principle: Put risk and reward side by side, in the right amounts
why: Sakurai defines game essence as push and pull: take risks to get rewards. In Space Invaders you can only hit an invader from where it can hit you, and in Super Mario Bros. the highest-risk moment next to a Koopa Troopa is the only time you can stomp it. Strategy is the same thing from the player's side: how they manage those risks to get the reward.
how_to_apply: For each core interaction, map how risk and reward change with distance, position and timing, and make sure the spot where the player can score is also a spot where they are exposed. Attach fresh risk to rewards, like a kicked shell that pays points but can bounce back. Tie effectiveness to closeness, as Darius does by capping on-screen shots so firing rate rises as you close in.
anti_pattern: Safe positions from which the player can still score; rewards with no attached risk; options that let the player wipe the screen from safety.
example: Space Invaders: the cannon must move under an invader to shoot it, and intercepting beats chasing. Super Mario Bros.: the stomp and the kicked shell. Darius: hanging back uses up your shots, closing in lets you fire more. Street Fighter II: the shoryuken is strongest when the opponent is closest.
review_question: At the exact moment the player can score, are they also exposed?
keywords: game essence push and pull risk reward core fun proximity danger opportunity tension strategy space invaders mario

principle: Give every action a downside that opposes its benefit
why: Danger and opportunity are two sides of the same coin. No motion feels complete until there is an opposing element (falling for flight, slowdowns for speed), just as player attacks and enemy attacks come as a set. An option that removes risk, like a three-way laser in Space Invaders, might look cool but kills the push and pull.
how_to_apply: List every verb with its risk and its reward. Where a downside is missing, add one: edge jumps that risk falling, dashes that cost control or stamina, long-range weapons with less ammo, strong attacks with longer recovery, flight that comes with falling or a requirement to fly. If you keep a risk-erasing option, counterweight it (limited ammo, enemies that cover the new angles).
anti_pattern: Actions whose benefit has no matching danger; strong attacks with little vulnerability afterward; flight with nothing to crash into.
example: Space Invaders three-way laser thought experiment. A one-punch fighter only gets push and pull once the kick recovers longer than the punch and can be countered on a miss. The first Ace Combat's long bridge: flying under it thrills because hitting the bridge or the water ends you.
review_question: For each verb in your game, what danger comes bundled with its benefit?
keywords: opposing force downside trade-off counterweight recovery cost vulnerability whiff punish two sides of the same coin mechanic pairing

principle: Make the riskiest play pay the most
why: Balanced correctly, risk and reward scale in almost perfect proportion: a more intense risk brings a more intense joy. A slow smash attack that leaves you open is a more commendable hit than a quick jab, so it deserves more damage and knockback. Sakurai feels Street Fighter II's heavy shoryuken, the riskiest variant, could have been even stronger.
how_to_apply: Rank your options by how much risk they demand (startup, exposure, accumulated danger, stake) and make the payoff climb with it. Give long-startup moves more damage and knockback, make multi-line clears require a tall stack, pay escalating points for chaining risky actions, and pay out more for higher wagered difficulty.
anti_pattern: Underpaying the riskiest variant; making the safe play the highest-scoring play.
example: Smash Bros. neutral vs. smash attacks. Tetris: clearing many lines at once needs a dangerously tall stack. Arcade greed scoring: Galaxian flagships after escorts, escalating points for eating fleeing ghosts in one go. Kid Icarus: Uprising's Fiend's Cauldron pays more for higher Intensity.
review_question: Is your riskiest option clearly your most rewarding one?
keywords: reward scaling risk proportion payoff high risk high reward commitment damage knockback greed multi-line clear jackpot

principle: Squeeze players with stress, then release it into growth
why: Games stress you out in order to provide relief. Stress alone isn't fun, but heavy pressure followed by sudden release brings great satisfaction. Most games run the loop stress (an obstacle), relief (it is removed), growth (a reward that makes you stronger) and progress (the next obstacle becomes possible). Relief, growth and progress are the fun, but they can't happen without the initial stress, and catharsis peaks when players straddle the line between victory and defeat.
how_to_apply: For every section, name the source of stress, the moment of release, the growth reward and the progress it unlocks, and fix any missing step. Use squeeze-and-release in moment-to-moment play too, such as holding a charge through a risky drift and releasing it for a burst.
anti_pattern: Weeding stress out to make the game comfortable; releases that give no growth and point to no next goal.
example: Kirby Air Ride: braking into a drift charges power, releasing at the curve's exit gives a speed burst (squeeze and release). EXP, skills and currency as rewards that prepare players for stronger foes.
review_question: Can you name the stress, the relief, the growth and the progress in this section?
keywords: squeeze and release stress relief growth progress core loop catharsis tension release pressure satisfaction

principle: Understand why something is fun before you copy or rebuild it
why: Copying a fun game won't feel original and can lose the very reason it worked. Because he understood the essence of falling-block puzzles (stack height is risk, a big clear is the reward), Sakurai pitched Meteos despite being bad at the genre and found its launching idea in five minutes. Borrowing hard-game systems without the pull that made them work fails too.
how_to_apply: Deconstruct (pick the fun part), analyze (state its risk and reward in one sentence), then rebuild (find a new verb that delivers the same payoff). Check whether your idea changes the concept or only renames the default action. When adapting or porting, carry the proven core over and spend effort on what the new format adds.
anti_pattern: Copying surface features; renaming the genre's action ('vaporized', 'demolished') instead of changing it; mimicking Souls-like or permadeath systems without creating a reason to push on.
example: Kirby Air Ride's one-button charge drifting came from deconstructing drifting. Meteos launches matched blocks instead of erasing them. Tetris has game essence and Pentomino doesn't. Mushiking's handheld version reused the arcade game's rock-paper-scissors core; the Famicom Donkey Kong kept the arcade game's essence.
review_question: Can you say in one sentence why your core action is fun, in terms of risk and reward?
keywords: deconstruct analyze rebuild originality imitation copying borrowing mechanics why is it fun genre essence adaptation porting ideas

principle: Make every rule earn its place by creating a new decision
why: A fighter with one punch and no walking has no push and pull; walking adds range, a punishable kick adds push and pull, and jumping, guarding and throwing each add depth. Long-running genres collect rules that add nothing, combos that decide a fight after the first hit leave the opponent nothing to do, and a button you only hold has little game essence.
how_to_apply: Build up from a minimal core one mechanic at a time and write down the new decision each creates; cut any that create none. At each project's start, list the genre 'givens' you inherited and re-justify each. In one-button designs, build on timing, reaction or hold-versus-release rather than mashing.
anti_pattern: Rules kept only because the genre always had them; mash-only or hold-only mechanics; systems where the outcome is settled after the first hit.
example: The one-punch fighter thought experiment. Street Fighter II gave each move a specific role. Smash Bros. replaced long combos with accumulated damage so every hit gets a different reaction, and every Smash has slightly different jump physics because he re-examines them. Kirby minigames: Crane Fever (release on time), Egg Catcher (hold to catch, release to avoid bombs).
review_question: What new decision does this rule create for players, and if none, why is it here?
keywords: mechanic depth givens conventions minimal core one button complexity rules decision push and pull combos mashing

principle: Let reads and clever plays, not raw stats, decide contests
why: What Sakurai calls game essence is mainly agon (competition), and in his view clever plays rather than physical advantage should decide the victor. Smash was built for interplay and improvisation rather than inputs alone; Mushiking's rock-paper-scissors battles are about reading the opponent; and reaction games gain push and pull once players can fake each other out.
how_to_apply: Give both sides counters and information: whiff punishes, guard-throw-attack cycles, specialties that can be read, signals that can be feinted. Tune so positioning, timing and reads can overcome stat or size advantages.
anti_pattern: Outcomes decided mainly by bigger numbers, or by whoever lands the first hit.
example: Mushiking: each Mushi specializes in one shape, so do you play your strong 'paper' or win by surprise? Quick Draw / Samurai Kirby: players fake the start signal. Smash Bros.' accumulated-damage rules.
review_question: Can a smarter read beat a stronger character here?
keywords: reads mind games bluffing feint interplay improvisation agon competition counterplay outplay skill expression rock paper scissors

principle: Offer choices with real upsides and real downsides
why: 'What downsides will you accept, and what upsides will you gain?' works in any game. Weapons with pros and cons broaden game essence, distinct sides create far more strategy than mirror matches, counter cycles with clear weaknesses and fitting costs enrich strategy, and players feel better when they choose their own path.
how_to_apply: Give every weapon, unit, character and route a clear upside and a clear downside on different axes (coverage vs. shot count, cost vs. power, range vs. ammo, safe-and-long vs. risky shortcut). Build counter cycles. Show the effect (attack range, spread) instead of only numbers.
anti_pattern: Options that are strictly better or interchangeable; showing differences only as numbers.
example: Gradius: the double cannon covers upward angles but fires only two shots and is weaker straight ahead than the laser. Strategy-game cycle: infantry lose to tanks, tanks to helicopters, helicopters to anti-air, anti-air to infantry. Errands with a safe long route and a dangerous shortcut.
review_question: Does each option have a reason to pick it and a reason not to?
keywords: trade-offs pros and cons weapon choice counter cycle rock paper scissors asymmetry options builds routes customization meaningful choice

principle: Place the best rewards beside the biggest hazards
why: In Gradius touching terrain costs a life, so enemies and power-ups placed beside it turn collecting into a risk worth taking. Flight thrills when there's a needle to thread, and a sky with nothing to crash into has no tension. In RPG dungeons, deeper means stronger enemies and better spoils, and dying loses what you found.
how_to_apply: Put power-ups, valuable enemies and shortcuts next to deadly geometry. Put ground, water and structures near flight paths and tie movement powers to the environment (launch off cliffs and ramps). Scale dungeon rewards with depth and make defeat cost the spoils so retreating is a real choice.
anti_pattern: Open sky or space with nothing to crash into; rewards sitting in safe spots.
example: Gradius power-ups near terrain. Flying under the first Ace Combat's long bridge. Kirby Air Ride's flight spots, with some machines that can fly and some that can't. 'Do you press your luck? Or get out while you still can?'
review_question: Is the best loot somewhere that makes the player nervous?
keywords: level design reward placement hazards terrain thread the needle flight press your luck dungeon depth spoils risky shortcut

principle: Let players choose how much risk to take
why: Strategy is how players manage risk, sometimes taking a bigger loss for an even bigger gain. Optional risk lets each player set their own stakes: classic arcade scoring makes the greedy play the dangerous one, partial cover lets you vary your exposure, and the Fiend's Cauldron lets you wager currency on difficulty.
how_to_apply: Offer optional risk with optional reward: press-on-or-retreat dungeons, escalating combo scores, wagers on difficulty, safe versus risky routes, partial cover. Map each system for ways to cut losses, raise gains, and trade a big loss for a bigger gain.
anti_pattern: A single fixed risk level; the safe play also being the top-scoring play.
example: Galaxian escorts, fleeing blue ghosts, crushing enemies with rocks instead of inflating them ('it's easy to get greedy'). Space Invaders bunkers. Kid Icarus: Uprising's Fiend's Cauldron.
review_question: Where can a confident player raise their own stakes for a bigger payoff?
keywords: optional risk greed wager stakes press your luck scoring chain player choice strategy minimize losses maximize gains

principle: Let skilled players turn last-moment danger into big payoffs
why: Parrying by waiting until the attack is about to hit turns massive risk into massive reward. Letting Tetris pieces be rotated and slid after landing lets players cling to life, which invites even greater risk. The shoryuken is invincible at startup and strongest near its base, so it pays most when the opponent is closest.
how_to_apply: Make parries trigger only at the moment of impact and pay heavily; give dodges a brief window where other actions are harder; add last-chance mechanics that let players survive at the edge; make reversals strongest at point-blank.
anti_pattern: Defensive options that work just as well early and safely; no way to recover at the brink.
example: Parries and dodges in action games. Later Tetris ports' rotate-and-slide after landing. Kid Icarus: Uprising's flick dodge, where drawing attacks in close and then evading is risk and reward. Space Invaders' Wall of Death: 'ultimate risk, ultimate reward'.
review_question: Can a skilled player wait until the last moment and be paid for it?
keywords: parry perfect dodge just frame last moment clutch cling to life lock delay reversal invincibility timing window

principle: Give enemies a purpose beyond being defeated
why: Kirby began with the idea that it would be fun to use enemies, because of risk and reward and the dual purpose enemies serve. Copy abilities then gave every enemy meaning and made each new encounter something to look forward to. Sizing up enemies by their look and behavior and exploiting weaknesses is both strategy and game essence.
how_to_apply: Give players a simple way to use on-screen enemies (inhale, grab, spit) and give each enemy type something distinct to take. Give enemies cues that hint at weaknesses and reward exploiting them with more than damage, such as a combo setup. Keep weakness systems simple for casual audiences.
anti_pattern: Enemies that are only obstacles to remove; overly complex weakness systems in a casual game.
example: Kirby's Dream Land inhale-and-spit (a tongue grab was the first idea) vs. Mega Man boss weapons, which are a reward for winning rather than using enemies. Kirby's Adventure copy abilities. Persona's weakness combos.
review_question: What can the player do with this enemy besides defeat it?
keywords: enemy design use enemies inhale copy ability weakness exploit dual purpose encounters combat rpg kirby

principle: Make bosses demand a strategy, and decide how authored it is
why: Bosses are the peaks of the climb and shouldn't just be stronger regular enemies; a boss should force a strategy and pay off when it works. Authored, mandatory strategies show crafted thought but feel like tutorials; free-form fights give freedom but can feel flavorless with less push and pull. Neither is wrong, but you must pick.
how_to_apply: For each boss decide up front: one authored solution, an ideal strategy found by trial and error, or many viable approaches. If authored, treat it as a tutorial in disguise; if free-form, add push and pull on purpose. Reward success clearly, and let aggressive positioning end the fight faster.
anti_pattern: Bosses that are beefed-up regular enemies; copying another game's boss structure instead of deriving it from your systems.
example: Nintendo-style bosses: hit the eye at the right moment, slash the stunned foe. Castlevania: any weapon, any way. Darius bosses: close-range rapid fire kills fast. Space Harrier's dragon only takes damage to the head.
review_question: Does this boss make the player form a plan, and do they get a reward worth it?
keywords: boss design strategy mandatory authored free-form weak point tutorial boss reward peaks encounter design

principle: Plan rewards early and make players earn them
why: Progress alone doesn't motivate players in modern games; rewards are the main source of their investment, and you can't reward players if you have nothing to give them. Motivation and reward are two sides of the same coin. A collection unlocked from the start has no joy, and movies used as rewards lose value once they are posted online.
how_to_apply: As soon as the bones of the game work, list what every enemy, mission and activity grants, when it arrives and where it is used. Gate characters, equipment and collectibles behind play, gamify unlocks (incoming challengers), and give casual players a grid of goals to work toward.
anti_pattern: Leaving rewards until late in development; unlocking everything at the start; relying on cutscenes or movies as the main reward.
example: Smash Bros. Ultimate's Spirits would have no joy if unlocked at the start. Smash fighters unlocked by beating challengers. Kirby Air Ride's Checklist, where clearing a square reveals its neighbors' conditions. Brawl's per-fighter movies leaked online and stopped being rewards.
review_question: Can you list every reward the game gives and roughly when each arrives?
keywords: reward plan unlocks collectibles motivation progression achievements checklist challenges earn it investment planning

principle: Turn rewards into growth the player chooses how to use
why: Release is only the first step: reward players with new ways to relieve the next stress, and choice boosts game essence. Getting stronger is the most effective in-game reward. Saved-up currency needs appealing things to buy, a few expensive high-impact items make players scrounge and plan, and crafted results must feel like profit.
how_to_apply: Pair every currency with desirable things to buy, including at least one expensive goal worth saving for. Show progress to the next reward (current vs. needed). Price crafting so the output is clearly worth more than its materials. Let players choose which skill or item to invest in.
anti_pattern: Infinite resources with no use; flooding players with money and minor gear; loops where collecting is the only activity; purely linear rewards with no choice.
example: Faxanadu: a few expensive shop items that each give a massive boost. Ys shows current EXP and what the next level needs. A mining game with infinite resources and no use would be pointless. Work games: work, earn, buy tools that make the next job easier.
review_question: What can the player spend this on, and does it help them face the next challenge?
keywords: economy currency sink shop upgrades growth progression crafting profit experience points skill choice rewards in sight

principle: Make losing part of the fun
why: A study found competitive FPS players feel relief when defeated and anxiety after a kill: quick restarts sweep away disappointment, and a kill that doesn't settle the match shows you a future where you're the one defeated. When both defeating and being defeated click, there's no better entertainment. Competitive games aren't only about dominating.
how_to_apply: Keep respawn and rematch times short, make the moment of defeat entertaining in itself, and write down how each death motivates a retry, aiming for 'I'll get you next time!'. Expect mid-match kills to raise the scorer's tension rather than relieve it.
anti_pattern: Assuming competitive fun is only the joy of dominating; long waits after death that let disappointment set in.
example: Overseas study of competitive first-person shooter players.
review_question: After a loss, does the player want another try, or want to quit?
keywords: defeat death respawn rematch relief anxiety retry motivation competitive fps losing fun one more

principle: Name your game's main source of fun; it may not be game essence
why: Game essence isn't the only thing that makes a game fun. Control feel, story, fandom, simulation, creation and rhythm can carry a game; Caillois adds chance, imitation and vertigo to competition; work games hook players with little push and pull; licensed games are judged on faithfulness first. Pushing essence too hard can cost flair and make a game a chore.
how_to_apply: Name the main source of fun and put the polish budget there (fine-tune control feel if control is the fun). Audit agon, alea, mimicry and ilinx. Then layer risk and reward where it fits: fall deaths and dangerous gathering in crafting games, strict timing in rhythm games, a work-earn-upgrade loop in task games.
anti_pattern: Assuming a compelling story alone makes a good game; judging a licensed game by fun alone; loosening judgment until nothing is at stake.
example: Ace Attorney, train simulators, Animal Crossing and beatmania (a hair late is a miss). PowerWash Simulator and House Flipper. Megami Tensei's computer-summoned demons as a licensed setting that suits a game. 'It's product value versus fun.'
review_question: What is the one main thing that makes this game fun, and is your polish going there?
keywords: sources of fun beyond game essence control feel story licensed games simulation crafting rhythm agon alea mimicry ilinx caillois work games

principle: Pay off risk tangibly, after the risky act, without snowballing
why: When he rebuilt drifting, a score bonus gave no tangible benefit and permanent power-ups let skilled drifters run away with the race; some speed was needed so the risk was rewarded. In a fighting game, stat growth would make the 'real' game start only at max level.
how_to_apply: Grant a useful, temporary benefit once the risky action is completed (a speed burst at the curve's exit), not throughout it. Avoid permanent stacking advantages in competitive play. If players can overpower themselves, reduce their rewards.
anti_pattern: Score-only rewards for risky play; permanent power-ups that let the leader run away; boosting throughout the risky action instead of after.
example: Kirby Air Ride charge drifting. Smash rewards with unlocks rather than character growth. World of Light gives fewer rewards when your Spirits overpower the fight.
review_question: Does the payoff arrive after the risk is survived, and does it fade before it snowballs?
keywords: reward timing tangible benefit snowball runaway leader speed boost temporary power-up drift payoff

principle: Raise the stakes as play goes on
why: Tetrominos falling faster over time heighten risk and make the game more exciting. In Space Invaders the fewer invaders remain, the faster they move, so careless clearing lets them reach you quickly; strategy (clear one column at a time from the ends) emerges from that one rule.
how_to_apply: Increase speed or pressure steadily across a session, and tie enemy speed or aggression to how many threats remain or to the player's own progress, so the order of clearing becomes a choice.
anti_pattern: Pressure that stays flat from start to finish.
example: Tetris speed-up. Space Invaders: survivors speed up as their numbers drop.
review_question: Does the pressure climb as the session goes on, partly because of what the player did?
keywords: escalation rising tension speed up difficulty ramp pressure emergent strategy space invaders tetris

principle: Leave room for players to beat the system within the rules
why: Strategy is how players minimize losses and maximize gains, and getting gains without losses is fun and memorable; just following the path laid out isn't. Some of the best moments were never planned, like Space Invaders' Wall of Death, probably a bug. A deliberately lucrative, hard-to-beat enemy becomes a special objective.
how_to_apply: When testers find a balance-breaking trick, ask whether it stays inside the game's rules and whether finding it is fun before patching it. Consider a deliberate within-the-rules shortcut or a rare, lucrative enemy with high HP or a tendency to flee. Keep blocking anything that amounts to rewriting game parameters.
anti_pattern: Patching out every exploit by reflex; letting players rewrite game parameters.
example: Dragon Quest metal slime farming. Dark Souls enemies lured into falling to their deaths. Resetting for a result. Space Invaders' Wall of Death (Nagoya Attack).
review_question: Is there anything a clever player can discover that the designers did not spell out?
keywords: exploits cheat the system emergent strategy metal slime farming bugs as features rare enemy discovery player agency

principle: Give every contest a stake that people care about
why: In a contest where only one side can win, having someone to root for makes it far more exciting; Smash's tiny spectator wagers work because they create investment, not because of the points. Without a leaderboard 'you're just fighting', so results need an incentive to aim higher. Races get heated when you can see the opponent's progress, and a real chance of failure made a live performance thrilling.
how_to_apply: Let spectators pick a winner before a match, show standing that moves with performance, keep both players' progress visible in races, and keep real stakes (no restarts) when showing play live.
anti_pattern: Spectator modes with no stake; ranked play with nothing to climb.
example: Smash Bros. online spectator wagers. Sakurai and Arino Kacho starting each retro game at the same moment. Kid Icarus: Uprising played live with an orchestra at Intensity 9.0, where a Game Over would have stopped the show.
review_question: Does everyone watching or playing have something riding on the outcome?
keywords: stakes investment spectators wager rooting leaderboard incentive race visible progress live performance tension

principle: Praise good play explicitly and give scores a meaning
why: Items and progress are expected by design, so they don't tell players they did well; games are meant to be fun, so praise matters. A score recast in a meaningful unit (an age, money, a power rating) changes what the whole game means, and having something to strive for is what makes games fun.
how_to_apply: Add crowd cheers for big launches and KOs and a gasp for near-misses, allies who comment on feats, generous labeled bonuses, and celebratory effects aimed at the scorer. Present scores in a unit that fits the fantasy and count gains up on screen.
anti_pattern: Counting item drops and progress as all the praise needed; a bare score counter added by default.
example: Smash Bros. crowd and KO confetti; Dynasty Warriors commanders; Forza bonuses even for wrecks; Brain Age; Burnout's Crash Dollars; Global Smash Power.
review_question: When the player does something great, what in the game tells them so?
keywords: praise feedback cheers bonuses score presentation units brain age achievement acknowledgment celebration

principle: Vary each session so players adapt instead of converging
why: Shaving tenths of a second has game essence, but Sakurai wanted Kirby Air Ride to expand the possible play types rather than reward one perfect method. Games repeat content, and randomness makes each play different and challenges players to handle a range of situations; chance (alea) is one of play's four elements.
how_to_apply: Add a mode built for variety (a sandbox with differing power-ups and events), vary probabilities instead of fixing results where repetition goes stale, and where draws are random let players choose among two or three, each with a reason to matter.
anti_pattern: Designing only around perfection and time-shaving; purely random draws with no player choice.
example: Kirby Air Ride's City Trial, whose rules later powered Smash Run. Smash Bros. random items. Gacha with two or three draws to choose from (his suggested application).
review_question: Will the hundredth session play differently from the first?
keywords: variety randomness replayability sandbox play styles optimal strategy convergence alea random draws gacha choice

principle: Side with what's fun as a game over realism
why: A realistic driving experience leaves little room for creativity; real drifting is slower than grip driving, but making drifting fun makes the game fun. If you forget that fighting games are nothing like real fighting, you drift from the essence you want. Realism still earns its place as information: floors that look hard and hits that sound painful.
how_to_apply: When realism and fun conflict, choose fun, and make risky actions rewarding even if they wouldn't be in real life. Borrow realism for readable information (mimicry), not for the rules.
anti_pattern: Copying real-world rules into the game because they are accurate.
example: Kirby Air Ride drifting (Sakurai's driving hobby gave him no cues). Smash's exaggerated fighting.
review_question: Is any rule here only because reality works that way?
keywords: realism vs fun simulation exaggeration mimicry fantasy driving fighting game design for fun

principle: Pick the target player first, then set how much risk to allow
why: Sakurai's theory is that as you increase game essence, you reduce a game's broad appeal. He made the first Kirby deliberately simpler to reach newcomers, slowed Brawl for a casual Wii audience, and went the other way with Kid Icarus: Uprising because casual players were already served. Who you target should follow from the game's design and concept, and there is no one right answer.
how_to_apply: Write down the target player in terms of experience ('beginners', not 'children'), decide how much push and pull they want, then set the risk dials to match. If you go hardcore, make it an explicit goal rather than the default.
anti_pattern: Tuning risk to your own skill; assuming more depth is always better for everyone; defining the audience by age or gender instead of experience.
example: Kirby's Dream Land vs. Super Mario Bros. Melee's speed was harsh on new players and even gave some players tendinitis, so Brawl was slowed. Kid Icarus: Uprising targeted hardcore players because Touch! Generations already covered casual ones. Sakurai suspects 'super casual' players who find even Dream Land too hard are a huge opportunity.
review_question: Who exactly is this for, in experience terms, and does the risk level match them?
keywords: target audience broad appeal accessibility casual hardcore beginners experience level difficulty target market

principle: Be kind to beginners: neutralize threats early and forgive small slips
why: A minor risk to an experienced player can be a massive brick wall to a newcomer. Being hit or missing a jump is a small mistake, so losing a life for it is too harsh. It is hard enough to get people to play at all, and a beginner who gets crushed before understanding the game will quit.
how_to_apply: Give beginners ways to stop threats while the risk is still low, a forgiving health pool, an escape from the steepest penalties, big targets that near-misses still hit, and an opening window where deaths cost little. Keep some penalty for real failure. In competitive play, let newcomers act and have fun before they get flattened.
anti_pattern: One-hit deaths, heavy control inertia or instant death for a missed jump in a game for newcomers; wiping every power-up on death; crushing someone who just came to try the game.
example: Kirby's Dream Land: inhale stops enemies early, the spit attack outranges the inhale, Kirby takes up to six hits and can fly over pits (falling still costs a life), and Whispy Woods is huge. Space Harrier's 'trial time'. Gradius's power-up reset makes players want to quit. Sakurai crushing a couple trying The King of Fighters '95.
review_question: What happens to a first-time player in their first five minutes?
keywords: beginners newcomers kindness forgiving onboarding penalty harshness health flight assist first time player

principle: Never let a player get permanently stuck
why: No matter how fun tense challenges are, the moment players give up, the challenge is worthless. In RPGs you can always level up, but in action games getting stronger won't win, and everyone has a breaking point. Games that force a restart because difficulty can't be changed mid-game have a fundamental design flaw, and an impossible spike after dozens of hours is to be avoided at all costs.
how_to_apply: Let players change difficulty at any time without losing progress. After repeated failures in one spot, offer an easier setting or a skip that counts as cleared, worded so it doesn't humiliate. Provide a floor that is nearly guaranteed to win. If a shipped game proves too hard, patch in an easier option. Teach newcomers explicitly how to turn difficulty down.
anti_pattern: Difficulty locked at the start; an impossible final spike; leaving the easy end of a difficulty system unexplained.
example: Kid Icarus: Uprising's Intensity 0.0 is nearly invincible, but players weren't told clearly that going below 2.0 lowers difficulty. Smash Ultimate's patch made Challenger fights easier and added Very Easy to World of Light. The Last of Us Part I's assists.
review_question: If a player fails the same spot ten times, what does the game offer them?
keywords: stuck difficulty settings change anytime skip stage easy mode assist dynamic difficulty breaking point accessibility

principle: Don't tune difficulty to your team; handicap yourself, then go easier
why: Developers know the game inside and out, so tuning to the best player on staff, or even the median one, leaves it too hard for players who won't spend all their time on your game. What keeps players going isn't other games being hard or you being able to scrape by in your own.
how_to_apply: Tune while handicapped: play one-handed, with lower health or stricter conditions, and make sure you can still clear it. Set difficulty a good deal below what feels right to the team, then lower it once more. Bring in people who have never played and use each one fresh only once; watch children play rather than asking them questions.
anti_pattern: Balancing around the most skilled staff member; calling the same outside tester back as if they were still fresh.
example: Sakurai plays with one hand when balancing. Elementary school play testers who came with friends and snacks.
review_question: Who set this difficulty, how well do they know the game, and were they handicapped?
keywords: playtesting difficulty tuning developer skill bias one-handed handicap fresh testers easier than you think curse of knowledge

principle: Get players back in control within seconds of failing
why: Interest cools fast between the moment the player thinks 'Ugh, I blew it!' and the moment they regain control, and quick retries raise tolerance for difficulty and hardship. The game moving on its own isn't enough; players need to be in control.
how_to_apply: Measure death-to-control time and cut it: a flashy, impactful failure effect of about a second, short loads, no non-interactive screens (if text must remain, let button presses advance it). Make sure enemies can't hit players the moment they respawn, but don't make respawning so free that the game feels mindless.
anti_pattern: Long death sequences, slow fades and loading before a retry; respawning into enemy fire; infinite respawns exactly where you died.
example: No specific title; he states it as a general rule. In competitive FPS play, quick restarts sweep away disappointment.
review_question: How many seconds pass between 'Ugh, I blew it!' and the player's next input?
keywords: retry respawn restart death time load times player time failure loop quick retry checkpoint

principle: Keep every option's peaks and valleys; never average them out
why: Balancing purely on strength trims advantages and patches weaknesses until every fighter is average, and average isn't fun. The more alike options become, the more they feel like the same character and the whole game turns bland. Divisive differences are healthy: you want players to say 'Then let's settle it in a match!'
how_to_apply: When something is too strong, first exaggerate its weaknesses instead of cutting its signature strength, and don't soften weaknesses in the same patch. Reject proposals that make a character more average. Push interchangeable options apart. This applies to move sets in non-competitive games too.
anti_pattern: Shaving strengths and filling in weaknesses until options feel alike; relying on mirror matches to dodge balance problems; backing away from distinctive designs because of social-media bias.
example: Smash Bros. tuning: Sakurai tells the team to keep fighters unique by amplifying shortcomings to offset advantages. Mario vs. Mario has no balance issues but limited push and pull. Fighters differ in movement speed, vulnerability and animation flair.
review_question: After this balance change, does every option still have a clear strength and a clear weakness?
keywords: character balance peaks and valleys uniqueness individuality asymmetry nerf buff roster homogenization mediocre average

principle: Fix balance with the narrowest change that keeps the signature intact
why: One attack has many components (power, speed, duration, windup, follow-through, range, hit size, animation speed, knockback, combo ability, shield damage, shield recovery), so it can be weakened without erasing what makes it special. Kirby's flight got too strong on the NES, and changing its context worked better than cutting it. After launch, touching core systems forces wide re-testing.
how_to_apply: List the move's parameters, mark the defining one, and change a secondary one instead: lengthen the vulnerable follow-through or shrink the hitbox. For an overpowered ability, try shrinking the play space, confining key fights to one screen or lowering its speed before removing it. Post-launch, adjust specific encounters or add an easier option rather than rewriting core AI.
anti_pattern: Flattening the stat that defines a move; cutting a signature mechanic outright; rewriting core AI or global difficulty in a late patch.
example: Smash: keep a move's attack power, lengthen its follow-through. Kirby's Adventure: a bigger info panel, single-screen mid-boss fights and slower flight. Smash Ultimate's narrow difficulty patch.
review_question: Is this fix touching the one thing players love about the option?
keywords: nerf adjustment parameters follow-through hitbox frame data rebalance context patch narrow fix signature mechanic

principle: Scale every penalty and reward to how good or bad the action was
why: Players are happiest when their behavior is compensated correctly, and each success and failure deserves a fitting consequence. A big penalty for a really bad choice can be fun, but you must ask whether the player can ever redeem themselves. Small slips deserve small costs, and failure should still cost something or respawning feels mindless.
how_to_apply: For every reward, penalty and damage value ask how good or bad the triggering action really was. Give irreversible choices an explicit recovery path and cost. Check whether a death that costs the player their build still leaves a realistic way back. Keep the mapping loose enough to surprise: polish out only what feels unreasonable.
anti_pattern: Permanent penalties decided only by scenario logic; a late death that leaves the player hopelessly underpowered; removing party members along with the gear invested in them; rationalizing every reward until the game is predictable.
example: Smash: slow smash attacks earn more damage and knockback than quick neutral attacks. Gradius: arriving late in the game with only a Double after losing power-ups. Score games paying more for stronger enemies.
review_question: Does this consequence match how good or bad the action really was, and is there a way back?
keywords: penalty fairness consequences punishment reward proportion redemption recovery irreversible choice death penalty

principle: Shape difficulty like a mountain trail, not a steady ramp
why: Keeping player and enemy strength in direct proportion makes progress a steady incline, which is a chore: it's just work. Real climbs have peaks to overcome and flat stretches to breeze through. Enemies that scale with the player remove any incentive to get ahead, and growth stages that dip in power create walls.
how_to_apply: Plot player power against enemy difficulty across the game and reshape it into deliberate peaks (bosses that demand a strategy) and flats (unexpectedly empty areas, spots to rack up gains). Don't level-scale enemies to the player. Check every growth stage for dips. Playtest the endgame for spikes.
anti_pattern: A straight diagonal of player and enemy strength; level scaling; an impossible spike at the very end.
example: The mountain-climbing analogy. Sodatete! Kouchuu Ouja Mushiking: care taken so growth stages don't hit a wall in battle.
review_question: Where are the peaks and the flat stretches on your difficulty curve?
keywords: difficulty curve pacing level scaling progression power curve peaks valleys breathers grind rpg balance

principle: If failure means repetition, give players a reason to push on
why: Most players won't enjoy repeating the same content forever; they continue because they want to see what comes next. If more players than expected hit a wall, they may see the same scenery again and again and quit. Dark Souls' pull partly rests on trust in its developer, which a copy doesn't inherit.
how_to_apply: For each likely failure point, list what players will replay on the way back, then shorten it or vary it (randomized equipment, items, events). Make the next area, story beat or reward visible or hinted. If you borrow permadeath or Souls-like systems, write down your own reason to push on.
anti_pattern: Mimicking hard-game systems without creating the pull; low-variety content players must repeat many times.
example: Roguelikes and roguelites vary each run after a defeat. Dark Souls players push on to reach what's next.
review_question: What does a player see on their tenth attempt at this section, and why would they want to keep going?
keywords: roguelike permadeath repetition retries motivation variety souls-like difficult games start over

principle: Layer optional depth over a simple core both audiences can use
why: In a mature market with few beginners, Kirby's Adventure had to satisfy both groups: novices can finish by inhaling and spitting, veterans dig into copy abilities. Making Ryu's full-command shoryuken essential would have split Smash players into those who can and can't do it. Shortcuts only experts use narrow a UI's appeal.
how_to_apply: Build a minimal core that can finish the game or compete, add depth on top, and verify a core-only playthrough works. Offer a one-button version of special inputs and give the full version a modest bonus (a bit more damage or invincibility). Keep novice extras optional and skippable.
anti_pattern: Requiring the depth system to progress; balancing so a hard input is needed to compete.
example: Kirby's Adventure copy abilities and optional one-button minigames on the map. Smash Bros. Ryu: one-button or command shoryuken. Kirby made for beginners but with enough 'oomph' that advanced players enjoy the controls.
review_question: Can someone using only the simplest controls finish or hold their own?
keywords: beginners and experts layered depth optional mechanics skill ceiling skill floor simple inputs command inputs accessibility

principle: Size complexity to your audience and lifespan; hold back what they can't feel
why: You can always add rules to boost push and pull, but overcomplicated rulesets are hard to grasp, so sometimes you must hold back. A game meant to last hundreds of matches still needs a certain level of complexity, but moves too hard to perform hide the push and pull. Constant risk made Kid Icarus: Uprising feel too hardcore, and Melee's speed was harsh on newcomers.
how_to_apply: Decide whether the game is for casual sessions or hundreds of matches and size its depth to match. Before adding a rule, check your target players could still grasp the game. Keep inputs easy enough to feel the push and pull, and lower speed and input density for casual audiences or laggy online play. Keep weakness and combo systems simple in casual games.
anti_pattern: Piling on rules for depth until the game is hard to understand; inputs so hard players cannot feel the push and pull.
example: The original Street Fighter (moves too hard) vs. Street Fighter II. Super Smash Bros. Brawl's slower speed. Kid Icarus: Uprising's land stages, too big and full of enemies with no respawn where you died.
review_question: Would your target player still understand the game after this rule is added?
keywords: complexity depth clarity learning curve casual competitive lifespan input density game speed rules bloat hold back

principle: Tune risk through explicit dials, not a vague difficulty knob
why: In Space Invaders the cannon's width is key to game balance because it determines how great your risk is; it is more than visual design. Kirby's approachability comes from specific dials: inhale range, six hits of health, flight, low inertia. Risk can also move between layers: easy dungeon exits can be offset by harder battles.
how_to_apply: List your risk dials (player hitbox size, partial cover, threat-neutralizing range, hits the player can take, escape tools, control inertia, game speed, target size, enemy durability, how freely players can leave) and set each deliberately. When you lower risk in one layer, decide whether to add it back in another.
anti_pattern: Treating character or hitbox size as purely visual; removing all tension along with exploration risk.
example: Space Invaders cannon width and bunkers. The hypothetical harder Kirby with a smaller inhale, one-hit deaths, no flight and more inertia. Kirby Super Star made standard enemies survive a few hits so stronger moves stood out.
review_question: Which specific dials set the risk in this game, and has each been set on purpose?
keywords: risk dials hitbox size health inertia game speed tuning parameters difficulty levers enemy hp target size

principle: Decide on purpose how much your game evens out skill
why: Competitive games are most fun when it's anyone's match. In casual games the most skilled player winning every time isn't fun, so catch-up systems are 'an absolute must', even if not quite fair. Smash wanted results to reflect skill, so it gives no stat help to trailing players and lets chaos (items, stages, Final Smashes) shake things up instead.
how_to_apply: Choose early: casual (everyone takes turns winning) or skill-reflecting. For casual play, give trailing players speed boosts or stronger items. For skill-reflecting play, leave core stats alone and route catch-up through chaos: make power-ups harder for the leader to get, charge comeback meters faster for losers. Keep variable-strength systems in party modes, out of level-playing-field matches. For home play, tolerate quirks players can house-rule.
anti_pattern: Letting the best player win every casual match; raising attack or reducing knockback for players who are behind in a skill game; stat-altering systems leaking into serious competition.
example: Mario Kart's boosts and items. Smash: the leader has a harder time getting a Smash Ball and the Final Smash Meter charges faster for losing players. Smash for 3DS/Wii U's variable character strength powered Smash Run, Smash Tour and amiibo.
review_question: How much does this game help the player who is behind, and was that a decision?
keywords: catch-up mechanics rubber banding comeback handicap party game competitive fairness skill gap items mario kart smash ball

principle: Never let luck alone decide a player's loss
why: Players need to feel, to some extent, that they are responsible for their own failure; losing only to bad luck is hard to accept and wastes hard work. Random dodge chances can feel unfair, and players already suspect computers of cheating with lucky rolls. Randomness still has value when using it well takes skill or when it gives anyone a shot at a comeback.
how_to_apply: Give players ways to respond to or control random events, keep randomness out of strict skill contests, prototype strategy combat without random evasion first, and keep random elements that still demand skill. Seed random numbers with an unpredictable value such as the system clock so resets can't force results.
anti_pattern: Matches decided by a single roll; leaning on a luck stat players forget; random rolls that swing the same battle unpredictably.
example: Peach's Smash Attack, once random, is now chosen with up or down. The Hero's randomized command list stays because each command takes skill. Wizardry's 1981 luck stat. Smash items stay random for comebacks.
review_question: Could a player lose this purely because of a random roll?
keywords: randomness rng luck fairness random evasion dice responsibility for failure seeding variance

principle: Let difficulty be a choice with stakes, not a humiliation
why: The Fiend's Cauldron let players bet hearts on higher Intensity for bigger rewards, and lowered difficulty automatically after failure, which stings less than asking whether you'd like to switch to Easy and means nobody plays the whole game on Easy. Xevious gave players a hidden lever: destroying one enemy rewinds the enemy table. Offering help is right, but do it without humiliating.
how_to_apply: Let players wager currency to raise difficulty for proportionally better rewards and pay to lower it; on failure, ease off automatically and take part of the stake. Give in-world levers that push difficulty back. If players can overpower themselves, treat it as a self-chosen difficulty and pay fewer rewards. Lock difficulty-lowering assists behind an unlock step so nobody flips them by accident.
anti_pattern: Bluntly asking failing players to switch to Easy; assists that can be switched on by accident; difficulty systems that never reward strong play.
example: Kid Icarus: Uprising's Fiend's Cauldron (default 2.0, 0.0 nearly invincible). Xevious's radar-station enemy. World of Light's Spirits. The Last of Us Part I's locked Combat Accessibility options.
review_question: Does lowering or raising difficulty feel like a decision the player owns?
keywords: difficulty wager fiend cauldron intensity dynamic difficulty adaptive assist mode self-chosen difficulty dignity stakes

principle: Check balance with testers and data, but let feel decide
why: Nobody is better at an in-development game than its play testers, and real match data shows whether every option has a shot: Smash Ultimate's 87 fighters fell between 47.18% and 51.43% win rate. But win rates aren't everything; the true metric is how each fighter feels. Identical setups should come out even, or the game isn't fair.
how_to_apply: Staff dedicated testers, use online and tournament results where you can, and test mirror matches for built-in side advantages. Look at multiplayer matches as well as top-tournament usage. Make final calls on feel, and step in as director mainly when an option's individuality is threatened.
anti_pattern: The director entering every parameter alone; judging fairness from one part of the game or from tournaments alone.
example: Smash Bros. Ultimate's win-rate spread. Brawl had only four testers and no online data. Rock, Paper, Scissors: identical teams draw.
review_question: What do your testers and data say, and does each option still feel right?
keywords: balance testing win rate data analytics playtesters tournament multiplayer mirror match fairness telemetry feel

principle: Make CPU opponents human-paced, aggressive and beatable
why: CPUs that react faster than a human feel extremely unfair, and players already suspect computers of cheating. Players who pick a high CPU level want a strong opponent, but one that waits around or perfect-shields everything would be invincible and no fun.
how_to_apply: Add a reaction delay, let status effects like reversed controls briefly confuse CPUs before they adapt, bias high levels toward offense, and cap perfect shields and dodges. Test for contradictions between AI behavior modes.
anti_pattern: Superhuman reaction speed; high-level CPUs that turtle or defend perfectly.
example: Smash Bros. Ultimate CPUs have a 'reflex' and were tuned more aggressively than in past titles.
review_question: Could a human have reacted the way this CPU just did?
keywords: ai cpu opponents bots reaction time fairness difficulty levels aggression perfect shield computer players

principle: Show rank so most players feel they are succeeding
why: A leaderboard gives purpose, but for most players it means 'eternal humiliation': trying your hardest and landing 10,000th saps motivation, and seeing the gap to the world's best makes people give up. Matchmaking also has to balance finding a match against fair skill gaps.
how_to_apply: Show standing as a number that rises with skill, measured against the whole population. Hide the identity and score of the #1 player from general players. Give top players an elite tier that matches them with each other. Tune matchmaking range by region and time of day, widening only as needed.
anti_pattern: Raw position leaderboards for a huge player base; showing everyone their distance from the top; fixed matchmaking ranges.
example: Smash Bros. Ultimate's Global Smash Power and Elite Smash.
review_question: What does the typical player see when they check their rank?
keywords: leaderboard ranking matchmaking elo mmr global smash power elite tier motivation online competitive

principle: Re-check difficulty after late performance changes, on real hardware
why: Meteos' speed was tied to processing speed, so a late optimization sped it up and made it harder than the per-planet tuning intended. Mushiking was tuned on a dev board and its Mushi got hungry faster on the production unit. Smash Ultimate's CPUs felt too hard at launch, possibly for a similar reason.
how_to_apply: Find any gameplay timing tied to processing speed, freeze it before final tuning, and replay difficulty-critical content after every optimization pass and on the actual retail hardware. Take it seriously when several people independently report the same feel problem.
anti_pattern: Tuning only on a dev kit; assuming smoother performance is purely a win when game speed tracks processing speed.
example: Meteos, Sodatete! Kouchuu Ouja Mushiking and Smash Bros. Ultimate.
review_question: Has the final difficulty been checked on the final build on real hardware?
keywords: performance optimization processing speed frame timing hardware testing difficulty regression late changes

principle: Check that co-op doesn't make the game harder than solo
why: In two-player Darius the ships get in each other's way and power-ups only cover one ship, which actually makes it harder; arcade Contra's two-player scroll point sits far forward. Kirby Super Star solved jump-heavy co-op by making one player the lead the camera follows.
how_to_apply: Playtest co-op for power-ups budgeted for one player, players blocking each other, and a camera or scroll point that strands the trailing player. Consider a lead-and-helper structure where an off-screen partner warps back.
anti_pattern: Dropping a second player into single-player resource and camera tuning unchanged.
example: Darius and Contra two-player modes; Kirby Super Star's Helper system.
review_question: Is the game easier or harder with a second player, and is that intended?
keywords: co-op multiplayer two player camera scrolling shared resources helper balance

principle: Give mismatched players handicap tools, and use them yourself
why: The skill gap between players can be painfully large. Settings can even it out, asymmetric fail conditions turn a mismatch into shared fun, and human adjustments, like letting a child grab the Smash Ball, may be the most effective handicap there is. Going easy isn't impolite unless the other person wants you to go all out.
how_to_apply: Expose difficulty and resources (lives, health, aggression) as separate per-player settings, offer asymmetric fail conditions, include an automatic handicap option, and ease off when you play newcomers.
anti_pattern: Framing every mismatched session as a strict winner-and-loser contest.
example: The Genji and the Heike Clans: hardest difficulty and fewest candles for Sakurai, easiest and most for Arino. Sakurai losing on one hit while Arino played to game over. Smash's automatic handicap setting.
review_question: Can a strong player and a weak player both enjoy the same session?
keywords: handicap per-player settings asymmetric fail condition mismatched skill family play going easy local multiplayer

principle: Fix one clear concept before production, then steer by it
why: Production is long, and once fatigue sets in it is easy to forget what was supposed to be fun. Sakurai treats the concept as a lighthouse: change course midway and you get lost, throw away months of art and programming, and demoralize the team. The spec change to avoid above all is the one forced because the game is not fun. Design documents rarely convey the fun, so the director has to hold the direction until the team can feel it in the build.
how_to_apply: Before anyone builds content, write the concept as one statement of appeal (for example 'the fun of sending opponents flying'), and do not start production until it is that clear. Use the gap before full staffing to finish the design documents and win stakeholder buy-in. When doubt sets in, check the decision against the concept. Amplify emergent fun that heads the same way instead of switching direction.
anti_pattern: Starting production with a fuzzy concept, then scrapping work or changing direction because the game is not turning out as expected.
example: Brawl: between E3 and the October start of development Sakurai wrote the design documents and pitched each character to its original creator. Ultimate: he finished its proposal the day the last Smash for 3DS/Wii U presentation went out, to keep the team together. Kid Icarus: Uprising: the story was set before development really kicked off.
review_question: Can the director state the game's appeal in one sentence, and does every task in progress serve it?
keywords: concept vision lighthouse direction pillar core idea pre-production pivot change of direction restart scrapped work

principle: Prove the core fun in a bare prototype before full production
why: Some things only become clear once you build them, and the costliest surprise is learning in mid-production that the game is not fun. Concrete visuals and a playable core let the team move forward with confidence, and they sell the idea to the people who fund it far better than a document.
how_to_apply: Build only the core rules first: Smash's prototype had no special moves, dodges or items. Mock up key characters at their intended on-screen size with complete movesets. For a non-game or content project, finish two or three representative pieces at final quality as a go/no-go test, then show them to partners and rights holders. Pitch moving mechanics with animated mock-ups, not static text.
anti_pattern: Committing a team on paper alone, or waiting for final tools before anything moves on screen.
example: Dragon King: The Fighting Game already played by Smash's rules. Kirby Super Star's Fighter moveset and Final Cutter combo, sketched early in a Famicom dev tool, survived to release. The channel's three-episode pilot (C03, C11, D03) proved it was doable and won Nintendo's cooperation. The Meteos proposal used PowerPoint animations.
review_question: Has the core fun been played, not just described, before content production began?
keywords: prototype pilot vertical slice proof of concept mockup greybox validate fun early playable go no-go

principle: Hand players control and the core fun within the first minutes
why: The arcade rule: players should understand why a game is fun in the first three minutes, because they judge quickly and put a slow game down. Long prologues only delay play, and players want to take control and find out what the game is. Starting with the climax, not the backstory, is how Sakurai gets there.
how_to_apply: Time a first boot: a newcomer should be playing, and should grasp the core fun, within three minutes. Open on a climactic scene the player controls and explain how things got there later (a slice from later in the story, or a battle as other characters). Show early that the enemy means business. Let repeated presses of confirm lead straight into the main game. If the game must open on everyday life, keep it short and hand over control early.
anti_pattern: Logos, backstory, customs and relationships before the first input; telling the story strictly in order at the cost of a strong opening.
example: Final Fantasy VII opens like the run-up to a final dungeon. Kid Icarus: Uprising Chapter 1 drops you into an Air Battle and introduces Medusa in under a minute. Phoenix Wright puts you in a trial at once. In Smash Ultimate, pressing confirm repeatedly goes from the title screen to fighter select.
review_question: How long from first boot until the player has control, and does the core fun show itself within three minutes?
keywords: opening intro first three minutes onboarding prologue start with the climax in medias res hook cold open first impression

principle: Measure and maximize the time the player is in control
why: Games are full of fun experiences, and making players wait to reach them is, in Sakurai's words, a sin. Slowness is the one trap that could make nobody love a game. Some waits are unavoidable, but a wait that looks like someone dropped the ball irritates most. The longer the player is in control, the better.
how_to_apply: Time a session in three buckets: in control, not in control (cutscenes, loading, menus, transitions, forced animations) and empty time with nothing to do, then set targets to shrink the last two. Keep transitions but make them quick. Hide unavoidable loads in presentation or show a simple on-theme indicator. Cut the gap between 'Ugh, I blew it!' and regaining control: a punchy failure effect of about a second, then control back, with no enemies waiting on the respawn. Skip the trip home once an errand is done.
anti_pattern: Slow fades into black screens, long retry sequences, walking back to town, and load screens that feel like an oversight.
example: The first Resident Evil's door animations hide loading and build fear. The first Zelda's edge scrolling suited its era but could be quicker today. Errands should whisk the player back to town once the objective is done.
review_question: What share of a typical session is the player in control, and what is the longest stretch without control?
keywords: player time downtime waiting loading screens transitions retries respawn idle time dead time control time pacing

principle: Plan to trim: cut what you can't finish, lock what you can't lose
why: Few projects go to plan. Sakurai says a director creates but is also responsible for trimming the excess, offloading the 'heavy or flammable cargo' to get back on course. Costs peak at the end (testing, marketing, the most people), so a project that cannot make it should cut its losses before that. Features treated as extras get cut first under schedule pressure, including ones you will regret.
how_to_apply: Weigh candidate concepts partly by estimated development time. Keep a visible list of what the whole game still needs, not just each person's tasks. Decide early which features are must-ship (a hands-on tutorial, for example) and which are trim candidates. When a target such as a stable 60 fps is non-negotiable, pare content until it holds. Re-weigh remaining cost against realistic return before entering the expensive final stretch.
anti_pattern: Assuming the game will ship because everyone completes their own assignment; leaving a must-have feature until the end, when it gets cut.
example: Smash's four-player fighter was chosen over an RC adventure that needed two years. Kirby Super Star's 'Kagero Mansion' scenario was cut for schedule and ROM space. Smash for 3DS was pared down until four players, 3D and items ran at 60 fps. Ultimate's hands-on technique mode was cut for schedule, a lasting regret.
review_question: If the schedule were halved tomorrow, which features go first, and which are locked?
keywords: scope cutting trimming descoping must-have nice-to-have feature cut schedule triage cancel minimum viable kill your darlings

principle: Treat play time as a cost; build fun first and let length follow
why: Before buying, people weigh a game's hours against everything else they could do, so '300 hours of content!' can put them off. Time spent should be a result of how fun the game is, as with players who spend hundreds or thousands of hours in Smash. Every new game competes for that time with every past work and with low-effort phone content.
how_to_apply: Do not plan or market around an hour count. Write down the core fun experiences and the systems that reinforce them first, and size content after. Prefer dense, varied content to padding, and give a solo mode an appropriate length. If failure sends players back, plan what they will see on each retry so repetition still pays.
anti_pattern: Padding length to hit an hour target; leading the pitch with play time; copying hard-game restart loops without the pull of wanting to see what comes next.
example: Kirby Super Star's omnibus format answered 'too many games that took too long to beat'. One of Brawl's two concept pillars was a single-player mode that takes an appropriate amount of time to complete.
review_question: Is the length we are planning a by-product of the fun, or a number we are padding toward?
keywords: play time game length hours content volume padding session length time cost respect player time competition for time

principle: Teach by letting them play, and only what they don't already know
why: Nobody wants manual-style paragraphs, which Sakurai calls the worst option, or a detached training room that makes players think 'Give me the real game!'. Players who learn by overcoming real challenges are more engaged. Yet hand-holding that keeps telling people how to play makes them feel dragged along, and explaining conventions they already know wastes their time.
how_to_apply: Teach each action where progression first needs it: an early real obstacle that requires it, a small enclosed area that can only be left by using a new movement skill, short prompts along the opening path. Build a mode that doubles as training, tailored per character. Skip genre conventions (at most show the attack-button icon when the first enemy appears), but test onboarding with genre newcomers. Make prompts read the current button mapping, and lock the hands-on tutorial into the schedule.
anti_pattern: Walls of instructions; dummy practice stages before the game starts; constant prompts that take away discovery; prompts that break when players remap buttons.
example: Donkey Kong Country 3 spells out buttons with bananas in an early stage. Few FPS games say 'fire with R2'. Break the Targets! in the first Smash was built to teach each character's controls. Smash itself only has a non-interactive video, which Sakurai considers a compromise.
review_question: Is any lesson delivered as text or in a separate room instead of through a real challenge, and does anything explain what the player already knows?
keywords: tutorial onboarding teaching controls hand-holding training stage prompts learn by doing genre conventions button prompts

principle: Open with a constrained slice of the core, then add controls
why: Demanding every skill at once is too much for beginners. Starting Kid Icarus: Uprising with the third-person shooting would have required players to dodge, aim and fire right away, so it opens with a rail-shooter air battle: simple shooting with quick scenery changes.
how_to_apply: Begin with a restricted form of the core action, such as an on-rails segment, a single-screen fight, or the basic verb alone, and add free movement, dodging and depth systems afterward. Check that a novice can make progress with only the simple core. Consider a no-penalty 'trial time' for first-timers.
anti_pattern: An opening segment that requires the full control set.
example: Kid Icarus: Uprising's air battles come before its land battles. Kirby's Adventure can be finished just by inhaling enemies and spitting them out. Space Harrier's arcade 'trial time' let newcomers die freely for a set period.
review_question: Which controls does the first segment require, and could it require fewer?
keywords: ramp control complexity layering introduce mechanics gradually onboarding sequence skill progression simple start

principle: Name your audience and hook in one line before designing
why: Risk, controls and rewards all depend on who the game is for. Sakurai sets his own taste aside and treats each project as an assignment to fit a genre or goal. Defining the target by experience ('beginners') works better than narrow demographic slices, and the audience should be chosen from a view of the whole market, not from personal likes.
how_to_apply: Write one line that names the target player or the signature mechanic, the way each of his works is captioned ('tailor-made for newcomers'; 'Rack up damage, then smash foes off the screen!'). Define the audience by experience or need, note who already serves them, and then tune risk to match.
anti_pattern: Picking the audience from your own taste; defining it only by age or gender.
example: An experienced gamer made Kirby's Dream Land for newcomers, and someone bad at puzzle games made Meteos. Brawl was slowed for casual Wii players. Uprising targeted hardcore players because Touch! Generations already covered casual DS owners.
review_question: Can you say in one line who this game is for or what its hook is, and do its risk settings match that player?
keywords: target audience pitch one-liner elevator pitch hook positioning beginners core gamers market segment who is it for

principle: Offer, and pitch, something players can't get anywhere else
why: Every new work competes with all past works for people's time, so it needs something fresh. If a game is close to another, people may just play the original; pitching it as 'X, but with Y' invites that question and copycat accusations, and references mean different things to different generations. Borrowing a game's systems skips the hardest part of design, so the saved effort must buy extra appeal elsewhere.
how_to_apply: Open the proposal by describing your game's own core experience without naming another game. List the reasons a player would pick yours over the original, many rather than one, and check again near the end of development. Form the concept first and use market data only to check its risks. Save 'it's like X' for sequels and informal chats with people who share the reference.
anti_pattern: Riding an original's coattails; choosing what to make from what research says is selling.
example: Around the NES-to-SNES transition, research showed RPGs selling, so many companies crowded into the same market with Dragon Quest and Final Fantasy-like games. 'Mario' can mean the NES game, Mario Odyssey or just the character, depending on the listener.
review_question: Described without naming any other game, what does ours offer that nothing else does?
keywords: originality unique selling point differentiation homage clone comparison pitch competition fresh idea stand out

principle: Question every inherited "given" at project kickoff
why: Genres with long histories pile up rules that add nothing to push and pull, and creators take familiar features for granted. Asking why a convention exists shows what it is for and whether you can do better. Novelty that only renames the genre's standard action is not new.
how_to_apply: At kickoff, list the conventions inherited from the genre or your last game (jump physics, enemies to defeat, blocks that vanish, how bosses are beaten) and decide whether each still earns its place. For every new idea, ask whether it changes what the player does or only what it is called. Keep de facto control standards unless you have a deliberate reason to break them.
anti_pattern: Treating conventions as fixed; cosmetic novelty that renames the usual verb.
example: Every Smash has slightly different jump mechanics because Sakurai re-examines them. Meteos asked whether blocks really had to be erased and made them blast off instead. Uprising set out to rethink a TPS genre he felt was stuck in by-the-book theory.
review_question: Which of our rules exist only because the genre always had them?
keywords: conventions givens assumptions genre rules first principles rethink innovation defaults re-examine

principle: Spec enough to start; expect the fun to surface while building
why: Trying to picture and document the whole finished game can take as long as development, and some things only become clear in the build. Proposals often lack elements that later become essential, unplanned elements often become core sources of fun, and ideas everyone opposed on paper often work once built. Polish is part of making a game fun.
how_to_apply: Fix the concept and core rules, write enough spec to start, and settle details as implementation reveals them. Schedule polish as fun-making work, not cleanup. When a problem appears, the person who spots it reports it at once with everything they know; lay out every option and decide quickly.
anti_pattern: Documenting every detail before building; defending the document against what the build shows; saying 'I knew that was wrong!' after the fact.
example: On paper Monster Hunter is just 'hunt monsters, make gear from their materials'. Metal Gear Solid 3's wound-treatment system reportedly had only four supporters at proposal stage.
review_question: Which parts of the spec are still guesses, and which build will answer them?
keywords: specification design document GDD iteration documentation up-front planning emergent fun polish discovery spec change

principle: Write specs nobody can misread: units, frames, bracketed parameters
why: Several people tune parameters later, and terse names like 'X-velocity' invite misreading; you will not get far with tuning if you cannot explain things clearly. Specs do not work if speed cannot be conveyed, and identical values meant different things on hardware with different pixel counts.
how_to_apply: Keep tunable numbers out of code. In specs, wrap each tunable value in a plain-language bracket with a placeholder, for example '[Special startup X-velocity is O]', under the rule that anything in brackets becomes a parameter, and keep a list pairing each phrase with its value. Pick one unit of speed for the project and include it in every parameter name. Give timings in frames. Keep specs in a collapsible outline (character, then moves, then each move's spec).
anti_pattern: Unitless numbers, vague words like 'quick', and hard-coded values only a programmer can change.
example: Sakurai's bracket rule for character-specific specs. Kirby Air Ride's speeds are in km/h and look low because Kirby is only about 20 cm across. He has kept ideas and specs in hierarchical outlines since about 1993.
review_question: Could a teammate implement and tune this spec without asking you a single question?
keywords: specs parameters units pixels per frame tuning values notation design doc clarity outline hierarchy data-driven frames

principle: Write proposals hot and fast, one image and idea per page
why: A proposal must make the people who supply money and talent think 'We should definitely do this'. Nothing good comes from droning on, and a draft that sits loses its freshness. Single-topic pages move like comic panels, so even 200-plus pages go quickly, and categories show listeners where they are. Talking about an unfinished proposal vents the 'internal pressure' that gives it force.
how_to_apply: Itemize the outline, then write the whole proposal in one push without discussing it; consult others once the draft exists. Give each page one screenshot or diagram and about two lines of text, grouped into categories and subcategories with visible section markers. Cut graphs, research, grand-vision passages and the plan B. Talk around each slide instead of reading it. Judge each page's information, not the page count. If it is rejected, rework how it shows the appeal instead of blaming the reviewers.
anti_pattern: Walls of text read aloud; lingering on your grand vision; assuming fewer pages is always better.
example: Sakurai's Super Smash Bros. Ultimate proposal ran over 200 PowerPoint pages, nearly all with one image and two lines of text.
review_question: Does every page carry one idea backed by an image, and could the whole deck be presented at a brisk pace?
keywords: proposal pitch deck presentation slides design document format brevity speed internal pressure

principle: Commit to one ideal spec; leave Plan B out
why: Writing 'or we could do this' hands the decision to someone else. Standing by one idea shows you have thought it through and builds experience. Start from the ideal spec and course-correct for cost afterward; the proposal is the skeleton of the game, so don't bend it out of shape up front for development convenience.
how_to_apply: Before sending a proposal or spec, delete every alternative and keep the option you judge best overall, weighing ease of implementation and appeal yourself. Then invite team feedback and trim for cost together when concrete problems surface, falling back to an alternative only when they justify it.
anti_pattern: Hedged documents that leave both doors open; pre-emptive compromises that put developer convenience ahead of the player.
example: The hedge Sakurai rejects: 'We could do A. Or we could do B.' Design documents that come back prioritizing the developers' jobs rather than the player experience.
review_question: Does the document ever present two options where it should make a decision?
keywords: plan b alternatives decision commitment ideal spec hedging compromise cost-effectiveness proposal

principle: Plan rewards at the planning stage, and fit their type to the concept
why: You cannot reward players if you have nothing to give them, and a game without rewards or new developments is drab; rewards are the main source of player investment.
