Not every reward fits every concept: in a fighting game where characters grow stronger, the 'real' game seems to start only at max level.
how_to_apply: Once the bones of the game exist, list every reward type and roughly when it arrives, and add systems before production if the list is thin. Make sure saved-up currency has appealing things to buy. If stat growth would undermine the concept, reward with unlocks, collectibles, options and objectives. Let rewards help with the next challenge and offer choices. Don't lock content many players want from the start, and don't make shareable movies the payoff.
anti_pattern: Bolting rewards on late; growth systems that break a game built on a fixed baseline; going overboard with reward systems.
example: Smash unlocks fighters by having challengers appear to be beaten, and its coins buy no stronger gear. Its collectibles moved from costly trophies to stickers and spirits.
review_question: What does the player earn in the first hour, and does each reward type suit what makes the game fun?
keywords: rewards progression unlocks loot collectibles motivation compensation economy currency incentives reward plan

principle: Keep the next objective visible and within reach
why: Keeping rewards in sight and giving a clear objective both motivate players; Sakurai thinks it a shame when a game doesn't keep you thinking about the next reward. Objectives are rewards in their own right, and a hint of future developments makes even a short errand worth doing.
how_to_apply: Show progress as current versus required (EXP now and EXP to the next level) and make every action move it. Make key purchases few, expensive and powerful. Use a goal grid that reveals its neighbors' conditions as each panel clears. At several points in a playthrough, ask what the player is working toward; if the answer is unclear or out of reach, add a nearer objective. If there is no ending, place the goal so far away players can't see it.
anti_pattern: Hiding how close the next reward is; handing out so much minor loot that no purchase is worth saving for.
example: Ys shows current EXP and the EXP needed to level up. Faxanadu's few, expensive shop items each give a massive boost. Kirby Air Ride's Checklist reveals adjacent conditions as squares clear. Cookie Clicker's exponential growth keeps the end out of sight.
review_question: At any moment, what is the player working toward, and can they see how far they have left?
keywords: objectives goals progress bar next reward visible goal achievements checklist motivation clear objective

principle: Shape progression as peaks and flats, not a steady incline
why: A climb at one steady incline with unchanging scenery is 'just work'. Keeping enemy strength in direct proportion to the player's removes the point of getting stronger. Stress followed by release is a core source of fun, and breathers make the next squeeze land.
how_to_apply: Plot player power and challenge across the whole game and reshape it into peaks (bosses that demand a strategy and pay off with a clear reward) and flats (an unexpectedly empty area inside a dense zone, a spot to rack up gains, a short scene as a breather). Vary the scenery along the way. In open or multi-path games, don't scale every enemy with the player.
anti_pattern: Proportional scaling; bosses that are just beefed-up regular enemies; rest stops at fixed intervals as the only highlights.
example: Sakurai's mountain-trail analogy: real climbs have challenges to overcome and flat plains to breeze through.
review_question: Where are the peaks and the flats in our first hour, and does the player feel stronger after each peak?
keywords: pacing difficulty curve progression level scaling bosses breather rhythm intensity curve peaks valleys stress relief

principle: Write story around play: the protagonist's view, the player's victories
why: Game writing differs from other media in about four ways: story can get in the way of play, it unfolds from the main character's perspective, the hero almost always needs to win, and comrades cannot simply die or leave without upsetting party balance or costing the player items. Story is not game essence, but it drives players onward into risk when it uses interactivity.
how_to_apply: Start with gameplay, not story, and brief players while they play (in-play dialogue, with an option to turn it off). Trim long backstory about allies and villains. Never let a cutscene undo a fight the player just won; if a companion must leave, protect the balance and items the player invested. Tie story beats to the challenge ahead. Break these rules only on purpose.
anti_pattern: A cutscene loss right after a player victory; long side-character exposition; mission briefings that hold up play.
example: In Kid Icarus: Uprising, Pit runs through a door and play begins, and the story unfolds during play like a radio program. Sakurai's errand rewrite turns 'Go buy me some meat!' into a search for a missing girl.
review_question: Does any story beat stop play, undo the player's win, or take away something they invested in?
keywords: story narrative writing scenario dialogue cutscene loss party members exposition briefing protagonist perspective

principle: Keep cutscenes lean and purposeful, and never make them the reward
why: Long stretches of fairly irrelevant cutscenes make players impatient, and leaner cutscenes suit modern games. Cutscenes still earn their place when they carry emotion, tell the story more clearly or serve as a palate cleanser. Movies used as progression rewards end up online at or before launch, so they stop being rewards.
how_to_apply: Review every cutscene: keep deliberate breathers and beats that play cannot carry, and shorten or cut the ones that are just downtime. Treat showcase movies as marketing everyone can watch. Test any quick-time event with players very carefully before committing to it.
anti_pattern: Spending heavily on unlockable movies; quick-time events added only to keep people on edge; relying on slowness to build suspense.
example: Brawl's per-fighter movies, meant to reward progress through the Subspace Emissary, were posted online from pre-release copies, so Sakurai turned showcase movies into fighter reveal videos.
review_question: For each cutscene, what does it do that play can't, and would anyone miss it if it were half as long?
keywords: cutscenes cinematics movies CG cinematic QTE quick time event reward story scenes length downtime

principle: Let players skip, pause and speed through anything non-interactive
why: A player with no save data is not necessarily seeing a scene for the first time, and unskippable scenes are off-putting. People now watch video sped up, and everyone wants to enjoy as much as possible in as little time as possible. Players press buttons because they want something from the game.
how_to_apply: Make every cutscene, logo and the credits skippable from the first playthrough, all at once if possible. Make cutscenes pausable. Offer line-by-line skip and fast-forward, or let voiced lines play while the player keeps playing. Have any button press during a cutscene bring up a skip prompt.
anti_pattern: Locking skip until a second playthrough; scenes that can be skipped but not paused; buttons that do nothing during cutscenes.
example: Line-by-line dialogue skipping, which jumps to the start of the next line, is 'a real breeze'. Players get phone calls and visitors, so cutscenes must pause.
review_question: Can a player skip, pause or fast-forward every non-interactive moment, credits included?
keywords: skip cutscenes pause fast-forward text speed credits logos unskippable respect player time dialogue skip

principle: Collect every hard limit at kickoff and design inside it
why: Age-rating, platform, storefront, online-service, internal and licensor guidelines must be met or the game cannot ship, and when they block an intended feature players may blame the developer. Hardware and media limits decide what is possible. Discovering any of them after a feature is built wastes the work.
how_to_apply: At kickoff, list every guideline and hard limit (ratings, platform rules, regional rules on depicting gambling, storage size, processing headroom on the weakest target) and check planned visuals and features against them. Let the weakest platform set shared limits. Budget several adjustment rounds for region-sensitive features. If you write guidelines yourself, state their purpose and allow justified exceptions.
anti_pattern: Finding a guideline conflict after the feature exists; adding a feature the hardware cannot carry.
example: Smash's spectator wagers needed careful, repeated adjustments for regional gambling rules. Ice Climbers were too heavy for the 3DS. Ultimate's cartridge capped the ROM at about 16 GB, and compression fit the music into a quarter of its old space. A twin-stick peripheral would have added about 5% processor load to an Uprising already at the hardware's limit.
review_question: Which guidelines and hardware limits bind us, and has every planned feature been checked against them?
keywords: constraints guidelines certification ratings platform requirements compliance hardware limits memory budget storage regional rules

principle: Budget the hidden costs each feature drags in
why: Features cost more than building them. Growth and parameter systems multiply the test matrix (a game that takes dozens of hours to finish may need thousands to tens of thousands of hours of testing), every one-of-a-kind character mechanic needs its own programming, a demo becomes a second build to maintain and test, and online updates mean development has no clean end. Heavy content formats cap how much you can include.
how_to_apply: Before approving a feature, estimate its testing, code and maintenance cost. Schedule programmer time for each unique mechanic, reserve people for post-launch fixes, and plan a demo as a small separate game that needs QA. When volume matters, choose lightweight formats (an image plus a gameplay effect rather than a model and written description).
anti_pattern: Adding modifier systems late without their test cost; treating DLC and updates as free; making every collectible a fully modeled, written item.
example: Spirits made testing Ultimate a gargantuan task. Brawl's adventure mode needed a second parameter set for every fighter. Trophies inflated costs, while stickers and spirits let far more characters in. Smash for 3DS/Wii U released in 2014, but development only wrapped in spring 2016.
review_question: For the feature we are adding, how many test hours, code days and post-launch hours does it really cost?
keywords: hidden cost testing QA test matrix maintenance post-launch DLC updates demo production cost content format budget

principle: Deliver volume as short, distinct chunks with their own rules
why: When too many games took too long to beat, Sakurai built Kirby Super Star as an omnibus of quick scenarios, each with its own rules and theme, to offer lots of content without tiring players of any one style. Chunks that play alike lose the benefit.
how_to_apply: Split content into self-contained modes or segments, picked from a hub, each with a rule no other has. If two end up playing the same, cut or change one. Use fixed-length segments where you want music or events to hit exact beats, and give competitive sessions short, concrete goals.
anti_pattern: Two modes that play the same.
example: Kirby Super Star's cork board of scenarios; its first scenario, Spring Breeze, got the copy ability at a producer's request, and Sakurai still wishes it could be played without it, since nothing really sets it apart from the next scenario. Smash Run gives five minutes to collect power-ups before a showdown. Uprising's air battles last five minutes.
review_question: Does each mode or segment have a rule that no other has?
keywords: modes omnibus variety minigames episodic structure session chunking content structure hub scenarios

principle: Give every character and option an identity in a word or two
why: Characters that are basically the same are no fun; pushing each one far from a workable neutral creates strategy and memorability. Options with markedly distinct pros and cons set customization apart, and a feature that could be generic can become individuality instead.
how_to_apply: Define a neutral baseline for your rules, then push each character's parameters well away from it and give some a one-of-a-kind mechanic, with programming budgeted for it. Write a one- or two-word identity for every character, enemy and option; if you can't, push further. Give each option a clear trade-off and let players test it right away.
anti_pattern: Timid parameter nudges; options that differ in name only; eccentricity that makes something unusable.
example: Gordo is invincible, harmless and static, and becomes interesting only through placement. Every Ultimate DLC fighter has a unique system. Brawl gave each fighter its own Final Smash instead of a generic power item.
review_question: Can we describe each character, enemy and option in a word or two, and does each one play differently?
keywords: character identity differentiation uniqueness roster design parameters trade-offs customization distinct options

principle: Spend a sequel's head start on purpose, and make it clearly more fun
why: Making the same thing again roughly halves sales, and fans who see the same scale and content feel they have already played it. Games need a system, structure and tools before content can be made, so a sequel can spend that head start either on expanding the system or on a big lead in content.
how_to_apply: At sequel kickoff, list what carries over (team, tools, assets, hardware architecture) and decide where the saved effort goes. Write how the sequel is more fun and more impactful than the last game, and list concrete changes for every element. Re-examine inherited rules, and if the tempo changes, retune every parameter.
anti_pattern: Same scale and similar content; carrying old tuning into a faster game.
example: Melee's concept was to power up every element of Smash. Ultimate's 'Everyone is here!' was feasible because the team and tools carried over, and Sakurai listed 70 to 100 potential changes per fighter.
review_question: In one line, how is this sequel more fun and impactful than the last, and where is the carried-over effort going?
keywords: sequel follow-up franchise iteration reuse head start series continuity expansion new entry

principle: Make every button press visibly register the moment it happens
why: Play is a two-way flow: information goes from the player's hands to the computer and back to their eyes and ears, and the hand side is vital, so an action with no reaction feels lacking. Lag from TVs and networks can never be fully removed, but the game can still tell players right away that their input was received. Impact sounds must never feel late, because players need a reaction to their attack immediately.
how_to_apply: On the first frame after an attack input, jump to a clearly different pose instead of easing out of idle. Give every accepted press an unambiguous signal (pose, sound, highlight). In menus accept confirm from more than one button; during cutscenes let any press bring up a skip prompt. Shape hit sounds so they reach a strong level almost instantly. Count the frames from press to first visible change for every action and treat that number as a design value.
anti_pattern: Smoothly interpolating from standby into the windup, which delays the visible response; buttons that do nothing in some state; ambiguous feedback that leaves players unsure the press registered; impact sounds with a slow attack.
example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate: the pose changes drastically the instant a Smash Attack is pressed, then the fighter holds and shakes while charging. Zero Suit Samus's neutral attack comes out one frame after input. The Pong-style dial games that impressed young Sakurai moved objects directly on a bright, flashy screen.
review_question: How many frames pass between a press and the first visible or audible response, and does any press in any game state get no reaction at all?
keywords: responsiveness input feedback acknowledgement instant response press reaction dead buttons action reaction snappy controls input confirmation first frame

principle: Stop the action at every big moment: hits, boss defeats and deaths
why: Whether hit stop is present completely changes how heavy a hit feels. A boss stop (the screen stops and flashes) is vital for feeling the defeat. In many shoot 'em ups players die without realizing it; if their takeaway is 'Wait, I got hit?', the game has only told them something went wrong, a missed opportunity. Stops are relatively easy to implement and belong in every genre.
how_to_apply: Freeze attacker and target briefly when a hit lands. On a boss defeat, freeze and flash the screen before the defeat sequence. When the player takes damage or loses a life, pause for an instant so the point of impact is visible. For the biggest moments (finishing blows, boss kills) layer a full stop with screen shake, a flash and slow motion. Compare builds with and without the stop.
anti_pattern: Treating stops as minor polish; deaths the player never saw happen; stopping the screen everywhere at the same strength so big moments don't stand out.
example: Kirby's Adventure (NES) stops and flashes the screen when a boss falls and stops the action when Kirby loses a life. Fantasy Zone (1986) stops the screen for a second when you're hit; Defender (1980) builds the stop into its hit effect. Final Fight's hit stop defined its feel. Smash Ultimate's Finish Zoom extends the boss-stop idea, and finishing blows stop the screen completely.
review_question: When the player lands a hit, beats a boss or dies, does the game stop long enough for them to see exactly what happened and feel it?
keywords: hitstop hit-stop hit stop freeze frame impact pause boss stop finish zoom stop effect death pause slow motion heavy hits big moments

principle: Hunt down input lag across the whole display and audio chain
why: Even a game with great response time is ruined by display or audio delay. At E3 2018 the Smash Ultimate setup had enough lag to ruin the controls and nobody noticed until Sakurai did: many people don't recognize lag when they see it. Modern TVs and monitors do heavy image processing, and more post-processing means more lag; during a recorded session his shots kept going astray until he switched to a low-lag monitor.
how_to_apply: Before any playtest, demo, capture or event, press jump in a game that responds instantly (a 2D NES game, not a 3D one) on that exact setup and confirm the character moves the moment you press. Use Game Mode or Low Latency Mode, or turn off every picture enhancement. Check sound separately and use an analog or low-latency audio path if hit sounds arrive late. Convert latency specs to frames: 16.67 ms is one frame at 60 fps. Rule out display lag before retuning any timing.
anti_pattern: Trusting that someone else already tested the setup; judging lag with a 3D game; leaving TV post-processing on; retuning the game to compensate for a laggy screen.
example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate at Nintendo's E3 2018 Treehouse: Live. Special Crossover #2: Sakurai swaps to the monitor from his 'Mr. Sakurai Presents' recordings mid-session. Brawl's speed was lowered partly because frame skips stood out online the higher the input density.
review_question: Has someone checked this exact screen, capture and audio setup for lag today, using a game known to respond instantly?
keywords: input lag latency display lag delay game mode low latency mode TV post-processing audio delay frame delay 16.67 ms online lag netcode responsiveness demo setup

principle: Make attacks that look like they connect actually connect
why: In a fast game with coordinate-based movement, hitboxes mapped tightly to the sword or fist make attacks miss and players grow more and more stressed. Attacks that look like they should hit but don't, or keep hitting after the swing ends, feel wrong. Shaking the hitbox during hit stop, letting damage percentage change knockback on the early hits of a multi-hit move, or letting a stance change slide the target back all make hits that should connect miss.
how_to_apply: Make collision wider than the visible weapon in fast games and make sure each attack's range crosses the median line where opponents stand. During hit stop, shake only the rendered model. Give every hit but the last of a multi-hit move fixed knockback. Test strings against every reaction stance so the target's top node doesn't drift. When a hit feels off, adjust the hitbox and the animation together. Check reach in every direction and in ground and aerial versions.
anti_pattern: Pixel-exact hitboxes in a fast game; hitboxes that shake with the model; fixing a misplaced animation by stretching collision to meet it; assuming a combo works because it works at one damage level.
example: Smash Bros. attack collision is wider than the fighter's sword or fist. Mario's Super Jump Punch uses fixed knockback on its early hits. A neutral-attack combo missed because the hit fighter's top node moved back. Pyra's forward aerial collision was shortened because it kept hitting after the swing; Steve's grab arc was pulled closer; Sora's Sonic Blade lost reach when aimed upward.
review_question: Does every attack that visibly connects register, at every damage level and from every direction, and does anything keep hitting after the swing has visibly ended?
keywords: hitbox hurtbox collision attack range whiff missed hits fairness multi-hit combos connect hit detection generous hitboxes median line top node

principle: Keep every wait and transition hasty, but don't cut it out entirely
why: Making players wait is a sin. Slow fades followed by long black screens leave players without control and rob them of their time, and it is almost impossible to make a transition too fast. Removing transitions altogether feels jarring, though. Some load times can't be optimized away; what really irritates is a wait that looks like someone dropped the ball.
how_to_apply: Time every fade, black screen and non-interactive stretch, then trim each one to 'a hasty speed' that still reads as a transition. Hide unavoidable loading inside an in-world moment or a themed wipe; if you can't, show a simple, world-styled loading indicator straight away. Don't time presentation to development-build load times, which will change. Let any press during a cutscene bring up a skip, and let cutscenes pause.
anti_pattern: Slow, dreary fades and long black screens; hard cuts with no transition; a loading icon on top of a transition that is already hiding the load; presentation whose length depends on today's load times.
example: The original Resident Evil's doors hid loading, built fear and opened a little slower when zombies waited behind them. The first Legend of Zelda scrolls at screen edges so players see how the map connects (today it could be smoother and faster). Super Mario World's key transition adds mystery; Smash Ultimate uses random wipes into the victory screen.
review_question: How many seconds of a typical session is the player not in control, and does any wait look like a development mistake?
keywords: screen transitions fades wipes loading screens load times waiting player time black screen skip cutscenes pause downtime speed

principle: Make failure hit hard for about a second, then hand back control
why: Player interest cools fast between 'Ugh, I blew it!' and getting control back, and the longer the wait the more they lose interest. Quick retries raise their tolerance for difficulty. The loss should still really be felt, so the failure effect must be flashy and impactful, but short. The game moving on its own isn't enough; the player has to be in control.
how_to_apply: Measure the time from failure to control. Keep the failure effect flashy and to 'a second or so' (genre-dependent), then return control as soon as possible. Trim loads and non-interactive screens; if a step must remain, make it player-advanced. Don't respawn players into enemy fire. Keep some real cost so respawning never feels mindless.
anti_pattern: Long death animations, slow fades and loading between failure and retry; infinite respawns right where the player died; players losing again before they touch the controller.
example: No specific game is cited in the retry episode. In Kirby's Adventure the action stops when Kirby loses a life, and Fantasy Zone's hit stop gives an 'oh no!' moment, both short and clear.
review_question: How long from the moment of failure until the player can act again, and is the failure itself unmistakable?
keywords: retry restart death respawn failure effect game over quick retry player time loss feedback checkpoint frustration

principle: Specify, feel and verify every timing in frames
why: Games measure time in frames, and distance = time x speed, so frames are the basis for all movement. There is no stopwatch for frames, so a designer must train a sense of them to write precise specs and to notice when code or data errors make the build differ from the spec.
how_to_apply: Assume a target rate (at 60 fps, 60 frames is one second). Train by clapping '1-and-2-and-3-and': about 30 frames per beat, 15 per half beat. Anchor on known moves (about 15 frames from Smash Attack input to release, about 15 for a standard Tekken kick's startup, a bit under half that for a Street Fighter II heavy punch) and estimate from the 0/15/30 anchors. Write specs as frame numbers (attack start frame, total frames) and speeds per frame. Lock processing speed and frame timing before final tuning.
anti_pattern: Words like 'quick' or 'slow' in specs; frame counts nobody on the team can feel or verify; tuning balance while frame timing is still changing.
example: His NES and SNES games counted time in screen interrupts, so the 50 fps PAL versions ran at 5/6 speed. Meteos became harder than intended when processing speed changed late in development.
review_question: Is every timing in the spec a frame number, and could its author tell by feel whether the build matches?
keywords: frames frame counting frame data timing unit of time 60 fps startup frames specs spec sheet durations distance time speed 1-and-2-and

principle: Sell hit stop with shake, scaling and blending, not a bare freeze
why: A plain stop works, but in Smash hit stop is never just a stop; there is always some shake. Each technique is hard to notice on its own, but together they make hits feel much stronger. Scaling by strength plus a multiplier lets a sweet spot feel heavier than its damage and lets guest characters feel like their source games.
how_to_apply: Shake the victim more and the attacker less, moving only the rendered model. Shake grounded characters horizontally only and airborne ones in all directions, starting big and decaying over the precomputed stop length. Compute stop length from attack strength, then apply a per-move multiplier; lengthen it for lightning and shorten it in multiplayer. Increase shake when the camera is pulled back. Blend the victim into the damage pose over about four frames. Keep a sword attacker's animation creeping forward very slowly (per-attack toggle). Let hit marks keep animating and let the hit sound's main body finish during the stop.
anti_pattern: Shaking the hitbox; vertical shake on grounded 3D characters, which clips legs into the floor; one fixed stop length for every hit; a frozen victim snapped to a single pose.
example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate: the tip of Marth's sword gets a bigger stop than its base; Ryu's stops look bigger and Kazuya's smaller at equal damage to match their games; a strong sword swing's tip keeps inching upward during the stop. Final Fight's hit stop left a lasting impression.
review_question: During hit stop, does the victim shake more than the attacker, does duration scale with strength, and does anything still move or animate?
keywords: hitstop hit stop shake hit shake freeze impact multiplier sweet spot victim attacker hitbox damage pose blend hit lag hit pause

principle: Front-load the hit and make strong attacks pay for it in recovery
why: Lead-ins should move quickly into the attack for responsiveness, but if you want push and pull, strong attacks must leave the character proportionally vulnerable afterward or the game feels unrefined. Landing a slow, risky move is a more commendable feat, so it earns more damage and knockback. Recovery length is also a balance lever that can change a move without touching its signature power.
how_to_apply: Lay out each attack so the hit registers about 1/4 to 1/3 of the way in (about 1/5 for fast moves), with standard attacks finishing in under a second. Scale recovery with power; even Smash Attacks with large openings almost never exceed one second. When a move is too strong, lengthen its follow-through or shrink its hitbox rather than cutting what defines it.
anti_pattern: Strong attacks with little vulnerability afterward; slow windups that delay responsiveness instead of long recoveries that create openings; nerfing a move's identity when its recovery could change instead.
example: Super Smash Bros.: the quick, safe neutral attack against the slow, vulnerable Smash Attack that earns more damage and knockback; attack breakdowns marking hit, end and cancel points.
review_question: For every attack, where does the hit land in its timeline, and does a stronger move leave the attacker open for longer?
keywords: recovery end lag vulnerability startup active frames frame data attack timeline risk reward push and pull punish window move balance

principle: Return control when players expect it, using cancel frames
why: Cancel frames let players move, jump or attack again before the animation fully returns to standby, a bit of elbow room. Smash didn't have them until after Melee, so control only came back at standby, which felt a little heavy or rigid. Their timing has to match when people instinctively expect control back.
how_to_apply: Mark a cancel window in the latter part of each recovery. When an input arrives during it, blend from the current pose into the new action. Playtest whether the window lines up with when players try to act, and keep the recovery pose visibly held up to that point.
anti_pattern: Returning control only after the full return to standby; cancel windows so early that recovery stops meaning anything; snapping into the next animation instead of blending.
example: Super Smash Bros. through Melee had no cancel frames and felt a little rigid; later games mark where cancel frames end the recovery.
review_question: Do players regain control at the moment they instinctively try to act after each move?
keywords: cancel frames animation cancel interrupt recovery control return elbow room IASA rigid controls heavy controls blend into next action

principle: Shape the jump's rise, fall and air control to your game's goal
why: A jump is simple but full of choices, and the right one depends on what the game is for. Even with the same trajectory, changing a move's speed drastically changes how it feels. A gentle rise and fast fall suit variable-height platforming, a floaty jump helps when the height you shoot from matters, and a fixed arc turns every jump into a planned commitment.
how_to_apply: Build the jump from an initial upward velocity plus downward acceleration added every frame, with a maximum fall speed. Use separate rise and fall gravity. Decide air control on purpose. For slams, make the descent faster than the ascent. If jump and up-attacks share an input, keep a short, uniform pre-jump windup. For forgiving escapes, use a very strong burst then heavy gravity for a few frames before normal gravity. Ask each project whether you need a jump at all.
anti_pattern: One default jump reused across games; removing the pre-jump windup when up-attacks share the stick direction; a camera that hides jump height.
example: Super Mario Bros. (gentle rise, sudden extra gravity at the peak, hold for height); Metroid (slow rise, slow fall); Ghosts 'n Goblins (low jump, no mid-air steering); Zangief's Spinning Pile Driver falls faster than it rises from Street Fighter II Turbo on; Smash Ultimate and Kirby Super Star's burst jump.
review_question: Can you state what your jump's rise, peak, fall and air control are each for?
keywords: jump physics gravity jump arc rise fall speed air control variable jump height fall speed apex jump windup jump squat platforming

principle: Sell big impacts with screen shake tuned to the camera
why: Screen shake is just the ticket for conveying a big impact; a game without it can feel bland and even a tiny shake changes how hard attacks feel. But too much makes the screen hard to see, and in 3D a camera shake barely moves distant objects, so the amount needs real care.
how_to_apply: Author a few distinct presets (Smash uses large, medium, small, extra-small) with different axis behavior, not scaled copies. Start strong and decay with a little randomness. Shake the camera's look-at point as much as the camera or more. Scale amplitude by camera distance and field of view, and retune scenes with unusual FOV. Reserve it for impacts that deserve it, and pair it with a brief full-screen flash only for the heaviest ones.
anti_pattern: Shaking until the screen is unreadable; moving a distant look-at point so subtly nothing seems to happen; one shake scaled up and down for every impact; shipping big impacts with no shake.
example: Super Smash Bros.: small shakes vertical only, medium adds horizontal, large shakes more; Flat Zone's tight field of view made normal shake feel too big, so it was retuned. Sakurai has used shake often since Kirby's Adventure.
review_question: Does each impact class have its own shake, and does the shake look the same size at every camera distance?
keywords: screen shake camera shake shake presets trauma impact rumble field of view camera distance decay randomness screen flash

principle: Tune on-screen response so each character has its own weight
why: The same physical button can feel light or heavy depending on movement speed, inertia, jump physics, lag and frame rate: somehow you feel feedback with your hands. Control feel can be the fun by itself, like an RC car. Differences in speed, vulnerability and animation flair create push and pull and characters that feel wildly different. Inertia is also a risk dial: more of it raises game essence but narrows appeal.
how_to_apply: Decide each character's intended weight, then tune speed, inertia and jump physics to it and compare characters with identical inputs. Run them on one shared behavior and express differences as parameter sets. Reserve schedule time just to sense and fine-tune movement. Set analog tilt sensitivity per console.
anti_pattern: Assuming feel comes from hardware; characters that differ only in stats you can't feel; adding inertia without considering who it shuts out.
example: NES control-pad games that feel radically different; Family BASIC's SPRITE command, a controller-driven sprite with a little inertia, taught Sakurai lessons he used on Kirby's Dream Land; every Kirby Air Ride machine shares one behavior and differs by parameters; a hypothetical harder Kirby with more inertia.
review_question: With the same inputs, does each character feel like the weight you intended, and does moving feel good on its own?
keywords: game feel weight heavy light inertia acceleration movement speed control feel character feel button weight parameters momentum

principle: Frame the camera for the gameplay, not just to follow the character
why: With the camera's center point anchored to the character, it's hard to see how the character is moving: jump height disappears and dodges lose impact. Good framing improves presentation, and the right frame differs by game: look-ahead for side-scrollers, an anchored point only where precise realistic racing suits it.
how_to_apply: Track the center point less (or not at all) on the Y axis during jumps. Let the character drift off center during dodges and drifts. In side-scrollers show more space ahead. In co-op scrollers make one player the camera's lead and warp stragglers back. When a character is knocked flying, stop scrolling, then gently recenter once they settle. Treat camera inertia as a tunable value.
anti_pattern: Anchoring the center point to the character by default; full vertical tracking that hides jumps; giving every co-op player equal pull on the scroll.
example: Super Mario 64 (Mario rises on screen when he jumps) against Smash Ultimate with a fighter-tracking camera; Armored Core; Kirby Air Ride drifting; Kirby Super Star's Helper system and Space Jump; Kirby's Dream Land's 1990 design document; Kid Icarus: Uprising's swipe-to-spin touch aiming.
review_question: When the character jumps, dodges or gets launched, can the player see on screen how far they moved?
keywords: camera center point look-at point camera tracking framing look-ahead co-op camera off-center vertical tracking camera inertia knockback camera

principle: Keep controls simple and physical, and no busier than the game needs
why: By 1996 fighting-game command inputs had become extremely complicated, so Smash used a stick direction plus a button, which players pick up intuitively. Reading how far and how fast the analog stick moves gives the controls real physicality. One button can already carry a whole game, and each added input changes how it feels; the simplest approach often plays best.
how_to_apply: Map moves to direction plus button and use input timing (a quick flick) for stronger variants. Scale walk speed by tilt and trigger dashes with a fast flick instead of a double-tap or held button. Try the core action on one button before adding more. Make the dominant action's button the most prominent only when actions are unequal. On new hardware, list what the device uniquely does and adopt only the uses that fit. Lower input density for casual audiences or laggy online play.
anti_pattern: Long command strings; two-step or two-button basic actions; adding inputs because the hardware has them; rapid tapping as a core mechanic; high input density for a casual audience.
example: Smash's smash input and flick input ('Tap' in the N64 version); Kid Icarus: Uprising's flick dash and dodge and its context-sensitive attack button; Brawl not using every Nunchuk or pointer function; Kirby's one-button minigames; the GameCube controller's big A button.
review_question: Could a newcomer perform every core action within minutes, and does each input earn its place?
keywords: controls simple controls input design one button analog stick flick input tilt dash input density control scheme peripherals intuitive

principle: Never let a deliberate input feel canceled or misread
why: If a small forward nudge from an action drops the player off a ledge, it feels like their input was canceled. If jumps start instantly, players jump before they can input an up-attack on the same stick direction. Flick dashes have accidental dashes as a downside. Ambiguous responses leave players unsure what happened. Each of these breaks trust in the controls.
how_to_apply: Decide ledge behavior per action: keep short stepping attacks and forward dodges on the platform, let fast rushes carry over, stop long rushes late in the move, and use speed thresholds for rolling moves. For walking, consider requiring a push toward the edge or steering along near-parallel ledges. Keep a short, uniform windup where two inputs share a direction. Expose flick sensitivity as a setting. Playtest ledges and edge cases by feel.
anti_pattern: Characters that fall off every ledge unconditionally; ignoring momentum so it's easy to fly off the stage; inputs that silently do something other than what was meant.
example: Super Smash Bros.: Fox Illusion stops at the ledge; Falcon Kick goes over unless the ledge is reached late in the move; Drill Rush stops at the ledge late; Egg Roll uses a speed parameter; the unified jump windup protects Up Smash; Ultimate's flick sensitivity option.
review_question: Is there any situation where the player pressed one thing and the game did something else, like walking off a ledge or dashing by accident?
keywords: ledges edge behavior input intent canceled input accidental input ledge falling momentum jump windup flick sensitivity misread input forgiveness

principle: Build knockback as a tunable payoff with per-attack parameters
why: When launching opponents is the core mechanic, knockback is at the heart of the game essence and needs unorthodox detail to feel fun. A launcher should cause at least some reaction on a barely damaged opponent, multi-hit moves must connect at any damage level, and big launches after a struggle give a visceral thrill. Launches also have to stay readable on small screens.
how_to_apply: Compute knockback from attack damage and the target's accumulated damage. Give each attack a free launch angle, an optional modifier toward the attacker's direction of travel, a multiplier, a guaranteed minimum kept in check by scaling, and an optional fixed value. Let target weight and fall speed shape the arc. Cap launch speed for readability on the smallest target screen.
anti_pattern: Adding a minimum knockback without scaling, which makes launches too big; damage-dependent knockback on early hits of a multi-hit move; launches too fast to follow on a handheld screen.
example: Super Smash Bros.: Mario's Super Jump Punch (fixed knockback until the final hit); launch speed slowed in Smash for 3DS to stay readable on its LCD; Ultimate sped knockback up again. Kirby's Dream Land's 1990 design document already tied knockback distance to health.
review_question: Does every attack produce a visible, intended reaction at low, medium and high damage, and can players follow the launch?
keywords: knockback launch angle knockback scaling base knockback fixed knockback multiplier weight fall speed combos launcher hitstun

principle: Choose your frame rate on purpose and protect it
why: 60 fps and 30 fps differ in look and in how smoothly they control. 60 fps is ideal; 30 fps is a common, more than adequate standard, because drawing twice the frames costs half your visual performance. For Smash on 3DS Sakurai treated a stable 60 fps as an absolute must and cut content until it held. A port that keeps every element but drops frames loses its smoothness and mood.
how_to_apply: Pick the target rate early by weighing control smoothness against the rendering budget. If the game is timing-heavy, hold a stable 60 and pare content and effects rather than dropping to 30. Keep game speed independent of how many frames are drawn; a variable frame rate is not slowdown. Check high refresh rates against displays that can show them.
anti_pattern: Deciding the frame rate late; confusing frame drops with slowdown; tying game logic to a refresh rate that varies by region or platform.
example: Smash for 3DS kept four players, stereoscopic 3D and items at a stable 60 fps; the NES Ghosts 'n Goblins kept everything in place but lost its smoothness and creepiness; Smash Ultimate's stages were built for eight fighters at 60 fps.
review_question: Does the game hold its target frame rate in the worst case, and was that target chosen for the controls rather than by default?
keywords: frame rate fps 60 fps 30 fps performance budget stable frame rate slowdown variable frame rate smoothness refresh rate

principle: Use genre-standard controls, keep series rules stable, and allow remapping
why: De facto standards let you skip explanations and warm the handshake between human and computer. Changing a series' basic rules and controls with every release makes it harder to play. Designers once assumed their layout was best and nobody would change it, but players want the freedom to play their way.
how_to_apply: Map core actions to the genre's standard buttons unless you have a deliberate reason not to. Keep rotation rules, previews and similar fundamentals identical across a series. Ship a remapping screen: a drawn controller, pick the button with the cursor then the action, let several buttons share an action, and save named profiles. Expose stick and flick sensitivity. Remap awkward legacy schemes when re-releasing old games.
anti_pattern: Avoiding standards so you don't look like a copy; reinventing basic rules each sequel; fixed controls on modern controllers.
example: Western FPS games share nearly the same controls; old Tetris versions each felt different until the 2002 guidelines; Pac-Land's run-by-pressing scheme became easy after remapping in Arcade Archives; Smash's two jump buttons and named profiles.
review_question: Would a player of this genre know the controls without being told, and can every player change them?
keywords: standard controls conventions button remapping key config control profiles sensitivity settings de facto standards series consistency

principle: Retune every feel parameter when tempo, mode or hardware changes
why: Raising Smash Ultimate's tempo meant none of Smash for's parameters could be reused, jumps and knockback included. Fighters dropped into Brawl's Subspace Emissary with their versus specs didn't work. Different hardware changes what reads well, and a late change in processing speed can silently break tuning.
how_to_apply: When the game's speed changes, budget time to rebuild movement and combat values rather than porting them. Give characters a separate movement parameter set for very different modes. Let the weakest target screen set shared speed limits. Redo tuning if performance changes late.
anti_pattern: Carrying old tuning into a faster or slower game; one parameter set for incompatible modes; reusing raw speed values across platforms with different pixel counts.
example: Ultimate's tempo sits between Melee and Smash for; Brawl was slowed for casual players; Smash for 3DS slowed launches for its LCD; Meteos became harder after a late processing-speed change; PAL ports ran at 5/6 speed.
review_question: Since the last change in tempo, mode or platform, has every movement and combat value been re-felt, not just carried over?
keywords: tempo game speed retuning parameters sequels porting modes parameter sets platform differences balance retune

principle: State speeds in shared units and judge them against body size
why: Speed = distance / time, and specs don't work if the team can't share what a speed means. Pixel counts differ between platforms, so the same value gives different results. A speed that looks low in km/h can be fast for a tiny character.
how_to_apply: Pick one unit per project (pixels per frame for sprites; km/h or distance per frame for real-scale 3D), document it and put it in parameter names. Build at real-world scale if you want real speeds. Judge speeds against the character's own size. Practice estimating speeds by eye before checking the number.
anti_pattern: Speeds without units; reusing raw speed values across resolutions; judging speed only by the number.
example: Mario's top speed in Mario Bros. is about 1 p/f on a 256-pixel-wide NES screen (Sakurai's guess); Kirby Air Ride used km/h, which look low because Kirby is about a 20 cm square.
review_question: Does every speed in your specs have a unit everyone reads the same way?
keywords: speed units pixels per frame p/f km/h distance per frame scale movement speed specs parameters

principle: Treat the screen as a small window and spend it on play
why: A screen covers only about 30 degrees of the player's vision, so a wide world is squeezed into a narrow window and screen space is scarce. Realistic views like a cockpit camera shrink the space left for play, and tiny distant targets lack impact.
how_to_apply: Before choosing camera and field of view, decide what must fit on screen. Prefer views that leave more room for play. If targets look tiny, scale them up. Weigh VR's blur and head-turning costs, and favor it where gaze and heading differ.
anti_pattern: Choosing a view for realism at the cost of play space; tiny targets on a big screen.
example: Racing games mostly avoid the cockpit view; Kid Icarus: Uprising made standard enemies four or five times Pit's size; VR racing suits games where you look somewhere other than where you move.
review_question: How much of the screen is actually used for play in your main camera, and are targets big enough to read?
keywords: screen space field of view FOV camera view cockpit view target size VR screen real estate

principle: Offer comfort toggles instead of stripping presentation for everyone
why: 3D motion sickness comes from on-screen inertia the inner ear doesn't feel. Turning off footstep shake can help a lot, but a camera built to avoid sickness has little embellishment and looks less entertaining. Too much shake or blur also makes the action hard to read.
how_to_apply: List inertia-heavy camera effects (footstep bob, vehicle-frame sway, blur) and give each an option. Lock cockpit or vehicle frames in place in a comfort mode. Offer a blur-strength setting. Cap shake and flash so the screen stays readable. Recruit testers who actually get sick.
anti_pattern: Assuming the camera is comfortable because nobody on the team gets sick; removing presentation for everyone instead of offering options.
example: The common FPS option to disable vertical footstep shake; games that let players adjust motion blur.
review_question: Can a player prone to motion sickness turn off every inertial camera effect without losing the game's readability?
keywords: motion sickness comfort options accessibility head bob camera shake toggle motion blur setting vehicle sway

principle: Tune feel by hand, with exposed parameters and fast iteration
why: Sakurai learned how changes affect feel by tinkering with sprite inertia in Family BASIC. Feel is found by trying values and playing, and tuning is where you iterate most, so values must be easy to change and the build easy to test. Ledge behavior and similar details only show up by paying attention to feel in playtesting.
how_to_apply: Keep every speed, timing and force in parameters outside the code, name them in plain language with units, and push edits to builds in one step. Build debug commands for the setups you test most (set damage percentage, slow motion, hide background). Vary one value at a time and note how it feels.
anti_pattern: Hard-coded values that need a programmer for every tweak; tuning by spreadsheet without playing; slow conversion loops.
example: Family BASIC's SPRITE command; Smash parameters in Excel with one-button conversion; '[Special X-deceleration is O/frame]' bracket notation; Kirby Air Ride machines tuned by a few numbers; the Training Mode trajectory guide began as a debug feature.
review_question: How long does it take to change one movement value and feel the result in the build?
keywords: tuning iteration parameters prototyping debug tools game feel tuning inertia experiment playtesting feel parameter spreadsheet

principle: Snap to a big lead-in pose on the frame the button is pressed
why: A smooth transition from standby into the windup takes too long. Jumping straight to a big pose tells players at once that their input was recognized, and it cues the opponent to dodge. Network and TV lag can never be fully eliminated, but the game can still acknowledge the input immediately; in Smash, responsiveness comes first.
how_to_apply: Skip easing frames out of standby: make the first frame after input a drastically different windup pose. For charge moves, hold that pose and shake in place while the button is held. Light, spammable moves can have no lead-in at all. If a windup reads as slow, have the character pull directly into the right pose rather than lengthening the ease.
anti_pattern: Interpolating from standby into the windup 'so the animation doesn't skip'; windups whose first frames barely change the silhouette.
example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate: the pose changes drastically on the press of a Smash Attack, then holds and shakes while charging. Zero Suit Samus's neutral attack comes out one frame after input; Final Fight's jab is instantaneous. Sora's Sonic Blade windup felt slow, so Sakurai had him pull directly into the right pose.
review_question: Does the very first frame after an attack press show a pose clearly different from standby?
keywords: lead-in anticipation windup wind-up startup first frame snap pose input acknowledgment responsiveness no easing charge attack

principle: Animate where and when the attack's collision actually is
why: A designer can make any animation connect by placing collision, but a large gap between visuals and collision feels wrong, and if the animation itself is mispositioned it feels even more broken. Attacks that look like they should hit but don't, or that keep hitting after the swing, feel off. Because animation shapes game feel so much, animators can't leave gameplay to the designers.
how_to_apply: Give animators each attack's active frames and hitbox placement, and review attacks with collision displayed. Make the motion cross the median line where opponents stand and stay in the gameplay plane rather than angling toward or away from the camera. When a hit feels wrong, fix the arc or pose and the hitbox shape or timing together. Watch for stance changes on hit that move the target's top node.
anti_pattern: Animating without seeing collision; fixing a misplaced animation by stretching the hitbox; attacks angled toward the camera; a visible swing that outlasts its active frames without a reason.
example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate: Pyra's forward aerial collision was shortened because it seemed to keep hitting after the swing; Mythra's slash was aligned to a diagonal; Steve's grab arc was pulled closer; Sacred Arrow's blade was raised slightly so it wouldn't pass straight through opponents; a neutral-attack combo missed because the target's top node moved back.
review_question: With collision displayed, does every attack's visible strike sit where and when its hitbox is active?
keywords: collision hitbox animation alignment active frames attack range median line gameplay plane hit detection animator responsibility top node root motion

principle: Make the hit stop frame the attack's strongest, clearest pose
why: Hit stop freezes the instant of contact, so that pose is the most memorable; everything hinges on it. On a finishing blow the screen stops completely, so a weak pose there is no good. In games about trading blows, attack animations affect fun more than any others.
how_to_apply: Treat the contact frame as a key pose: include it in reference photos and review it on its own. On sword swings, start collision partway into the swing once the pose is strong, and let hit stop kick in after the blade has swung out a bit. Check the pose on both the left and right of the screen.
anti_pattern: Collision on the first frame of motion, so hit stop freezes a half-formed pose; hit stop before the sword has swung out, which loses the 'hit' feeling.
example: Super Smash Bros.: sword-swing collision doesn't start until the sword is partway through; Pyra's hit pose before and after Sakurai's silhouette correction.
review_question: If you pause on the frame where each attack connects, is it the strongest, most readable pose in the move?
keywords: hit pose contact frame key pose hitstop pose impact frame attack pose freeze frame sword swing collision timing

principle: Exaggerate past "OK": too much is just right
why: Attacks are small things on a small screen, so the usual problem is 'not anywhere near far enough'; if a pose looks OK there's still room to push. Game characters lose much of the information real people give off and no part of them truly exists, so big performances make up for it. Pushing beyond common sense is what gives animation its greatness.
how_to_apply: Push twists, reach and extension past natural limits, until the rig's weighting nearly breaks. Treat motion capture as a starting point and make it bigger. Make a sword swing more than 'just a sword swing'. Scale exaggeration to the character's on-screen size and camera distance.
anti_pattern: Stopping at 'OK'; dropping motion capture straight into the game; keeping poses within what is physically possible.
example: Kazuya's Roundhouse to Triple Spin Kick twists so far it could look like a bug, and Sakurai says they should have gone further; Virtua Fighter's upper and lower body sometimes face opposite directions; Kinji Fukasaku's over-the-top Clock Tower 3 cutscenes.
review_question: For each key animation, did someone try a bigger version, and is the shipped one the biggest that still reads well?
keywords: exaggeration too much is just right push poses motion capture mocap cartoon big performances information loss rig limits

principle: Reach key poses fast; don't let interpolation water them down
why: Animation tools interpolate conveniently, but 'convenience doesn't mean quality': in-between frames overpower the key poses and make an animation feel slow even at the same length. Time saved on in-betweens goes to the lead-in and the strike, and key poses shown for even one frame each still leave an impression when the attack hits.
how_to_apply: Scrub interpolated attacks and cut in-between time so the key poses arrive quickly. Pull the windup further back, hold the anticipation relatively long, then pass through the key poses in as little as one frame each. Give poses more energy than the reference. Judge snappiness by eye in game, not by frame count.
anti_pattern: Accepting default interpolation between reference poses; judging speed only by frame count; mushy in-betweens on fast attacks.
example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate: a kick recreated with straight interpolation felt too slow at 8 frames; the release version is still 8 frames and much snappier. Ryu's crouching heavy punch: forearm pulled back, anticipation held, the original's three key poses on screen one frame each.
review_question: Do your attacks hit their key poses quickly, or do in-between frames make them feel slow?
keywords: interpolation in-betweens key frames key poses snappy timing anticipation hold tweening easing curves slow animation

principle: Make the follow-through big, held and unlike standby
why: The hit is over in a fraction of a second; the follow-through takes the most screen time and shows what the character just did and how heavy it was. It is also the opening when the player can't act, so it must read clearly. The follow-through determines the impact of the attack itself.
how_to_apply: Keep the motion going with big movements that carry the strike's momentum before returning to standby. Hold a pose clearly different from standby. Give it its own trajectory instead of reversing the attack. Give landings a full follow-through, and place follow-throughs where they read from the game's camera.
anti_pattern: Interpolating straight back to idle; a follow-through that looks like standby; letting it fizzle out.
example: Ryu's uppercut follow-through in Smash Ultimate takes a different trajectory from the original's backwards playback; Sora's forward-aerial landing was reworked to follow through fully.
review_question: Does every recovery clearly show what move just happened and how heavy it was, right up to standby?
keywords: follow-through recovery animation end lag vulnerability weight momentum overlap settle return to idle

principle: Make the first damage frame an extreme pain pose
why: Hit stop holds the first frame of the damage animation, so it is what players actually see. A pose that looks nothing like standby makes it clear the character got hit even from far away, and both players feel the impact. 'The more punch, the better.'
how_to_apply: Author the hit-stop frame of each damage animation as an exaggerated, asymmetric pain pose, and segue into it with a quick blend from the pose at impact rather than a snap. Choose high, middle or low reactions by the nearest impact point and small, medium or large by strength, with a separate knockback set. Twist bodies in knockback so arms and legs read. Enter the damage animation immediately, even from special attacks.
anti_pattern: Damage poses close to standby; stiff bodies flying sideways; damage reactions that start late.
example: Super Smash Bros. damage reactions (nine ground types); Kirby's extreme damage pose in the Kirby Super Star design document; a fighter hit by a Final Smash should enter damage immediately; Wolf's damage face retouched for emphasis.
review_question: From the farthest gameplay camera, can you tell at a glance that a character just got hit, and how hard?
keywords: damage animation hit reaction flinch pain pose knockback pose hurt animation reaction set getting hit readability

principle: Pose for a clear, asymmetric silhouette from the game's camera
why: Smash is seen from the side, so profile silhouettes matter more than anything; one minor silhouette tweak can make a huge difference. Symmetric poses and plain sideways bends are dull, while a twist lets arms and legs read. A character's form should be exaggerated even in solid black, and if the basic pose is off nothing else saves it.
how_to_apply: Make all four limbs readable from the game's main view. Break symmetry unless it's deliberately comic. Twist the torso instead of bending it sideways; give torso, hips and legs different lines. Check poses on both sides of the screen and filled in solid black. Correct swing animations until the blade trail reads from the gameplay camera.
anti_pattern: Symmetric, front-facing poses; plain sideways bends; knockback bodies flying flat; horizontal slashes whose trails vanish from the side.
example: Pyra's pose before and after Sakurai's correction; Smash knockback poses twisted so limbs read; Sora's forward aerial, where upper-body twist brings more information to the pose; the Pit figma posed default and adjusted.
review_question: Filled in black and seen from the gameplay camera on both sides of the screen, is every key pose asymmetric and instantly readable?
keywords: silhouette pose posing asymmetry twist S-curve readability profile line of action dynamic pose solid black test

principle: Specify each animation's frames and key poses before animators start
why: Getting animation ideas across to the team is vital, and timings should be chosen with the game's push and pull in mind before animation begins. Four values are often enough for animators to start. A director needs a feel for frames to prepare this data and to catch errors when the build differs.
how_to_apply: Keep an animation list: every animation described in text with its length and when the attack occurs; mark loops like idle and walk 'Loop' or 'Any'. For each attack specify the standby pose, the attack pose, the attack start frame and the total frames until it can be canceled. Add photographed figure poses for key poses and source-game screenshots where relevant. Treat the spec as a first step; animators fill the gaps.
anti_pattern: Leaving timing to animators; describing timing in words; treating the director's spec as the finished animation.
example: Super Smash Bros. fighter spec sheets: an animation list plus photographed figure poses, 70 to 80 pages per fighter on average.
review_question: Does every animation request state its length, its attack start frame and its key poses?
keywords: animation list animation spec frame data timing sheet attack start frame total frames brief reference photos direction

principle: Judge animation in motion, at gameplay size and camera
why: A model can look warped when paused, and 'fixing' it kills the animation's energy. Motion that works up close feels far too understated when the character is small or far away. Faces in Smash are often too small to make out, and blade trails can nearly vanish from the side.
how_to_apply: Review attacks at full speed, at real in-game size and from the gameplay camera. Turn down corrections for distortions that only show in freeze-frames if the move reads in motion. For detailed checks use slow motion, hidden backgrounds and dev-mode transparency for capes and clothing.
anti_pattern: Approving animation in a close-up model viewer; correcting freeze-frame warps; judging faces at a size players never see.
example: Kazuya's twist looks like a bug when paused but reads well in motion; Smash Ultimate's developer mode can make capes translucent to check poses; slow-motion effect reference with backgrounds disabled.
review_question: Was this animation approved while playing at gameplay camera distance, or only in a paused close-up?
keywords: animation review in-game size camera distance freeze frame playback speed dev tools transparency slow motion review

principle: Keep blends short; use them for cancels, segues and directional poses
why: Blending lets the same follow-up animation start naturally from very different poses, but making animation too smooth reduces rhythm and impact, and automatic blends can distort the pose.
how_to_apply: When a cancel arrives, blend from the current pose into the new animation. Segue into damage poses with a quick blend (about four frames in Smash). Keep blend durations short and check them for distortion. Blend a fixed center stance with poses around a circle for directional moves. In full 3D, layer upper and lower body, place feet on terrain and let slopes affect turns.
anti_pattern: Long, smooth blends that sap rhythm; trusting automatic blends unchecked; snapping between unrelated poses on cancels.
example: Super Smash Bros.: idle-to-walk and attack-to-walk both look natural with the same walk; shield shifting blends circular movement with the center stance. Sakurai notes blending matters less in fast Smash than in fully 3D games.
review_question: Are your blends short enough to keep rhythm and free of distorted in-between poses?
keywords: animation blending crossfade transition cancel blend blend duration layered animation foot placement directional blend

principle: Squash and stretch while keeping volume constant
why: Rotation and translation are everywhere, but scaling is often overlooked; with it a bouncing ball feels almost touchable, and squash and stretch gives objects texture and life. Keeping mass roughly constant is what sells it: 3D Kirby squashed only vertically lost his physical presence.
how_to_apply: Add squash to landings, crouches and bounces and compare with and without. When squashing on one axis, widen the others. On 3D models, sculpt the squashed shape (an oval-track profile, a blend shape) instead of scaling one axis. Use shape animation for cartoon squeezes a skeleton can't do.
anti_pattern: Squashing vertically without widening ('your oval will end up dull'); treating rotation and translation as the whole toolkit.
example: Kirby has squashed on crouches and landings since the Game Boy; Sakurai's Daily Report asked for side volume on the 3D model; Tom and Jerry-style squeezing might need shape animation in CG.
review_question: Where landings, crouches and impacts squash, does the volume stay about the same?
keywords: squash and stretch scaling volume preservation mass bounce landing crouch blend shapes shape animation

principle: Move bodies like bodies: two axes, linked joints, bent wrists
why: A head turned on one axis looks mechanical and a one-axis wrist twist looks like a drill. Connected parts move together in reality. Wrists that follow a straight line from the arm look limp, and a perpendicular grip on a swung object makes a character look like an action figure.
how_to_apply: Layer a dip (X) or tilt (Z) onto every Y-axis turn of heads, wrists and torsos. Move the shoulder and collarbone with a twisting wrist. Bend wrists rather than keeping them in line with the arm. Pose anything swung with the forearm in a diagonal grip. Plan head turns with the eye line, and reduce the head turn once the eyes carry part of the look.
anti_pattern: Single-axis organic rotation; straight wrists; perpendicular grips on swords and bats; full head turns animated before the eyes exist.
example: Sakurai's own head turn; revving a motorcycle (shoulder and collarbone move with the wrist); Sora's losing clap, limp until the wrists bent; diagonal versus perpendicular weapon grips.
review_question: Does any organic motion rotate on a single axis or move a joint without the joints connected to it?
keywords: two-axis rotation head turn wrist twist joints collarbone shoulder grip fingers diagonal grip organic motion eye line

principle: Give mechanical motion personality: off-center pivots, wobble and recoil
why: Designers tend to move things in straight lines and smooth circles, but animation means putting a soul into something unmoving, and software defaults look bland. A slightly shifted rotation axis feels a little erratic and organic, a wobble makes a straight shot fun to watch, and recoil makes firing feel forceful.
how_to_apply: Move the pivot of thrown or spinning objects and swung weapons slightly off the geometric center or grip. Layer a small looping offset onto straight-flying projectiles. Snap guns or cannons back on each shot. Hand-tune rotation timing (offset the two axes, add an occasional counter-motion) instead of trusting generated curves. Make quick mock-ups during review to show the alternative.
anti_pattern: Straight-line moves and center-point rotations left as the software produced them.
example: Kirby's Shotzo 'wobbly cannonballs' (a six-frame offset loop); Smash Ultimate's bomb throw spins on an off-center axis; Pyra's Blazing End axis was moved off the sword's grip; Star Force's side cannons pull back with each missile.
review_question: Which moving objects still follow straight lines or spin on their exact center, and what would give each one personality?
keywords: pivot center of rotation off-center axis wobble projectile motion recoil function curves software defaults personality secondary motion

principle: Build rigs that allow exaggeration from the start
why: Rigs that lock arms to the torso make adequate animation impossible. Joints are naturally limited to 180 degrees, but bending past straight adds oomph; backward-bending joints make IK flip, and fixes like extra joints cost processing and need cartoon-minded animators. Convenient tools also set mental limits.
how_to_apply: Decide early whether the style needs exaggeration. Rig shoulders to move forward and back and the upper and lower body to rotate independently. Budget extra joints or an extended skeleton for limbs that bend past straight, watch for IK flipping, and hire or brief animators with cartoon sensibilities. Where processing is tight, lock finger joints and swap preset finger patterns.
anti_pattern: Letting a standard rig decide what poses are possible; adding exaggeration needs late, when the rig can't support it.
example: The first Smash (or Dragon King prototype) had arms rigged directly to the torso; Sakurai proposed past-straight joints at the start of Smash development, but processing load and staffing left it unsolved.
review_question: Can your rig hit the most exaggerated pose your style calls for, and was that decided before animation began?
keywords: rig rigging skeleton joints IK FK range of motion exaggeration extra joints processing load fingers

principle: Keep faces toward the viewer in side-view games
why: Without mirroring, the character on the right faces away, so you can't see their expression and get little information. Pure profile views aren't fun to look at and hide the face for half the movement. Non-realistic tricks like moving the mouth to the side of a profile face can express a character better than anatomy.
how_to_apply: Mirror the animation set when a character changes facing instead of turning the model around. Angle runs and similar moves diagonally toward the camera. Plan for flipped handedness and quick item hand-swaps; skip mirroring for asymmetric characters such as sword fighters. Make emblems and lettering mirror-safe. Try placing the mouth on the side of the face in profile.
anti_pattern: Expressive characters showing the back of their head on one side; runs in pure profile; rejecting a technique only because it isn't realistic.
example: Smash Bros. adopted flipped animation after Brawl; Kirby's run angles toward the camera; Street Fighter II mirrored sprites and IV kept it; Mega Man Legends and Sonic put the mouth on the side of the face.
review_question: Can players see the face of every expressive character from both sides of the screen?
keywords: flipped animation mirroring facing side view face visibility handedness profile mouth manga conventions

principle: Push facial expressions a step past done, shaped by anatomy
why: CG loses information, so 'too much is about right' for realistic and cartoony faces alike; most artwork Sakurai received had expression shifts that were too small. Details tied to anatomy sell an expression. Where the source has no facial range, putting the source first matters more than adding faces.
how_to_apply: Once an expression feels done, make it one step bigger and judge it at in-game size. Show eye white above and below the iris on wide eyes, offset upper and lower teeth, and size mouth shapes to the jaw. Retouch key expressions before modeling. If the character only blinks in the source, carry emotion through body movement.
anti_pattern: Subtle expressions on small on-screen faces; inventing faces the source character lacks.
example: Smash Ultimate: Wolf's damage face retouched to suit a wolf's jaw; Kazuya's brows pulled up to look angrier; Steve only blinks, so his movement does the work; a Sora costume's damage expression was too weak.
review_question: At the size players see them, do faces read clearly, and do they stay true to the source?
keywords: facial animation expressions faces exaggeration eye whites teeth jaw retouch expression strength

principle: Give movement weight, and give fast motions enough frames to register
why: Motions that are too fast don't land: Kazuya's wings retracting in two frames had no impact. Normal legs can't keep up with very fast movement. Weight shifts and solid landings make movement believable, and slipping feet read as wrong.
how_to_apply: Add frames to secondary motions that vanish before they register. For speeds a walk cycle can't support, use bounding or sliding locomotion. Shift weight forward in walks to improve weight and silhouette. Keep feet planted on landing. Add squash on landings.
anti_pattern: Sped-up realistic leg cycles; secondary motion too quick to see; sliding feet.
example: Kid Icarus: Uprising's Pit bounds and slides because normal legs couldn't keep up; Kazuya's wing retraction got more frames; Pyra's walk shifts her weight forward; Sora's landing foot moved too far.
review_question: Is any motion so fast it never registers, or so smooth it has no weight?
keywords: locomotion walk run cycle weight landing foot sliding secondary motion frames wings bounding

principle: Honor the source's feeling, not its literal frames
why: 2D poses don't survive a literal move to 3D, and copying a source exactly can miss what makes it feel right. Sakurai's rule is to honor the feeling and do what works best, keeping signature poses and limits where the source has them.
how_to_apply: Keep a source character's signature poses and quirks, but change what the new medium needs: a different first frame for momentum, a new follow-through path instead of reverse playback. Put source screenshots next to your version and compare feel, not just shapes. Keep source limitations (a face that only blinks) and compensate elsewhere.
anti_pattern: Playing source poses forward then backward in 3D; matching a reference exactly but missing the character.
example: Ryu's uppercut in Smash Ultimate; Kazuya's spin kick twist and knocked-down pose kept from his original game; Steve's blink-only face; the Nakoruru Mii costume revised until it felt like her.
review_question: Does each adapted move feel like its source in play, even where the frames differ?
keywords: source material faithfulness adaptation 2D to 3D guest characters licensed characters signature moves honor the original

principle: Check every variant: ground and air, every direction, both facings
why: Variants drift apart: Sora's Sonic Blade had drastically different ground and aerial poses and lost reach when aimed upward, which counts as a bug. Poses look different on the left of the screen than the right, and a stance change on hit can push a target out of a combo.
how_to_apply: Play ground and aerial versions of every special side by side, comparing poses and reach. Test attacks aimed in each direction. Review poses on both screen sides. Run multi-hit strings against every reaction stance.
anti_pattern: Reviewing only the default version of a move; assuming mirrored or aerial variants inherit correctness.
example: Smash Ultimate: Sora's Sonic Blade fixed for pose mismatch and upward reach; a neutral-attack combo that missed because of a stance change.
review_question: Has every move been checked in its ground, aerial, directional and mirrored versions?
keywords: animation QA variants ground aerial versions directions mirrored poses stance combos consistency

principle: Find and communicate poses with a physical figure
why: Handling a physical figure teaches what makes a pose cool and which angle works best; there's no formula for posing. A posed, photographed figure communicates key poses to animators more clearly than words, and showing beats telling in feedback.
how_to_apply: Keep a posable figure at your desk and practice posing it, including zooming it around ('bundodo'). For specs, pose it, photograph it, cut out the silhouette and raise the contrast. In reviews, show a posed figure or a retouched frame rather than describing the change.
anti_pattern: Describing poses only in text; polishing details while the base pose is off.
example: Sakurai's Pit figma; Smash spec sheets with photographed figure poses; Sora's forward aerial explained with a posed figure.
review_question: When you ask for a pose change, do you show the pose instead of describing it?
keywords: posing action figure figma reference photos bundodo pose reference feedback visual direction

principle: Make everything players must read stand out from decoration
why: In an action game players must always know where solid ground, opponents and threats are, and a perspective 3D view makes collision hard to recognize. Elaborate backdrops easily steal attention; his standing note to stage artists is that the backdrop is outshining the terrain. He still wants the stage to look good, because visuals sell the game, so gameplay gets the slight edge rather than total victory.
how_to_apply: Highlight every collision surface in a debug view and check it reads at a glance in the normal view. Push non-colliding scenery back with aerial perspective and weaker contrast, then repair the overall look. Check that platforms, projectiles, costumes and fighters in shadow or vignetting stay visible, and that the floor doesn't overpower projectiles. Desaturate screenshots to see what actually stands out. Give dangerous attacks a visual tell players can react to.
anti_pattern: A backdrop that outshines the terrain. Drop-through platforms, costumes or fighters that vanish into dark or busy scenes. Fixing readability only by fogging out the background until the stage looks bad.
