example: Smash stage reviews with collision marked in red; Mishima Dojo fighters in shadow checked with a desaturated image; Hollow Bastion's floor toned down so Greninja's Water Shuriken stays visible; the P8 Enderman costume pitched as a game of 'find the Enderman'; Punch-Out!!'s yellow eyes as a dodge cue.
review_question: In a grayscale screenshot of a busy moment, are terrain, characters, platforms and projectiles the most prominent things on screen?
keywords: readability clarity legibility terrain collision backdrop background foreground contrast aerial-perspective visibility platforms projectiles telegraph tells

principle: Keep characters visible inside their own effects
why: Effects are needed for impact, but characters easily get lost in a sea of them. In 2D you can draw characters above effects; in 3D, forcing characters to draw on top creates depth disparity and looks wrong, and lowering the effect's priority instead can leave you seeing only terrain. So the fix has to live in the shape of the effect itself.
how_to_apply: Review each big effect with the character inside it at gameplay camera angles. Leave gaps around the body. Make the parts of a surrounding effect that sit between camera and character lower than the parts behind it. Add an outline to character models. Cut layered effects or background atmosphere that bury fighters, and make scattering elements like hit stars fly far enough not to hide behind bodies.
anti_pattern: Forcing 3D characters to render on top of effects. Lowering hit-mark draw priority until terrain hides them. Layered throw effects or super-move backdrops that hide the fighters.
example: Terry stays clear inside Power Dunk's crown effect; Falcon Punch keeps Captain Falcon partly visible; the inner peaks of Chrom's Up Special differ in height seen from front and back; Sora's down-throw effects were thinned because they hid the fighters.
review_question: Pause on the biggest effect each character makes: can you still see the character's pose?
keywords: effects occlusion draw-priority display-priority outline characters visibility buried sea-of-effects vfx aura

principle: Never let color alone carry gameplay meaning
why: If a game is built mainly around color, players with color blindness can't play it, because certain hues look alike to them. The same problem hits power-ups and interactive stage objects in any genre, not just puzzle games. He treated this as essential before he could call Meteos complete.
how_to_apply: Run screenshots of every color-coded element through a color-blindness simulation filter (Photoshop includes one). Where hues merge, separate them by brightness, not just hue, without making them so dark they vanish into the background. Also check whole screens in black and white. Keep each screen to one dominant color theme rather than a mishmash.
anti_pattern: Puzzle pieces, pickups or team markers told apart by hue only. Darkening pieces until they disappear against the background. A jumble of competing colors on one screen.
example: Meteos blocks checked with a protanopia filter and redesigned with significant brightness differences while staying visible on each planet's background.
review_question: Through a color-blindness filter and in grayscale, can every gameplay-critical element still be told apart?
keywords: color-blindness colorblind accessibility protanopia deuteranopia brightness value hue color-coding grayscale black-and-white

principle: Give every character a silhouette that reads even in solid black
why: Of the ways he knows to make an imaginary character look cool, the silhouette is the one he stresses most. Characters are often small on screen and seen from one main angle, so an ambiguous outline, or one that resembles another character, fails. Exaggerated shapes are also what establish a character, as with Nakoruru's hair and ribbon or Sonic's big head and skinny limbs.
how_to_apply: Fill each character and key pose in solid black and compare the whole cast side by side. Exaggerate signature features (hair, ribbons, gloves, head size, limb thickness). Check key poses from the game's main viewpoint, with all four limbs readable and on both sides of the screen. Brighten extremities such as hands, feet or socks so movement reads. Sharpen shapes that have gone soft.
anti_pattern: Realistic proportions that blur together at game size. Two characters with near-identical outlines. Symmetric, front-facing poses that hide the limbs.
example: Nakoruru's emphasized hair, ribbon, gloves and legs; Sonic's head and limbs; the Mii maid outfit's socks colored white so movement reads; Devil Kazuya's too-rounded wing silhouette sharpened; Sora's back jump given a more energetic silhouette.
review_question: Filled in solid black, is each character's form exaggerated, readable and impossible to confuse with anyone else?
keywords: silhouette shape-language character-design readability outline exaggeration solid-black extremities poses distinct cast

principle: Give effects contrast with crisp shapes and dark accents, not glow alone
why: Additive blending adds an element's colors to the background, pushing it toward white. Layering it gives decent results from simple visuals, 'but that's it': the effect lacks impact and contrast, can be too bright, and vanishes on light backgrounds. Keeping the whole game dark to show effects off still falls short. Opposing elements make any image stand out, like straight lines in a curvy design.
how_to_apply: Build each effect around solid polygons or simple images as the focal point, with additive glow as support. Mix dark elements (black accents, a dark backdrop behind a hit mark) into bright effects. Test every effect on your brightest and darkest backgrounds. When processing is tight, mixing white and black pixels makes an effect show on any color.
anti_pattern: Effects made only of bright additive layers. Darkening the whole game so effects show. Low-contrast effects that disappear on white or bright stages.
example: Smash Ultimate builds all its effects around crisp shapes for a clean, anime-style look; Sora's Blizzaga got dark elements because it vanished on bright stages; Kirby's Dream Land's inhale effect mixed white and black pixels.
review_question: On the game's brightest background, does every effect still pop with a clear shape and contrast?
keywords: vfx effects additive-blending contrast pop dark-elements black crisp shapes polygons anime glow bright-background

principle: Fit each hit mark to its hit: size, place, layers and duration
why: Hit marks exist for clear visual feedback and fun, so they should be flashy in proportion to the impact. They must appear where the attack and target hitboxes actually met or they look wrong, which a pulled-back camera with large hitboxes makes tricky. Quick repeated hits need short marks, and even big ones should resolve fairly quickly. Hitstop gives the mark extra time to animate.
how_to_apply: Scale size and flashiness by attack strength. Spawn the mark at the real contact point and check placement in game. Layer a main flash, a shockwave behind the target, an upward spray and material extras such as sparks for machines, without clutter. Keep durations short, shortest for rapid hits. Let the mark keep animating during hitstop while the characters freeze. Adapt any borrowed effect to your own camera distance and hit frequency.
anti_pattern: One generic spark for every hit. Marks floating where nothing connected. Lingering effects that pile up. Cartoony marks pasted unchanged onto realistic subjects. Copying a lavish effect from a game with different hardware, camera distance or hit rates.
example: Smash Ultimate's hit marks with shockwaves, upward sprays, sparks on mechanical opponents and dark backdrops; the hitstop effect that shows the flight path the hit player can slightly adjust; Sora's hit stars sent flying farther so they don't vanish behind Donkey Kong.
review_question: Does each hit mark's size and length match the hit, appear exactly where it connected, and clear before the next hit?
keywords: hit-marks hit-effects hit-sparks impact feedback contact-point hitbox hitstop layering duration vfx combat

principle: Flash for impact and status, with internal contrast and fixed color meanings
why: A full-screen flash adds impact the way screen shake does, because it covers a large area; a character flash emphasizes a change in that character's status, and he calls both crucial. Adding white or one color evenly lowers contrast, since the same amount goes onto dark and light areas and they average out, and a white flash makes the character vanish on light backgrounds.
how_to_apply: Add shadows or dark elements into hit flashes so the character keeps internal contrast. Give each status one flash color or treatment and keep it consistent. Use rim lighting to signal states like invulnerability. Scale flash strength with camera distance so close-ups don't flash most of the screen. Keep flashes to a single brief moment and full-screen flashes mild. Check them on real LCDs, whose response time changes how they look.
anti_pattern: Flashing a character pure white. One flash color meaning several things. Full-strength flashing when the camera is zoomed in.
example: Smash Ultimate's shadowed hit flash, built from a mockup Sakurai drew; white flash for invulnerability while getting up; yellow flash for the window after a throw when the character can't be grabbed again; rim lighting for damage types; Kirby's Adventure freezing and flashing the screen when a boss falls.
review_question: Can a player name what each character flash means, and does a flashing character stay readable on a light background?
keywords: flash flashing hit-flash white-flash screen-flash status invulnerability rim-lighting internal-contrast boss-stop photosensitivity

principle: Treat effects as essential and study them frame by frame
why: Effects pack a great deal of information into an instant, so they fly by unnoticed at full speed, yet remove them and the game looks plain. The same game can feel quite different with different effects. Careful observation is a shortcut to building them well.
how_to_apply: Add debug slow motion, a background-off toggle and on/off toggles for each display element. Record your effects and reference games' effects and step through them to see shapes, timing and layering. A/B a key scene with effects off. Give swings, punches and kicks trails or blur. Add celebratory flourishes aimed at the player who scored.
anti_pattern: Skimping on effects because they're only on screen for an instant. Judging effects only at full speed.
example: His long montage of Smash Ultimate effects in slow motion with backgrounds disabled; blade trails, without which attacks lack oomph; confetti in Ultimate's KO explosion praising the player who landed the KO.
review_question: With effects turned off, does the scene look noticeably plainer? If not, are your effects doing enough?
keywords: effects vfx slow-motion frame-by-frame study reference debug background-off juice polish celebration confetti

principle: Let each character's look express its essence and its mechanics
why: Characters must be well established, and that takes everyone assigned to one understanding its core essence and drawing it out further; it can't be done by one person. Each character should be describable in a word or two. Visual details are where that identity, and the rules behind it, become visible to the player.
how_to_apply: Write a short core-essence statement per character and share it with everyone on that character. Make effects and trails carry the move's character: an emphasized edge where a sword's tip is stronger, a frenzied trail for a heavy blade, no fade-out for a blade that emits light. Show state changes on the character's body. Let poses express personality. Where a system has hidden rules, consider an effect that shows them.
anti_pattern: A generic trail or effect shared by every character. A design that matches the reference but misses who the character is. Identity left to the planner alone.
example: Marth's tip-emphasized trail, Ike's frenzied trail, Travis's unfading beam katana; the hitstop effect that shows the knockback path a hit player can adjust; Kirby drawn slightly plumper and recolored when he holds a copy ability; copy hats that boosted Kirby's appeal.
review_question: Could a player guess what this character is about, and what its moves do best, from its look and effects alone?
keywords: character-design identity core-essence personality expression mechanics visual-language trails status cast strengths

principle: Prefer expressive exaggeration over literal realism
why: Game characters lose much of the information real people convey, and nothing in them truly exists, so 'too much' is 'just right'. Manga and anime conventions often express a character better than realism, and can even be cheaper to produce. You can't fix what you don't notice, so question inherited conventions.
how_to_apply: Exaggerate signature features and expressions past where they feel done, judged at in-game size. Try manga conventions such as a mouth on the side of the face in profile, animated by swapping cels. Use shape animation for squash and stretch through gaps. Review models at the angles players see, and question default anatomy that reads less expressively.
anti_pattern: Rejecting a technique only because it isn't realistic. Keeping an inherited modeling convention without asking whether it reads.
example: Mega Man Legends' profile mouths; Sonic's side-of-face mouth; Kirby's and Jigglypuff's Smash mouths remodeled for a more expressive profile; Wolf's damage face pushed to suit his jaw.
review_question: Where did we choose realism by default, and would an exaggerated or manga-style version read better at game size?
keywords: exaggeration stylization manga anime cartoon expression realism profile mouth squash-stretch too-much-is-just-right

principle: Size characters and targets for the screen they're played on
why: A screen covers only about 30 degrees of the player's vision, so a target of realistic size can be a speck. Tiny targets on a big screen lack impact as entertainment, and on a handheld they make players stare at a small area. Big targets also forgive beginners' slightly off-target attacks.
how_to_apply: Decide how much of the screen gameplay and targets should occupy before fixing camera and field of view. Scale enemies up if they look tiny. Make bosses in beginner games big enough that slightly off-target attacks still hit. When characters are small on screen, push their exaggeration and carry their appeal elsewhere, such as HUD portraits.
anti_pattern: Choosing a camera for realism that leaves little room for play. Pinpoint distant targets on a handheld.
example: Kid Icarus: Uprising's standard enemies at four or five times Pit's size; Whispy Woods made big for Kirby's newcomers; Smash HUD portraits because fighters are often small.
review_question: On the real target screen, are the things players must hit and watch big enough to read and to feel?
keywords: screen-size scale enemy-size field-of-view fov handheld targets impact beginners on-screen-size

principle: Unify mixed art styles around one visual concept
why: Artists on one team must produce the same visual style whatever their specialty, and characters imported as-is from different sources look like 'a fight between live action and animation'. The more advanced the visuals, the more unifying style costs, but it's a necessary step.
how_to_apply: Before production, have your strongest artist make a few image boards (world, scenery, characters, items) and build every model and the lighting from them. When mixing styles, meet in the middle: slightly desaturate pure primaries and make them respond to light, add material texture to flat cartoon characters and ease texture on realistic ones, tweak proportions where matchups look silly, give everyone the same refinement pass, and ground stylized features in how they'd work if the character really existed. Apply the same check to animation, effects and audio. Vet a new technique before adopting it mid-project.
anti_pattern: Each artist working in a personal style. Official designs imported unchanged. A trendy technique adopted mid-project that the staff don't know and the game doesn't suit.
example: Mario's denim overalls; Bayonetta's adjusted proportions; R.O.B.'s added detail; Donkey Kong's and Yoshi's eyelids closing instead of comic pupils; Meta Knight's mask reshaped to sit beside realistic fighters; Kirby Super Star's mid-project CG backgrounds, which didn't fit.
review_question: Lined up in one frame, do all characters and assets look like they belong to the same game?
keywords: art-direction style-unification consistency image-boards concept-art crossover mixed-styles cohesion live-action-and-animation

principle: Draw the light an asset reflects, not just the asset
why: Everything we see is light reflected into our eyes; it isn't as simple as seeing a red thing as red. A tree with a brown trunk and green leaves isn't finished, even if lighting is someone else's job. Cheap lighting techniques also let you fit more objects on screen than heavy per-object shaders would.
how_to_apply: Make lighting part of an asset's definition of done. Light groups of repeated assets with colored light, brighten the spots that would catch more light, vary hue slightly across copies, and add atmosphere that does more than flat fog. Enrich flat backgrounds with contrast and hue-shifted light. Let stylized colors respond to scene lighting. Check that character lighting on each stage isn't too dark.
anti_pattern: Calling an asset done with base colors only. Copy-pasted assets with identical color. Flat, evenly lit backgrounds. Bright primaries that look the same under any light.
example: The cut-and-pasted forest improved with colored light, sprayed highlights, hue variation and atmosphere; the Spirits cave retouch with a hue-shifted reflective glow; Hollow Bastion's character lighting brightened.
review_question: Can you tell where the light in this scene comes from and what color it is?
keywords: lighting light color hue-variation atmosphere backgrounds environment-art shading definition-of-done colored-light

principle: Judge visuals on the final composited frame at gameplay distance
why: Drawing each material's texture on its own won't create cohesive visuals. On modern hardware the post-processed frame, with blended hues and reflections, decides quality more than any single model: what matters is how everything comes together. Many problems, such as even spacing, square outlines, mismatched proportions or wrong scale, only show in the whole frame or from the gameplay camera.
how_to_apply: Approve art in the game with all post-processing on, not in a model viewer. Review scale and lighting on full screenshots. Check assets both up close and from the gameplay camera. Line up mixed characters in game rather than against their source art. Step back from details regularly. On high-end projects, give one person responsibility for post-processing and final output.
anti_pattern: Polishing props in isolation. Approving assets one at a time. Getting lost in minor details.
example: The same stage in Melee (each object its own distinct color) and Ultimate (blended hues, reflections off the water); the Mishima Dojo wall that only looked square and evenly spaced from far away; Bayonetta looks odd beside her original art but right in the game.
review_question: Was this asset approved in the final frame, at the distance and lighting players will see it?
keywords: final-output post-processing compositing framebuffer whole-image cohesion review gameplay-distance big-picture

principle: Spend detail where players actually look
why: Console hardware is weaker than people think, so you must separate major elements from minor ones. Players mostly watch the center of the screen and the playable surface, and how much an environment means depends on how closely the gameplay makes them scrutinize it. A bit of playfulness is fine if deadlines and performance hold, but detail nobody will see is waste.
how_to_apply: Rank assets by how much they're seen: the area in front of the camera and the stage surface first, off-screen foundations last. Budget each model by its on-screen size, raised for models also shown up close elsewhere. Put environment detail where cautious play makes players look, and where the camera actually reveals background. Build LOD only when the gain is worth the labor. Build stage art for the worst-case load.
anti_pattern: Turning car tires deep in a backdrop. Over-investing in elements that are tiny on screen. Detail spread evenly regardless of attention.
example: Smash skyspheres detailed in front of the camera; the Inkling stage's turning backdrop tires toned down; Dark Souls' frequent deaths making players scrutinize every nook, versus the same art at Sonic's speed; Ultimate's stages built to hold 60 fps with eight fighters.
review_question: Is the most detail where the player's eyes actually spend time during play?
keywords: budget optimization lod detail-allocation major-minor performance screen-center environment-art presence

principle: Raise graphics and gameplay together, because graphics multiply fun
why: Environments are massless mirages until gameplay gives them presence: a game where you die often makes players scrutinize every corner. In the other direction, on crowded storefronts a banner decides whether anyone looks at your game, so visuals that don't draw players in mean nobody plays. Calling visuals irrelevant to gameplay won't matter if nobody buys the game.
how_to_apply: Build environment art alongside the mechanics and match its density to how closely play makes players look. Treat storefront banners and key art as critical. When readability and beauty conflict, keep both and give gameplay the slight edge.
anti_pattern: Writing graphics off as irrelevant to fun. Finishing art in isolation from how the game is played.
example: Dark Souls and Sekiro versus the same graphics at Sonic's speed; Steam banners; Smash Ultimate's roughly 115 base stages recreating the worlds of dozens of games.
review_question: Would a player scrolling a storefront stop on our key art, and does our gameplay make players look at the art we spent the most on?
keywords: graphics fun presence key-art banner storefront marketing appeal environment gameplay

principle: Direct art by showing, and approve whatever meets the goal
why: Palette, contrast, mood and shape are hard to put into words, and showing communicates more clearly than telling, especially over email. A retouch takes him about five minutes, ten at most, which beats explaining. But a retouch is direction, not final art, and his goal isn't to make everything match his own ideals.
how_to_apply: Send a quick paintover, retouched screenshot, mouse sketch, posed figure or density reference beside the original, with one line on what to change and why. Make notes concrete: which axis, which spacing, which repetition. Flag tiny flaws the moment you see them. State each asset's core goal in one sentence and approve anything that meets it. If several rounds don't converge, ship it and move on. Keep physical models of the characters for artists.
anti_pattern: Long text descriptions of visual changes. The director retouching everything. Swinging direction back and forth each round. Rejecting good work because it differs from your mental image.
example: The Spirits cave retouch (duplicate the layer, boost contrast, shift hue, erase where light hits, harmonize); the Mishima Dojo wall feedback; the hit-flash mockup; a figure posed to show Sora's forward aerial; the flame density reference for Pyra.
review_question: Does every piece of visual feedback include an image, and does each asset have a one-line goal to approve against?
keywords: art-direction supervision feedback retouch paintover mockup reference-image sketch figure review approval iteration

principle: Stage explosions as flash, blast and smoke, then let them finish
why: Spitting out a single blast of fire is tempting but flat. An instant flash tells players something intense just happened, the crisp blast is the key part, and smoke plus a natural conclusion show where it happened. For pure gameplay, clearing the smoke instantly would be better, but a shorter explosion lacks impact, so the damage window is kept short while the visuals run their course.
how_to_apply: Open with an instant flash whose light rays reach well past the blast radius, mixed with black elements, plus a shockwave and a flare. Follow with a crisp roar of flames from the center with sparks. Keep the hitbox active for only part of the blast. Let black smoke take over as the flames wane, and end with flickering sparkles. Add a screen flash or shake only where it suits that explosion. Make ground variants whose blast spreads upward and whose shockwave follows the floor.
anti_pattern: One fire sprite for the whole explosion. A pure white flash that disappears on white backgrounds. Cutting the explosion short. A hitbox that lasts as long as the visuals.
example: Star Force's five-frame explosion (flash to smoke to gone); Smash's standard explosion; Young Link's bomb on the ground; extra smoke added so Sora's Final Smash explosion reads; slight gusts of wind around Smash explosions.
review_question: Does each explosion have a distinct flash, blast, smoke and ending, with a hit window shorter than the visual?
keywords: explosion explosions flash blast smoke shockwave flare sparks phases vfx bombs screen-flash ground-variant

principle: Sell scale through materials, saturation, atmosphere and density, not shape
why: A huge object and its plastic model share shape and color, and CG objects naturally look like scale models: more saturated, glossier, less affected by ambient light, flatter in material. Big things looking small is the usual failure. Shallow depth of field and high saturation are exactly the tricks that make photos look miniature. Effects suffer the same way: a big flame without density reads as a candle.
how_to_apply: Fix materials before shape: enlarge texture loops and painted detail, lower saturation on realistic assets, shrink gloss area and strength, match normal-map detail to real size, add dirt and mixed hues to big mechanical or monotone surfaces. Lower saturation and add haze with distance, so the nearest objects are the most saturated. Avoid depth-of-field blur. Give large effects more loops or smaller particles. Use placement and surroundings to establish size.
anti_pattern: Small texture loops, oversaturated or glossy large objects, normal maps at the wrong scale. Full saturation on distant giants. Big flames built from a few large shapes.
example: Off-color tile spots and grass hue variation that betray a small object; the miniature photo trick (blur top and bottom, raise saturation, cut blue); Pyra's sword flames given a density reference because they looked like a candle.
review_question: Viewed in-scene from gameplay distance, does each large object or effect read as huge, or as a toy?
keywords: scale sense-of-scale miniature saturation gloss specular texture-loop normal-map aerial-perspective haze depth-of-field density

principle: Honor the source's feeling instead of copying it literally
why: An exact copy of one reference can match and still feel wrong, because what fans love is a feeling. He wants to 'honor the feeling and do what works best', which sometimes means moving closer to the original and sometimes mixing in newer details. In licensed work, faithfulness and satisfying fans' love come first.
how_to_apply: Get original production material and put source screenshots next to your version. Compare palette, saturation, relative brightness of costume parts, eye shape and signature poses. Combine the classic design with selected newer details. Stay close where the source shows a lot and invent where it shows little. Don't invent facial range the source lacks; carry emotion through movement instead. Get the rights holder's permission for changes.
anti_pattern: Matching one source version exactly but missing the character. Freely rewriting an established character. Inventing expressions that contradict the source.
example: The Mii Nakoruru costume revised from a literal KOF XIV match; Kazuya's knockdown pose and Final Smash moved toward his original game; CG shots pushed toward FFVII: Advent Children, starting by lowering saturation; Steve's only facial animation is a blink; Game & Watch LCD patterns used as reference.
review_question: Next to the original, does our version feel like the character fans remember, even where details differ?
keywords: faithfulness source-material adaptation licensed fan-service reference original crossover authenticity homage

principle: Protect players' eyes: cap glare, flashing, blur and depth of field
why: Bright glowing elements are hard on the eyes, regulations now keep flashing mild, too much blur makes it hard to tell what's going on, and trying to focus on something blurry can be physically uncomfortable. The more natural a blur, the less discomfort. Inertia-heavy camera motion makes some players sick.
how_to_apply: Raise contrast on glowing areas like magma but cap their brightness. Keep full-screen flashes brief and mild, scaled down when the camera is close. Use pre-drawn blur textures on spinning parts, keep artificial blur subtle and offer a strength option. Remove depth of field and focus pulls except where truly needed. Offer toggles for camera embellishments such as footstep shake.
anti_pattern: Searing magma or full-screen strobing. Heavy motion blur that hides the action. Depth of field everywhere as cheap atmosphere.
example: World of Light's magma kept from getting too bright; a focus shift removed from Sora's fighter reveal; the Spirit Train stage's built-in wheel and rail blur; the spinning blur he regrets leaving off Kirby Air Ride's Wheel.
review_question: After an hour of play, is anything on screen glaring, strobing, fuzzy or nauseating, and can players turn it down?
keywords: eye-strain comfort accessibility photosensitivity flashing glare motion-blur depth-of-field dof motion-sickness options

principle: Check color on matched screens and on the displays players use
why: Each monitor shows color differently, even the same model from the same maker, and room lighting changes perception; for artists and supervisors any variance is fatal. Games end up on ordinary TVs, so calibration devices only go so far. Older games were made for CRTs, whose glow and dithering look different on today's panels.
how_to_apply: Set up one shared reference screen everyone can see and calibrate monitors by eye against it. Retire monitors that crush shadows or flatten contrast. Light art areas neutrally. Check flashes and dark scenes on real LCD TVs. When porting or imitating retro art, judge it as it looked on a CRT.
anti_pattern: Assuming everyone sees the same colors. Moody tinted office lighting. Approving art on a monitor that hides shadows.
example: The Mewtwo image on two monitors, one losing the right-hand shadow; an office lit in yellow whose art came out bluish; checkered pixel patterns that read differently on a CRT.
review_question: Was this art approved on the team reference screen and checked on an ordinary TV?
keywords: color-calibration monitors color-disparity lighting reference-screen tv crt display lcd art-review

principle: Make imaginary objects feel real through weight, light, use, placement and air
why: To a creator a game world is a massless mirage; players feel it as real only because visuals, audio, programming and parameters work together, which he calls 'expression'. A regular table and a miniature have the same shape; presentation and arrangement decide which one you see. Imitating reality also packs in information: floors look hard, windups look powerful.
how_to_apply: For each prop decide texture, light response, weight, use and placement, not just shape. Add environmental wind so cloth and foliage flutter, and small gusts around explosions. Make broken things irregular (no perpendicular cuts, uneven spacing, no copy-pasted fragments) and keep debris out of the space characters move through. Do a top-down plausibility sweep: windmills turning with the wind, debris spread naturally, light shafts through broken ceilings, motion that isn't excessive.
anti_pattern: Objects that only look like the thing. Forgetting invisible forces like airflow. Manufactured-looking breakage.
example: The table and the miniature table; Smash's environmental wind; the Cloud Sea of Alrest windmills that once turned against the wind; the Mishima Dojo destructible wall.
review_question: Does every object in the scene sit and behave the way its real counterpart would, including in the wind?
keywords: expression believability physicality weight airflow wind props destruction plausibility mimicry realism

principle: Give each weapon its own trail, and fix the swing until it reads
why: Attacks lack oomph without blade trails, so getting them right has a tremendous impact. But a trail that simply traces a fast swing looks angular and can be nearly invisible from the side, so the animation usually has to change too.
how_to_apply: Build trails as a polygon ribbon swept behind the blade like a folding fan, with a translucent, fading tail. For swings that finish in one frame, show a single flat trail image and let hitstop hold it on screen. Check every swing from the gameplay camera and adjust the animation rather than using plain horizontal slashes. Design each trail for its weapon. Extend a similar blur to punches and kicks.
anti_pattern: One generic trail for every sword. Plain horizontal slashes that vanish from the side. Raw path-tracing that looks angular.
example: Lucina's standard blue trail, Marth's emphasized edge, Ike's frenzied trail, Pit's two-color trail, Pyra's flames, Travis's beam katana trail with no fade.
review_question: From the gameplay camera, does every swing leave a clear trail that says what kind of weapon it is?
keywords: blade-trails sword-trails swing-trails weapon-trails slash motion-blur ribbon vfx melee

principle: Get the most out of every particle
why: Particles always cost processing, however powerful the hardware, so his teams set rules: they must appear in the largest numbers at the lowest cost. Billboards are cheap and perfect for intangible effects like flashes of light, but look wrong from some angles. Effects are always moving, so looking quick and fierce matters more than fine detail.
how_to_apply: Keep particle lifetimes short and compensate with higher speed. Pack several particles into one billboard and draw billboards somewhat large. Stagger spawn timing across emitters and offset positions so particles don't overlap. Build flashes and particles from camera-facing billboards with sparks on top. Orbit the camera around billboarded objects and switch to models where they look odd. Use Y-axis billboards carefully. When processing is scarce, use hand-placed animation frames or random picks from preset patterns.
anti_pattern: Long-lived particles that crowd the screen. Piles of overlapping particles. Many tiny particles you can't afford. Effects that look too skinny from misused Y-axis billboards.
example: Steel Diver's bubbles packed several to a panel; Kirby's Dream Land's enemy-defeat stars hand-placed per frame; Super Mario 64's billboard iron balls and King Bob-omb's billboard body; Smash food items that look odd when the camera rotates.
review_question: Is every particle short-lived, fast, non-overlapping and doing visible work?
keywords: particles particle-budget billboards sprites optimization performance vfx lifetime spawn stagger y-axis-billboard

principle: On small, low-color canvases, give every pixel and color a job
why: With few colors and 16x16 sprites, every choice shows. Odd-sized shapes have a true center line, so a 15x15 circle looks rounder than a 16x16 one. A third color is best spent on edge softening or a reflection, and the background decides how well soft edges work. Art made for one display can read differently on another.
how_to_apply: Draw round or symmetric sprites at odd dimensions. See how far an outline plus one highlight carries a material before adding colors. Spend extra colors on anti-aliasing against the real background or on reflections. Mix light and dark pixels so small effects show on any background. Design emblems and shared parts that survive mirroring. When imitating retro art, remember its dithering was made for CRTs.
anti_pattern: Even-sized small circles. Mesh shading on something meant to read as round. Decorative colors with no job.
example: Kirby's 16x16 Game Boy sprite; outline plus highlight reads as a bubble, solid black plus highlight as a cannonball; the Maxim Tomato's 'M' and Dee Jay's 'MAXIMUM' pants survive mirroring; Waddle Dee and Waddle Doo share a back half.
review_question: Does every color in this sprite do a job (shape, highlight, edge, reflection), and does it still read flipped and on its real background?
keywords: pixel-art sprites palette limited-color odd-dimensions anti-aliasing dithering retro mirroring 16x16 crt

principle: Mix every sound by how relevant it is to the player
why: Sound effects play almost constantly, so each one needs a deliberate loudness, flashiness and discernibility. Judging only by the physical size of an action gives the wrong result; what matters is a sound's importance to the game and to the player character. Match-deciding events and direct feedback come first, ambience last.
how_to_apply: List every sound and rank it by relevance, then set volumes in that order. Smash's order, loudest first: KO; hits given or taken, and perfect shields; special-move activations and voices, with explosions between hits and specials and louder the bigger they are; dodges, shield blocks and ledge grabs; attack swings without impact and dashes; landings; jumps; walking; ambience lowest of all. Within a tier, scale by strength. Balance voices carefully, because clear speech cuts through everything. When voices or channels are limited, decide in advance which part yields.
anti_pattern: Volume set by how big the action looks. Ambience or chatter masking gameplay sounds. Every sound equally loud.
example: Smash's KO sound is the loudest because it is crucial to push and pull and decides the match; Link's quiet footsteps versus his quiet sword swing pose the question of which comes first.
review_question: Is the loudest sound at any moment the one that matters most to the player right then?
keywords: mixing mix priority volume loudness relevance hierarchy sound-effects sfx balance

principle: Make impact sounds hit instantly and clear out fast
why: Players need a reaction to their attack right away, so an impact sound must never feel late. Echo makes a sound feel stronger, but in fast battles with four or eight players, overlapping tails make it impossible to tell where each sound starts and everything gets buried in a sea of noise. Hence his policy: strong attack, light reverb.
how_to_apply: Shape hit sounds with a short attack that reaches a strong level almost immediately (not literally starting at peak volume). Trim reverb tails. Cut rapid jab sounds to the shortest length that still reads as consecutive hits. Time heavy hits so the main body of the sound plays during hitstop and is over when action resumes. Review in the busiest mix, not one sound at a time. Make sure the punch survives speakers that drop bass, and that the playback chain isn't delaying it.
anti_pattern: Impact sounds that swell in late. Long echoing tails that sound great solo and turn the mix to noise. Reviewing hits only in isolation.
example: Smash impact waveforms: loud at the start with a short tail, revised from the sound team's pre-check versions; jab sounds pared down; strong-hit sounds timed to finish inside hitstop; impact sounds arriving late through home theater systems.
review_question: In the busiest scene, can you hear exactly when each hit lands, and is its sound finished before the next one starts?
keywords: impact hit-sounds attack envelope transient reverb tail hitstop latency punch sfx combat mix

principle: Treat audio as essential, never as bolt-on polish
why: He can't think of a single masterpiece with bad audio, though masterpieces with bad graphics, or even without coherent game essence, exist. When people remember a game they loved, its music and sound effects are often the first things that come to mind; audio is what hits you right in the heart. Even old games with nothing but simple noise-based effects had well-constructed audio.
how_to_apply: Schedule and budget music and sound alongside graphics from the start. List audio changes for every character or major asset at kickoff, as you do for art and moves. Construct every sound deliberately, even with limited technology. Use what new hardware makes possible to do something the old one couldn't. Tie presentation to music, for example by starting play as a stage's musical intro ends. Benchmark against the sounds you remember from games you loved.
anti_pattern: Leaving audio until the end. Assuming players won't notice.
example: Kirby's Dream Land's Sound Test, stages that begin right after their musical intro and Kirby's victory dance; Melee's streamed, orchestral tracks; the 70 to 100 planned changes per Smash Ultimate fighter, covering audio as well as graphics and moves.
review_question: If players remembered one sound or melody from our game, what would it be?
keywords: audio-quality importance music sound-design memorable budget schedule priority masterpiece

principle: Answer every input and every feat with sound
why: If a player acts and the game gives no reaction, it feels lacking. Swing, dash and footstep sounds exist as feedback for button presses, and landings are a reaction. Items and progress don't specifically say 'well done', so praise has to be added on purpose, and it works best when it heightens what the player already feels.
how_to_apply: Give every accepted press a clear signal, sound included. Keep input-feedback sounds audible even at low mix priority. Add crowd reactions tied to skill: cheers for big launches and KOs, a subtle 'oh!' for near-misses like a barely caught ledge. Let spectators clap along to victory music. Consider vibration matched to the frequency of impact sounds.
anti_pattern: Silent actions or menus. Praise limited to item drops. One generic 'Good!' for everything.
example: The Smash crowd's gasp when someone barely grabs a ledge; Kirby Air Ride's spectators clapping along to the dance music; Sakurai's own HD Rumble experiment matching vibration to impact sounds.
review_question: Is there any press, success or close call in the game that makes no sound at all?
keywords: feedback input-feedback responsiveness praise crowd cheers reactions near-miss rumble haptics

principle: Exaggerate action sounds; keep material and ambient sounds realistic
why: Real punches would sound like a bunch of slaps, and fighting games are nothing like real fighting; forget that and you drift away from the game essence you want. Realistic sounds have their own power: they give meaning to things simple graphics can't show, such as the weight of wood and stone. Ambience works best fairly realistic, even in cartoony games. But the more realistic the visuals, the stranger exaggerated sounds feel.
how_to_apply: Decide each sound category's job: selling impact (exaggerate) or conveying material, weight and place (keep realistic). A/B real recorded hits against exaggerated ones. Give simple-graphics games distinct material sounds. Layer realistic ambience even under cartoon art. Set the overall exaggeration level against how realistic your visuals are, and unify audio across mixed sources the way you unify art.
anti_pattern: Literal realism in combat audio. Cartoon sounds over photoreal visuals. Simple visuals backed by generic sounds that carry no material information.
example: Street Fighter II's wildly fake impacts, in the tradition of Showa-era film sound; Minecraft's thunks that help you picture what you're building; hits that sound painful as a form of imitation that enriches a game's information.
review_question: For each sound, is its job impact or information, and does its realism level fit both that job and the visuals?
keywords: exaggeration realism fiction non-fiction foley impact material sounds stylization sound-design

principle: Never leave dead silence; keep ambience quiet but alive
why: Ambient sounds are the least important and take the lowest priority, so they must never cover the sounds that matter. But if the player stops for a second and hears dead silence, there's no atmosphere, and games should make players feel they've entered another world, especially in first-person or over-the-shoulder views. A handful of well-chosen sounds can imply a whole world beyond the screen, and players with good speakers notice whether ambience is well made.
how_to_apply: Mix ambience at the lowest priority. Stop in every area and just listen, and add layers wherever it's silent. Give realistic visuals a soundscape (wind in leaves, feet on dirt, clinking armor), each layer at an appropriate level. In simulations, call a few simple off-screen sounds to suggest activity. Check ambience on good speakers. Put extra effort in for first-person and over-the-shoulder games. Keep music from standing out too much over detailed visuals.
anti_pattern: Silence whenever the action stops. Ambience so busy it buries key effects. Foreground chiptune-style music fighting dense, realistic visuals.
example: Smash stages played with the volume raised to reveal their many quiet ambient sounds; a train simulator's clattering doors and shuffling feet; NES-style music over modern games sounding noisy and 'off'.
review_question: If you put the controller down anywhere in the game, what do you hear?
keywords: ambience ambient-sound atmosphere immersion soundscape room-tone background-sound silence world-building

principle: Finalize sound on cheap TVs and several setups, not studio speakers
why: Most players hear the game through small TV speakers that lose low frequencies, so impacts hit less hard and details tuned in a pristine studio can become inaudible. Each listening environment reveals different problems. A fixed reference keeps standards steady; change your headphones mid-project and it's hard to stay consistent with everything checked before.
how_to_apply: Compare important sounds on headphones, PC speakers and an inexpensive TV before approving them. Watch sounds whose punch lives in the bass. Check good speakers for ambience quality. Keep the same reference gear all project. Don't tune so hard for weak speakers that you lose your creative vision. Check audio latency separately from video. Check every audio feature you rely on exists on each hardware variant you ship.
anti_pattern: Signing off on big studio speakers alone. Swapping reference headphones mid-project. Over-correcting until the mix loses its character.
example: His order of checks: headphones, PC speakers, then most importantly a cheap TV; the Switch's built-in speakers sit low on the list because they're already clear and many handheld players play muted.
review_question: Has every key sound been approved on a cheap TV as well as on headphones and PC speakers?
keywords: monitoring speakers tv-speakers headphones listening-test reference mastering low-frequency bass latency hardware

principle: Never make sound the only carrier of critical information
why: Many players play handhelds with the sound off, or somewhere they can't hear the game; a player who can't hear the audio has no idea when enemies are firing. The reverse holds too: audio and vibration cues can carry information to players who can't easily see it.
how_to_apply: Give every audio warning a visual tell players can react to, and treat sound as a reinforcing layer for critical events. Where it helps, offer audio and vibration cues as accessibility options, such as a sound near a spot you can jump to or an item you can pick up, and combat cues.
anti_pattern: Incoming attacks signaled only by sound. Key information delivered only in voice.
example: A crossover host who couldn't hear the game audio and so couldn't tell when enemies were firing; Punch-Out!!'s yellow eyes as a visual dodge cue; traversal and combat audio cues and vibration cues in a modern accessibility menu.
review_question: Muted, can a player still see every warning? And does sound add the information it should for players who rely on it?
keywords: accessibility redundancy muted deaf hard-of-hearing visual-cue audio-cue telegraph warnings captions haptics

principle: Build the soundtrack on a few memorable themes
why: He thinks too many songs get produced for a single game, and admits he's guilty of it too. Huge soundtracks are harder to remember and harder to get excited about. A song has more impact if people can remember its melody, so restraint and arrangement beat sheer volume.
how_to_apply: Write one main theme early and plan where its arrangements appear across the game. Cut or merge tracks that have no melody players could hum. When arranging, keep the main melody intact so that humming the arrangement is humming the original.
anti_pattern: A new, unrelated song for every scene. A soundtrack nobody can hum.
example: His habit of writing a main theme and arranging it throughout the game; the Star Wars theme as the reason a familiar melody shouldn't change from film to film.
review_question: Can a playtester hum the main theme after a session?
keywords: music soundtrack main-theme leitmotif melody arrangement memorable hummable restraint

principle: Match music tempo and mood to the action and the player's feeling
why: Some tempos fit a game's content and others don't. Even among similar fighting games, the right tempo depends on the speed of the action, and scenes within one game need their own tempos and rhythms. Songs work best when they complement how the player is feeling. Tempo is everyone's concern, not just the composer's.
how_to_apply: Count BPM by clapping along (one clap per second is 60 BPM, two is 120) and note a target per scene. For fast battles, start from roughly 130 to 170 BPM, with near-200 tracks as rare exceptions. Set tempo by your game's actual speed, not its genre. Write one line per scene on what the player should feel and check the music supports it. Consider tying tempo to game state if you can afford it.
anti_pattern: One tempo for the whole game. A genre-default tempo that doesn't fit the actual pace. Music that works against the player's mood.
example: Smash battle arrangements at a little over 120 BPM, 130 to 170 on average, a few near 200; the first Dragon Quest's dungeon music slowing the deeper you go.
review_question: For each scene, what is the music's BPM, and what is the player supposed to feel there?
keywords: tempo bpm music mood pacing rhythm adaptive-music scene-music feeling

principle: Brief sound work with concrete roles, shared references and examples
why: Audio has no physical form and you can't approximate it with your voice, so vague requests fail, especially in text over remote work. Not everyone knows every sound, even a real one. A reference track is a fast way to set direction, but composers often can't tell which parts to keep. A director may know what he wants and still lack the musical language to say it.
how_to_apply: Decide what feedback and feeling each sound must give before requesting it. Describe its role concretely ('strong attack'). Compare only to universally known sounds ('a jet engine') and link an example for anything specific. Use onomatopoeia only as an extra clue next to a concrete description. Give one reference track with what to keep and what not to copy. Route musical feedback through a sound director. Agree on terms like 'main melody' by playing the reference together.
anti_pattern: Emails asking only for more 'clang' or 'boom'. 'Make it like this' with no notes. Assuming everyone knows the sound in your head.
example: God Hand's 'Gene's Rock-a-Bye', requested in the style of The Ventures but without their famous riff; the Athena arrangement that kept coming back opposite to his notes because he and the musicians meant different melodies by 'main melody'.
review_question: Could the sound designer tell from your request alone what the sound is for and what to borrow from the reference?
keywords: audio-direction sound-feedback brief reference-track communication onomatopoeia sound-director composer commission

principle: Approve the sound that serves the game, not the one in your head
why: It's not just about creating 'good' sounds but finding the right type of sounds for your game. Delivered sounds may differ from what you imagined and sometimes sound even better. A reference can save work or create more, and fixating on it closes off other possibilities. Having a clear idea of the goal from the start is what makes this judgment possible.
how_to_apply: Judge drafts by whether they fit the game and the scene, not by how closely they match your idea or the reference. List two or three other directions before locking a reference. Balance multi-environment fixes against your creative vision. If an existing song fits the theme exactly, consider licensing it as-is.
anti_pattern: Rejecting a fitting sound only because it differs from your mental image. Every draft a cheap imitation of one reference. Sounds that impress in isolation but are wrong for the mix.
example: Sakurai approving sounds quite different from his original idea; Ore no Shikabane wo Koete Yuke licensing the song 'Hana' because blooming and wilting flowers fit a family cursed with a two-year lifespan.
review_question: Are we judging this sound by whether it serves the game, or by whether it matches what we pictured?
keywords: approval judgment flexibility fit references fixation licensing creative-vision review

principle: Shape music structure around gameplay timing
why: Music and play share a timeline: a match countdown, a typical match length, a segment of known length, or a fight whose length varies. When the structure fits, music can be timed to the exact beats and moods of a scene; when it doesn't, intros get talked over and climaxes land at the wrong moment.
how_to_apply: Brief composers with gameplay-driven rules: an intro that covers any start countdown (or music that starts after it), big dynamic shifts for a dynamic game, a build to a climax at the end, a length that fits the typical match with only a little loop, and a loop point before or after the intro. Use fixed-length segments to sync music to beats. Plan cue points where music waits for or follows variable-length events. Start play as a stage's musical intro ends.
anti_pattern: Loops that restart mid-match. Music cues that ignore when the action actually happens.
example: Smash's '3, 2, 1, GO!' intro rule and its two-minute (two and a half in Ultimate) target length; Kid Icarus: Uprising's air battles of known length with music timed to their beats; the PRESS START orchestra following his live mid-boss kill.
review_question: Where do the countdown, the climax and the loop point fall relative to how long a typical play segment lasts?
keywords: music-structure loop intro countdown match-length cue-points sync adaptive-music beats composition brief

principle: Ground characters with audible, varied, material-aware footsteps and landings
why: In many 3D games footsteps are barely audible, which makes characters feel like they're hovering instead of walking. Landing is a reaction and deserves more presence than the jump. Believable sounds feel best, and one sample repeated over and over sounds mechanical.
how_to_apply: Make footsteps clearly audible. Give each character unique footsteps. Match landing and walking sounds to footwear or costume and to the floor material. Record several variations of repeated sounds and rotate them. Make landings louder than jumps.
anti_pattern: Near-silent footsteps. One footstep sample for every surface. The same sample on every step.
example: Cloud's landing sounds differ by costume; every Smash fighter got unique footsteps.
review_question: Walk a character across every floor type: do the steps sound grounded, varied and right for the surface?
keywords: footsteps landing foley surfaces materials variation randomization movement-sounds grounding

principle: Script every vocalization; keep battle voices short, sparse and non-competing
why: Recording a fighter's voice takes about an hour, but the result goes straight into the game and players hear it constantly, so writing and directing dialogue carries a lot of responsibility. Anything not in the script won't get recorded. Long lines or excessive chatter in battle draw too much attention and break immersion, and clear speech cuts through other sounds.
how_to_apply: List every grunt and line (attacks, jumps, damage reactions, special and super moves, reveal lines). Bring reference audio from the original game and prefer the original or current series actor. Keep combat lines short and infrequent, and check how loud or feral voices overlap. Brief and warm up actors before they enter the booth. Record banter-heavy casts together when schedules allow. Budget heavy editing time after recording. Where you can, deliver dialogue as voice during play so players needn't stop.
anti_pattern: Missing grunts. Constant battle chatter. Voices that compete. No editing time. Patching lines recorded in a different room.
example: Smash's one-hour sessions per fighter (two at most with reveal or story lines); extra care for Bowser's and Donkey Kong's overlapping voices; Kid Icarus: Uprising's cast recorded together for banter; his own channel voiceover re-recorded only as a last resort because a new room sounded different.
review_question: Is every vocalization scripted, and does any voice line overstay its welcome or clash with another during play?
keywords: voice voice-acting vo dialogue barks grunts recording script casting editing localization chatter

principle: When arranging beloved music, treat the original as players heard it as right
why: Listeners come for one familiar song out of a great many, so an arrangement that turns out totally different disappoints. The song you hear when playing the original is what's right, even when it strays from musical convention, quirks and hardware-driven structure included, and arrangers must not detract from each player's memory of it. Recreated sounds should match how they came out of the original hardware.
how_to_apply: Keep the main melody intact. Decide which melody is 'main' by what players heard and remember from play. Preserve odd sections. Mirror structure the hardware forced, such as an instrumental where the original lost its vocals. Keep separate language versions distinct. Recreate how a sound came out of the original cabinet, not just the raw file. Review for mistranscriptions of the original score.
anti_pattern: 'Correcting' quirks. Rewriting a melody because it feels old-fashioned to you. Copying the raw audio file when players remember the cabinet.
example: Athena's section that hits on-beats the first time and off-beats the second, reproduced in Smash; Psycho Soldier's English arrangement going verse, instrumental, verse because the original switched to the internal audio processor after verse one; Ryu's impact sounds tuned to sound like the arcade cabinet.
review_question: Would a longtime fan humming our arrangement be humming the original?
keywords: arrangement remix cover nostalgia original fidelity melody licensed-music fan-expectations

principle: When voices or channels are scarce, plan what yields and fit timbre to role
why: On the Famicom, music and sound effects shared the same five channels, so part of the music often had to cut out whenever an effect played, and composers gave each role the waveform that suited it. The same budgeting applies wherever polyphony, memory or storage is limited, and features can differ between hardware versions.
how_to_apply: Decide in advance which music part drops when a sound effect needs a voice. Give crisp tones to melodies, mellow tones to bass and noise-like sounds to hits and explosions. Test compression on big audio sets early, before cutting content. Check every hardware variant or region supports the audio features you rely on, or provide a fallback.
anti_pattern: Letting effects steal the melody at random. Discovering missing audio features on a regional version.
example: The Famicom's two pulse, one triangle, one noise and one DPCM channel; Super Mario Bros. 3's timpani sample; NES cartridges losing expansion audio; Smash Ultimate's music library compressed into a quarter of the space it took in Smash for.
review_question: When every voice is busy, what drops out, and was that our choice?
keywords: polyphony channels voice-stealing chiptune famicom nes timbre compression memory hardware-limits

principle: Let players reach and choose the music they love
why: Each generation has its own version of a series, and so its own music, which made one song per world feel wasteful. Some players also want to enjoy the music from the start rather than earn it as a reward.
how_to_apply: Where your game celebrates many sources, offer several tracks per world and let players choose. Don't lock music many players want behind progression. Give options such as menu-music frequency.
anti_pattern: Locking favorite music behind long progression.
example: Brawl's My Music; Smash cutting back on music used as rewards; adjustable menu-music frequency after beating Ultimate.
review_question: Can players hear the music they came for without grinding for it?
keywords: music-player jukebox unlocks my-music options player-choice rewards

principle: Showcase game music live with the performance at the center
why: He believes live music can stir emotions you can't find elsewhere. In a concert the performance is the point, and video after video distracts from it. Live, one-time stakes are what make a gameplay performance thrilling.
how_to_apply: Gather far more candidate songs than you have slots and narrow them down by listening together. Use game footage only occasionally. Size each edition so it fits beside development work. If gameplay joins the performance, keep real stakes and plan cue points for variable timing.
anti_pattern: Video after video during a concert.
example: PRESS START: ten annual concerts from 2006, 14 to 16 program pieces (about 60 songs counting medleys); his Intensity 9.0, zero-defense Kid Icarus air battle played live with the orchestra; Melee's orchestral tracks leading to those concerts.
review_question: In this showcase, is the audience's attention on the music?
keywords: concert orchestra live-performance showcase curation press-start events

principle: Let players skip and pause anything they are not controlling
why: Logos, opening movies, intermissions and cutscenes are moments when nobody is playing. Creators want every sequence seen, but a player with no save data may still have seen it before, and not being able to skip video is flat-out inconvenient. Phone calls, visitors and dinner pull players away mid-scene, and making players wait is, in his words, a sin.
how_to_apply: Let one press skip a whole non-interactive sequence (company logos, opening movie, intermissions, cutscenes, credits), including on a brand-new save. Show a skip prompt the moment any button is pressed during a cutscene. Let players pause in the middle of any cutscene. If you write company or platform logo guidelines, make skippable the default. The only accepted exception for pausing is an online game that keeps advancing.
anti_pattern: Locking the skip until the scene has been watched once; cutscenes that can be skipped but not paused; unskippable logos or credits; cutscenes that ignore button presses.
example: Ep 180 lists logos, opening movies, intermissions and cutscenes as things to make skippable all at once; ep 233 adds the credits; ep 104 asks that any press during a cutscene at least bring up a skip prompt.
review_question: On a fresh save, can a player skip every logo, movie, cutscene and the credits with one press, and pause any cutscene?
keywords: skip cutscene skippable unskippable pause cutscene company logos opening movie credits intermission player time skip prompt

principle: Let players read and advance text at their own speed
why: People read on-screen text and subtitles quickly and zipping through text feels good. Staged, voiced scenes cannot move at the pace a reader wants, like the difference between turning a book's pages and watching a film. Everyone wants to enjoy as much as possible in as little time as they can, as video playback-speed settings show, while others want to slow down, so support both.
how_to_apply: Make one press finish the current text box instantly and the next press advance it. In voiced cutscenes add a skip that jumps to the start of the next line as well as a skip for the whole scene, or a fast-forward. Where possible, deliver dialogue as voiced lines during gameplay so players never stop to wait. Playtest text pacing with fast readers.
anti_pattern: Forcing every player through text or cutscenes at one fixed, slow pace; a text crawl that cannot be completed early.
example: Line-by-line dialogue skip that jumps to the start of the next line, which Sakurai calls a real breeze (211). Kid Icarus: Uprising tells its story during play like a radio program, with an option to turn it off (125).
review_question: Can a fast reader complete each text box with one press, and skip a voiced scene one line at a time?
keywords: text speed advance text dialogue skip line by line fast forward typewriter text crawl voiced dialogue during gameplay reading speed

principle: Ship in-game button remapping in every game, however simple
why: Button settings are a necessity for some players. Modern controllers are not simple and players arrive with diverse mindsets and experiences. Consoles do not offer per-game remapping, and a console-wide remap such as Switch's affects every application and can leave actions with no button. Designers once assumed they had found the best controls so nobody would need to change them; players want the freedom to play how they like.
how_to_apply: Build a key config screen that draws the controller graphically. Let players select a button with the cursor, then pick its action from a list. Allow several buttons to share one action, and let each be reassigned separately. Save layouts under player profile names chosen before a match, stored on the controller where hardware allows. Where actions can go on the directional buttons, confirm a remap with a long press so short presses still navigate. Show each action's default button, split maps by context (aiming, swimming, menus), and make sure no essential action can end up unbound. Keep genre-standard defaults.
anti_pattern: Fixed controls on a modern controller; leaving remapping to the console; press-the-button-to-assign screens that capture the menu's own exit button; vertical lists where players lose track of which button does what.
example: Smash Bros. draws every controller, uses cursor assignment, has two jump buttons and name-based profiles for guest players (197). The Last of Us Part I confirms remaps with a long press and shows the default button beside each action (55). Sakurai remapped Pac-Land's press-A-to-run-right, mash-B-to-run-left scheme to D-pad movement and A to jump (156).
review_question: Can a player rebind every action in-game, save it under their name, and never leave an action without a button?
keywords: button remapping key config rebind controls control settings custom controls profiles input mapping accessibility controller layout

principle: Answer every button press, and accept confirm on several buttons
why: Players press buttons because they want something from the game. Play is a two-way flow from the hands to the computer and back to the eyes and ears, and an action with no reaction feels lacking. Everyone plays their own way; if L also confirms, players can even play one-handed. Feeling around for which button does what is a downside, but it beats unresponsive controls.
how_to_apply: In menus, accept confirm from the main button plus another such as a shoulder button. In games with one or two actions, put each action on several buttons instead of leaving most dead. During cutscenes, respond to any press with a skip prompt. Give every accepted press a clear sound, highlight or animation. For each state (menus, gameplay, cutscenes), list which buttons do nothing and give them a sensible reaction unless silence is deliberate.
anti_pattern: Buttons that produce no reaction; ambiguous feedback that leaves players unsure whether the press registered.
example: Using L as an extra confirm or action button allows one-handed play (104). Smash Bros. has two jump buttons (197).
review_question: In each game state, which buttons currently do nothing, and is that silence deliberate?
keywords: responsiveness unresponsive dead buttons confirm button redundant inputs one-handed play feedback button press reaction menu input

principle: Make the game playable without reading a single word
why: Pictures are recognized much faster than text and parsed largely through intuition, while words must be read and then understood. Many players will not read the on-screen language. Typical interface design sometimes lets mashing confirm reach the game by accident; Sakurai sets it up on purpose because the idea is rarely considered.
how_to_apply: Put a picture or character on every major menu icon. Give each section a color. Set the default cursor on every screen from the title onward so pressing confirm repeatedly starts the main mode, tutorial included if there is one. Switch the game to a language you cannot read and try to navigate it; fix any screen where you get lost.
anti_pattern: Text-only menus that become unusable without the language; default cursors resting on Options or Exit.
example: Mashing confirm in Smash Bros. Ultimate goes from the title to Smash mode's fighter select, in Kirby Air Ride to the first Air Ride stage, and in Kirby Super Star to the first scenario with its tutorial. With menus switched to Korean, the icon pictures still help somewhat (240).
review_question: If every word were in a language you cannot read, could you still reach and start the main mode?
keywords: wordless clarity icons pictures language independent default cursor mash confirm quick start localization nonverbal UI

principle: Size and lay out text for every language and the real screen
why: The right text size varies by language: kanji need larger but fewer characters, English is legible small but runs longer, and French longer still. A layout designed only for English leaves translations too small. Handheld developers who check on the real device quickly spot text that is too small, which is why handheld games tend to use larger fonts. Icon menus are hard to fit in wider languages. Text that is too big stops looking stylish.
how_to_apply: Leave room in every text area for each target language's glyph size and string length. Read every screen, in every language, on the actual target display, including the handheld itself. Mock up labels in your longest language before locking a layout. Keep the interface clean so text has room to grow, and offer a font-size setting where space allows, along with subtitle size options.
anti_pattern: English-only layouts; approving text on a large dev monitor only; text so large it no longer looks stylish.
example: Japanese, English and French text compared (33). Smash Bros. icon menus fit Japanese well but were hard to fit in languages that take more horizontal space (147).
review_question: Has every screen been read, in every language, on the smallest real display the game ships on?
keywords: text size font size localization translation string length readability handheld subtitles legibility typography language layout

principle: Write help text and names in plain words, never the item's name
why: Menu items are usually one or two words that often do not say what they do. Help text exists for people who do not know the term, so describing Options as Go to the Options misses the point, and he says it happens quite often. Being clear in a few words is hard, so you must drill down to the essential meaning. Names follow the same rule: player-facing names should follow how the player experiences the thing.
how_to_apply: Show a one-line description of the highlighted item, for example at the bottom of the screen. Rewrite it without the item's own words: Options becomes Adjust a variety of game settings. Cut excess words, translate meaning rather than words, and reread as someone who does not know the term. Name modes by what the player does (Play Solo, not 1P Mode), drop jargon like config or key repeat, and name moves in input order (Up Special), even if internal labels differ.
anti_pattern: Help text that repeats the item's name; technical terms; internal labels shown to players.
example: Options described as Adjust a variety of game settings; Play Solo versus 1P Mode (229). Players see Up Special because the direction is input first, while the internal label is SpecialHi (22).
review_question: Does any help line reuse its own item's name, or any menu use a term a newcomer would not know?
keywords: help text tooltips menu descriptions microcopy UX writing plain language jargon mode names naming 1P mode

principle: Offer comfort and accessibility options, grouped, previewed and safe
why: Accessibility means design that makes a game more convenient and playable, including for players with disabilities, and players come with diverse needs. Motion sickness comes from on-screen inertia the inner ear never feels. Removing presentation for everyone makes the game less entertaining, so make it optional. Assists that lower difficulty can be switched on by accident, and a player who gives up gets nothing from your challenge.
how_to_apply: Add a dedicated Accessibility menu that also links relevant options from other menus, with presets that switch groups on at once. Put difficulty-lowering options behind an extra unlock step. Include subtitle size, background, speaker names with colors and speaker direction; a screen reader for all text; colorblind and high-contrast modes; a magnifier; footstep head-bob off, locked vehicle frames and a center dot for motion sickness; a blur-strength slider; flick sensitivity; a cutscene-vibration toggle; and difficulty changes at any time without restarting.
anti_pattern: Stripping effects for everyone instead of offering toggles; assists a player can switch on by accident; cutscene vibration that cannot be turned off; difficulty locked at the start.
example: The Last of Us Part I's accessibility suite (55). FPS footstep-shake toggles and locked cockpit frames (129). Blur strength in options (192). Smash Ultimate's adjustable flick sensitivity (154). Changing difficulty mid-game (213).
review_question: Can a player prone to motion sickness, a color-blind player and a player who cannot read small text each set the game up comfortably, without restarting?
keywords: accessibility options settings subtitles screen reader motion sickness head bob colorblind high contrast difficulty assists presets haptics comfort options

principle: Make choosing fast by cutting steps to the most common choices
why: Of all inputs, menu selection is the one Sakurai most wants to be quick. Tapping the analog stick over and over is unsatisfying, while a clicky D-pad feels nice, and tactile feedback makes even selection more immersive. New devices are new opportunities to speed things up. But the more advanced the shortcuts, the less beginners use them, and the UI can lose broad appeal.
how_to_apply: Count the inputs to the most frequent choices and reduce them. Support D-pad navigation with crisp one-step movement and a distinct, clicky feel per step. Add shortcuts as optional accelerators layered over a simple default path. When a platform adds a wheel, touch or gyro, prototype using it to jump through lists, but adopt only uses that fit. In equipment screens, offer a one-press equip-strongest.
anti_pattern: Menus that require repeated stick taps; expert-only shortcut systems as the main way to navigate; shoehorning every function of a new peripheral.
example: Since the GameCube and Melee, Sakurai has suggested a clicky scroll wheel, then called a jog dial, for fast menu selection; it was passed on because wheels are bigger than you would think (169).
review_question: How many inputs does it take to reach the three most-used options from the title screen?
keywords: menu navigation fast selection shortcuts input count D-pad analog stick scroll wheel jog dial clicky tactile menu speed

principle: Size menu elements by how often players use them
why: Size shows which modes take priority, so players reach the most-used options fastest; it is all about ease of access. The GameCube controller follows the same idea with a big A button and small X and Y, so you feel which button to press. Weighting has costs: it loses versatility when all options matter equally, and icon menus are harder to translate.
how_to_apply: Rank options by expected use; make the top ones the largest tiles or icons and shrink rarely used ones. Make a game's dominant action the most prominent. Keep a plain, equal list when options really are equal. Mock icon labels in the longest target language early.
anti_pattern: An equal-weight list when a few options dominate; unequal weighting when everything is used equally.
example: Menus from Meteos onward, including Smash Bros., use icons of varying size; the GameCube controller's big A button (147).
review_question: Does the size of each menu item match how often players actually use it?
keywords: visual hierarchy icon size menu tiles importance priority big buttons layout weighting major minor elements

principle: Settle clarity versus style per game, and organize menus like drawers
why: Clarity and style are arguably contradictory, and clear UI does not always mean good UI, or vice versa. Persona's UI is the most stylish he knows yet hard to parse, but swapping it for traditional menus would lose its appeal. A UI is like a drawer that should be organized sensibly when pulled open. Feature-packed games need drawers on top of drawers, and crafting games leave players drowning in materials.
how_to_apply: Decide early where the UI sits between clarity and style from the game's content and setting. Group related items and plan a window hierarchy proportional to the amount of content. Review each menu for visual guidance, element size, window hierarchy, brightness and saturation, and typeface. Then improve usability wherever it does not break the chosen style.
anti_pattern: Assuming the clearest UI is automatically best; replacing a signature style with generic menus purely for readability; flat menus for huge feature sets.
example: Persona 5's menus; Minecraft players building warehouses as makeshift item folders; Sakurai's own drawers on top of drawers (18).
review_question: Where does this game sit between clarity and style, and does every menu follow that decision?
