keywords: clarity vs style menu organization information architecture window hierarchy nested menus UI checklist Persona

principle: Keep the HUD informative without crowding the play area
why: A HUD is useful but can crowd the screen, and every game solves that its own way. Markers that track characters would be an eyesore if always visible. Japanese games tend to show more information and overseas games tend to be more restrained for immersion; Sakurai keeps everything on as a player. On CRTs only about 490 of 525 scanlines were usable, so screen edges were assumed unseen.
how_to_apply: Let tracking elements hide themselves based on distance and situation. Turn HUD panels semi-transparent when a character moves behind them. Keep essential information out of edges a display may crop. Offer HUD size with a preview, and HUD hiding for players who want immersion. Make HUD space earn its place.
anti_pattern: Always-visible markers; HUD elements that cover the characters they overlap; essential information at the very edge of the image.
example: Smash Bros. player cursors auto-hide by distance and situation, and the HUD turns semi-transparent when a fighter overlaps it (254). Kirby's Adventure enlarged the bottom info panel, which limited vertical space and showed each copy ability's picture (11). The CRT safe area (252).
review_question: Does any HUD element cover a character or stay on screen when it gives the player nothing?
keywords: HUD heads-up display clutter auto-hide transparency safe area overscan screen edges minimal HUD immersion

principle: Put navigation information where the player is already looking
why: Sakurai often feels he is just playing on the mini-map while the beautifully rendered world goes unseen. Opening and closing a full-screen map again and again is frustrating. The player sees only a small part of the world, and the more realistic the game, the harder the environment is to read. Consider where players look, and even more, what they will be thinking.
how_to_apply: In playtests, note where eyes go; if they mostly watch the mini-map, move the needed information into the main view. Try a translucent full-screen map players can keep up while moving, with one button for a map-only view. Add in-world guidance such as corner-sharpness markers, shape terrain to lead players, design how a 3D map shows height, and offer optional aids like destination arrows, ledge vibration and audio cues near jump or pickup spots.
anti_pattern: A mini-map so essential it pulls eyes off the world; making players repeatedly open and close a full map.
example: Mystery Dungeon's translucent full-screen map; Forza's visual guidance for corner tightness; Subnautica's vertical map (119). The Last of Us Part I's navigation assistance and traversal audio cues (55).
review_question: During normal play, are players watching the world or the corner map?
keywords: mini-map map design navigation waypoint markers map overlay in-world guidance gaze wayfinding traversal cues

principle: Show loading honestly and in your world's style, never timed to dev builds
why: Nobody likes watching Loading linger, and today's players have little interest in waiting, but a wait is easier to accept when the game shows it is loading. Some presentations hide loading perfectly, like Resident Evil's doors, where an icon would ruin the illusion. Load times usually shrink between development and release, so presentation tied to them breaks. What irritates most is a wait that feels like someone dropped the ball.
how_to_apply: Build one minimal, animated indicator styled after your world that can appear anywhere for any duration, and show it immediately when a load cannot be disguised. Use load-masking transitions only if they still work when final loads are shorter, and never put an icon on top of one. Time every fade and black screen and cut each to the fastest version that still does not feel abrupt; keep a short transition rather than none.
anti_pattern: Silent waits; plain Now Loading text; presentation timed to today's slow dev loads; slow fades into long black screens.
example: The first Resident Evil's door-opening transitions (78, 246).
review_question: When the game loads, does the player instantly see that it is working, in a way that fits the world?
keywords: loading screen loading indicator spinner load times transitions fades wipes black screen waiting Now Loading

principle: Never let color alone carry information players need
why: If a game relies on color alone, color-blind players cannot play it, because certain colors look alike under color blindness. Meteos was the one game of his where color coding really mattered, and he would not call it complete until it was playable for color-blind players.
how_to_apply: Run every color-coded element through a color-blindness filter (Photoshop includes one). Where hues merge, separate them by brightness, without making them so dark they disappear into the background. Back color up with shape, icon or position, and offer colorblind or high-contrast modes.
anti_pattern: Gameplay-critical items told apart only by hue.
example: Meteos blocks checked under a protanopia filter and redesigned with big brightness differences (214). The Last of Us Part I's High Contrast Display (55).
review_question: Under a color-blindness filter, can every gameplay-critical item still be told apart?
keywords: color blindness colorblind mode accessibility protanopia contrast brightness high contrast mode color coding

principle: Treat fonts, frames and icons as worldbuilding, but keep them legible
why: Two games with the same essence and content can target different audiences just by changing UI or font, which is much easier than redesigning characters or environments. Fonts and UI are the package the world is wrapped in, and frames, icons, colors and decorations add atmosphere too. Modern taste leans minimalist, but fonts still deserve careful thought.
how_to_apply: Mock up one representative screen in several styles (slick, cute, horror, flashy, digital, regional or historical) and pick the one that fits the world and audience. Budget time for a custom font if nothing fits. Theme backgrounds, frames, icons, loading indicators and wipes, not just the typeface. Check every themed font and frame for legibility at real screen size before locking it.
anti_pattern: Menus and fonts as neutral afterthoughts; default fonts left in place; text styled until it cannot be read.
example: One options screen shown as slick, cute, horror, flashy, digital, Japanese, Victorian, Chinese and South Asian (111). Loading indicators that evoke the world (78); themed wipes such as Smash Ultimate's random victory-screen wipes (246).
review_question: Would a screenshot of the options menu alone tell someone this game's world and audience, and can every word on it still be read?
keywords: fonts typography UI style theming worldbuilding art direction menu frames tone and manner legibility custom font

principle: Show what an option will do before the player commits
why: When customization is part of the fun, the work of customizing must be fun, and it feels like a chore unless players can see what the work will get them. Numbers alone are less intuitive. The right HUD size depends on preference and TV setup, so a preview window is a quality-of-life feature within the quality-of-life features.
how_to_apply: Draw the effect on screen, such as a weapon's attack range, instead of only a stat. Show pros and cons side by side. Give visual settings a live preview, show a dark and a bright reference scene on brightness or HDR screens, and let players change them mid-game to compare. Let players test a build immediately, ideally swapping on the fly. Put a short looping clip beside each new skill's description.
anti_pattern: Differences shown only as numbers; settings whose effect cannot be seen until later.
example: The Last of Us Part I's HUD-size preview and HDR screen (55); drawing attack range on the customization screen (182); short clips beside skill descriptions (85).
review_question: Can a player see the effect of each setting or part before leaving the screen?
keywords: preview settings preview customization screen stat visualization compare equipment options live preview skill video

principle: Keep the next goal and the distance to it on screen
why: It is a shame when a game does not keep you thinking about the next reward. Showing current EXP against the amount needed shows how far you have come and how far is left, and the number rising with each enemy keeps you pushing. Sakurai says he wishes he had done more of this in his own games.
how_to_apply: Display current versus required values for the next reward on the main screen and update them on every gain. Consider a checklist where clearing an objective reveals the neighbors' conditions. At several points in a playthrough, ask what the player is working toward right now; if it is unclear, show it.
anti_pattern: Hiding how close the player is to the next reward.
example: Ys (TurboGrafx-16 version) shows current EXP and EXP needed (23). Kirby Air Ride's Checklist reveals adjacent conditions as you clear squares (59).
review_question: At any moment, can the player see what they are working toward and how far they have left?
keywords: progress bar experience to next level goals rewards visibility objective display checklist achievements

principle: Color-code menu sections, one dominant color per screen, fit to tone
why: Pictures and color convey more information than words and are understood through intuition, so a color per section tells players where they are. A mishmash of colors on one screen often turns into a mess. Lots of color can make a game feel aimed at younger players, so tone and manner come first.
how_to_apply: Give each top-level menu its own color and theme all its submenus in it. Put large images on panels so players learn options by picture. Keep one dominant color theme per screen; large character art is the exception, since the images become memorable. Set saturation to fit the game's tone and audience.
anti_pattern: Many competing colors on one screen; a bright scheme that overrides the game's tone.
example: Smash Bros. Ultimate's main menu: Smash and its submenus are red, Spirits and its submenus green. Smash for 3DS/Wii U's character-art panels mixed colors but stayed readable (133).
review_question: Can a player tell which menu section they are in from color alone, with no clash of colors on the screen?
keywords: color coding menu colors section colors palette saturation tone and manner visual navigation

principle: Make large inventories quick to sort, tell apart and equip
why: Lots of items is good for collecting, but players pile up so much that choosing becomes slow, and look-alike icons make them struggle. Crafting games leave players drowning in materials; Minecraft players build warehouses as their own folders. As a heavy player, a way to sort purchases into folders is the thing Sakurai always wants most.
how_to_apply: Add sorting and categories, make every weapon, part and icon clearly distinct by sight, and include a one-press equip-strongest option, which he calls essential. In libraries or launchers, let players make folders.
anti_pattern: Look-alike icons; unsorted inventories; no automatic equip.
example: Customization screens (182); Minecraft warehouses (18); digital libraries (58).
review_question: With a late-game inventory, how many seconds does it take to find and equip the best item?
keywords: inventory sorting categories folders item icons auto-equip equip best library organization crafting materials

principle: Make HUD elements react to play and carry character appeal
why: A HUD should be both easy and fun to use. Fighters are sometimes tiny on screen, so faces turned toward the audience boost their appeal, and moving backgrounds suggest burning spirit where a flat image would not. Meters that change or break with the game state make the HUD informative and fun, and in 3D it is hard to track which opponents you have hit. Even a conventional score feels better counted up point by point.
how_to_apply: Put character portraits in the HUD posed toward the player; animate their backgrounds, for example with upward UV scrolling. Swap meters per ability or mode and visibly break them when a vehicle or character is destroyed. Show icons for hard-to-track facts such as opponents hit or defeated. Animate score gains as a running tally.
anti_pattern: Flat, static HUD art; a score that snaps to its new total.
example: Smash Bros. HUD faces with UV-scrolling backgrounds from Brawl on; Kirby Air Ride's ability meters that break with your machine and icons for opponents you hit; Meteos' alien head that spins faster with the Speeder (254). Counting scores up point by point (200).
review_question: Does the HUD change when the game state changes, and is it fun to look at?
keywords: HUD animation portraits meters reactive UI score counter tally juice feedback character appeal UV scrolling

principle: Present scores and ranks so improvement feels meaningful to most players
why: High scores should feel as good as possible. A unit of measurement changes what the number means (Brain Age, Crash Dollars, Global Smash Power). Raw leaderboard positions tell almost everyone below first that they are losing; landing 400th or 10,000th saps motivation, and nobody wants to hear they are in x-millionth place.
how_to_apply: Choose a unit that fits the fantasy and the direction that suits it (lower is better for an age). Show standing as a number that rises as players improve, measured against the whole player population. Do not show general players the world number one. Consider an elite tier that rewards top players and keeps them matching each other.
anti_pattern: A plain score counter by default; raw position leaderboards for huge player bases.
example: Smash Bros. Ultimate's Global Smash Power and Elite Smash (170); Brain Age, Wii Fit Age, Burnout's Crash Dollars and Tecmo's Game Deviation Value (200).
review_question: Does the typical player's rank display make them want to play another match?
keywords: score presentation leaderboard ranking GSP rating units motivation inverse ranking percentile elite tier

principle: Use text effects for emotion, and let translators restyle them
why: In text-heavy games, changing how certain letters or words appear conveys emotion and adds flavor, which makes such effects almost essential; one text size feels almost wasteful given comics' techniques. But languages emphasize things differently, so native speakers should decide what reads naturally. Effects may not suit very serious titles.
how_to_apply: Support inline markup for size, color, animation and font on individual words. Store the tags in the localizable script so translators can add, move or remove emphasis without a programmer. Offer several speech-bubble styles and a few clear emotion symbols.
anti_pattern: Effects hardcoded where translators cannot change them; one flat style through an expressive, text-heavy game.
example: Japanese comics' kakimoji and manpu, such as a bead of sweat or a vein mark (93).
review_question: Can a translator change where emphasis falls in a line without asking a programmer?
keywords: text effects rich text markup dialogue emphasis localization translators speech bubbles kakimoji manpu

principle: Give one director the final say; never settle design by majority vote
why: In creative work, more votes don't make an answer right. Majority decisions converge on the safest, most mediocre ideas, and ideas everyone opposed in planning often turn out fun once built. A team usually has one director because the role charts the game's path, and split opinions or unclear goals derail it. That power demands a balanced view and good information, or direction turns into dictatorship.
how_to_apply: Name one person who holds the whole-game vision and makes the content calls. If you split the role (co-leads on a jam team, say), write down exactly who decides what. When the team is split, the director decides and explains the reasoning. Polls are fine as input or out of curiosity, but the decision and any later adjustments stay with the director. If the person with the vision believes in an unpopular idea, build it and judge it in the game.
anti_pattern: Counting hands on design questions; co-directors with no clear final say; a leader barking orders with paper-thin reasoning.
example: Metal Gear Solid 3's wound-treatment system reportedly had only four supporters on its team at first, yet it is fun in the finished game. Sakurai polled his team on Mii Fighter maid outfits out of curiosity; they went with A, and he then made a director's call to color the socks white because brighter extremities make movement easier to read.
review_question: For each open design question, can everyone name the one person who will decide it?
keywords: director final say decision-making majority vote democracy consensus design by committee authority one vision co-director lead designer

principle: Hold the concept steady and steer with small, frequent corrections
why: Sakurai calls the concept a lighthouse: change direction midway and the team gets lost, months of art and programming get thrown away, and morale drops. But individual decisions set the trajectory toward that light, and a wrong one should be corrected rather than defended, so frequent slight adjustments keep the project on course. Many teammates won't feel a new game's appeal from documents until it's playable, so the director has to keep them oriented.
how_to_apply: Before production, write the concept as one sentence of appeal (his examples: the fun of sending opponents flying, the thrill of sprinting down a straight path) and don't start full production until it's that clear. When fatigue or doubt sets in, check decisions against the concept instead of changing course. Correct individual calls as soon as you see they're wrong, amplify emergent fun that still heads toward the concept, and before scrapping a part, count the months of work and the morale you'd lose. Keep restating the concept to the team.
anti_pattern: Changing the game's direction because it isn't turning out as expected; clinging to a known-bad decision because it was already made; swinging the direction back and forth with each round of feedback.
example: People have told Sakurai after a project shipped, "Now I see what you were getting at", which is why he says design documents alone rarely convey the fun.
review_question: Has any recent change altered what the game's core appeal is, or only how we get there?
keywords: concept vision direction course correction pivot change direction midway lighthouse steering iteration spec change emergent fun north star

principle: Raise problems the moment you see them, with facts and a fix
why: Players can only complain; developers can still fix things. Staying quiet and saying "I knew that was wrong!" afterwards only satisfies your ego and upsets teammates. Decisions are only as good as their information: act on an incorrect premise and everything after it is wrong. The worst case is someone who struggles silently and says at the deadline that they can't do it, losing the time an early fix would have saved. Pairing each problem with a proposed solution keeps the environment constructive.
how_to_apply: Make it a team rule with no exceptions: tell someone who can act, right away, with everything you know, and don't waste time arguing about how to bring it up. Bring the problem and at least one possible fix as a set. Flag being stuck well before the deadline with an honest status, and treat that report as a baton pass. If the team decides to keep things as they are, ask for their reasons and accept them.
anti_pattern: Saving objections for after the project; struggling silently until the deadline; only saying "this isn't good"; teams arguing over how to raise a problem instead of raising it.
example: Sakurai prefers that people tell him everything they know, leaving nothing out, because the less accurate the information, the more likely the decision is a mistake.
review_question: Is anyone stuck or worried about something the decision-maker hasn't heard yet?
keywords: raise issues early speak up escalate report problems blockers stuck honest status bad news proposed solution transparency psychological safety

principle: Decide on the spot instead of putting decisions off until later
why: Each decision is a fork that sends the team down a long production path, and every minute they wait is a minute the issue stays unresolved. Wanting to be careful and get second opinions is understandable, but there often isn't time for that hesitation, and a quick, firm decision helps more of the team than you'd imagine. Delaying a key member's decision can put their whole team behind schedule.
how_to_apply: Make sure someone with the authority to decide is in each decision meeting, and push them to decide before it ends. If you're the decider, make the call as soon as a teammate brings you the issue; if information is missing, research it right away. Put every option on the table, pick the one that works in the short and long term, and leave leeway to correct it.
anti_pattern: Ending a meeting with "I'll have to decide on this later!"; long deliberation while the team is blocked.
example: Sakurai says he tries to make a call as soon as a team member comes to him, doing any research he needs on the spot.
review_question: Which decisions are open right now, and who is waiting on each one?
keywords: decision making decide quickly decisiveness indecision blocked waiting meetings postpone defer analysis paralysis fast calls

principle: Show, don't tell: give visual feedback as quick retouches and sketches
why: Changes to palette, contrast, mood or pose are hard to put into words, and text-only notes, especially remote ones, get misread. Showing communicates more clearly than telling, and a retouch that takes about five minutes, ten at most, is more efficient than a verbal explanation. Concrete visuals early in a project also help the team move forward with confidence.
how_to_apply: For any visual note, spend 5-10 minutes on a rough paintover, a mouse sketch, a photo of a posed figure or a diagram, and send it side by side with the original plus one line on what to change. Label it as an example of the direction; the artist still does the release-quality work. Save retouches for what words can't carry, because nobody can retouch everything.
anti_pattern: Long verbal descriptions of visual changes; treating the director's retouch as final art; trying to retouch every asset.
example: Sakurai retouched Smash Bros. Ultimate backgrounds (a Spirits exploration cave with a too-understated palette, the Marx boss fight, a World of Light path) in Photoshop using only a mouse, and posed a figure to show how upper-body twist adds information to Sora's forward aerial.
review_question: Does every visual note on this asset come with an image that shows the change?
keywords: paintover retouch draw over redline visual feedback art direction supervision show don't tell sketch mockup reference image posed figure

principle: Make every note concrete enough to act on without guessing
why: Vague notes make people guess what's in your head, which costs them extra work and extra rounds. Specific notes let the team fix each problem. For things that can't be drawn, like sound, an email asking for more "clang" or "boom" tells people you had something in mind but not what. Words also mean different things to different people, so notes can come back as the exact opposite of what you asked for.
how_to_apply: Name the exact change: the axis, the spacing, the repetition, the frame. For sound, state the role ("this is a strong attack"), compare only to sounds everyone knows ("like a jet engine") and attach a link to a real example. With a reference track, say which quality to keep and which signature element not to copy. When revisions keep contradicting your notes, play the reference together and check you mean the same thing by the key terms. If you lack a craft's vocabulary, route notes through someone who has it. Send notes as bullet points.
anti_pattern: "Make it look better"; onomatopoeia-only sound notes; assuming everyone knows the sound or song you have in mind; repeating the same note louder.
example: Arrangements of the Athena theme kept coming back opposite to Sakurai's feedback because he and the musicians meant different melodies by "main melody". On the Mishima Dojo wall he asked for the X-axis to stay flat with jagged edges only on Y and Z.
review_question: Could the recipient act on each note without asking what you meant?
keywords: specific feedback actionable notes vague critique sound feedback audio references onomatopoeia shared vocabulary terminology misunderstanding bullet points

principle: Give feedback to everyone involved at once, in the open
why: Relaying intent down a chain (director to planner to programmers) can return the polar opposite of what was meant. When every discipline hears the same explanation, everyone understands the goals, anyone unsure knows what to do whatever their role, and visibility improves on large projects. Seeing the feedback others get, not just your own, lets the whole team learn and avoid the same missteps.
how_to_apply: When reviewing a feature, gather everyone who touches it (planner, programmers, modelers, animators, effects, sound, and their leads), show the build on a big screen, use a mic if the room needs it, take questions at the end, and let anyone sit in. Hold group reviews within each discipline. When a review needs changes, explain them to everyone involved, not only the person who asked. Keep these sessions speedy, or the extra meeting time stops paying off.
anti_pattern: Briefing only the planner and hoping it trickles down; private critique the rest of the team never hears; group meetings that drag on.
example: After instructions relayed through planners on Kid Icarus: Uprising came back reversed, Sakurai required every relevant member to attend his feedback from Smash Bros. for 3DS/Wii U onward: about 30 people on average, up to 50, in a room with a huge monitor.
review_question: Did everyone who will touch this feature hear the feedback first-hand?
keywords: group review feedback session all-hands telephone game relay miscommunication visibility shared critique dailies review meeting

principle: Answer every review request the same day it arrives
why: The longer a reply takes, the longer teammates wait, and delaying a key member's decision can put their whole team behind. Quick replies make the second and third review rounds easier, while putting them off makes the next day more miserable. Late-night reviews also wreck the reviewer's sleep.
how_to_apply: Use one predictable channel (his is an email titled "Review Request", sent once the production work is finished), handle requests first come, first served, and reply the same day, ideally right after the review you're on. Set a delivery cutoff so reviews don't start late at night (his was 8 PM). Block a fixed daily period, such as mornings, with no reviews so your own work gets done.
anti_pattern: Unread review requests piling up overnight; being open to reviews all day so your schedule breaks into pieces; starting reviews at 11 PM.
example: Sakurai replies to every review email within the day no matter how many pile up. For this channel, HIKE had to deliver by 8 PM, and each episode got about six to eight rounds of bullet-point feedback.
review_question: Is any review request or approval older than one working day?
keywords: review turnaround approvals same day response latency bottleneck supervision inbox cutoff time focus time feedback loop

principle: Write specs teammates can build from without guessing
why: Spec sheets carry the detail that programmers, animators and other staff build from, and anything vague gets misread or never made. As Sakurai puts it, it's not just you who needs to understand your game. Exact numbers, units and visuals let values land close the first time and let you spot errors when the build doesn't match the spec.
how_to_apply: For animation, give an animation list with each move's length and when the attack becomes active, posed-figure photos for key poses, and four values per attack: standby pose, attack pose, attack start frame, and total frames until it can be canceled. Write timing in frames, not "quick", and give every speed a unit. Put each tunable value in plain-language brackets ("[Special startup X-velocity is O]") so programmers know what to expose. Script every grunt before a voice session. Tell artists and animators each piece's gameplay role (which surfaces have collision, when a hit lands). Tidy your private outline before it goes on the shared server.
anti_pattern: "Fast" or "slow" instead of frame counts; speeds without units; terse parameter names others misread; a raw personal idea dump posted as the spec.
example: An average Smash fighter's spec includes 70-80 pages of posed-figure images, and Sakurai's rule is that anything inside brackets becomes a parameter.
review_question: If you handed this spec to a new teammate, what would they have to ask you?
keywords: spec sheet design document GDD requirements animation brief frame data parameters units handoff documentation clarity planner

principle: Start specs from the player's ideal, then negotiate feasibility with programmers
why: Design documents often come back prioritizing the developers' jobs, but players only care whether the game is good and won't cut you slack because development was hard. Hedging with "we could do A, or we could do B" pushes the decision onto someone else. The proposal is the game's skeleton, so don't twist it out of shape for efficiency up front: start from the ideal and course-correct for cost.
how_to_apply: Choose the one option you judge best and delete the Plan B from proposals. Flag every choice made for development convenience and keep it only if players won't suffer for it. Bring programmers in to balance the ideal against what's technically feasible, take the team's suggestions with an open mind, and fall back to an alternative only when real problems appear.
anti_pattern: Specs that put ease of development ahead of the player; proposals that list alternatives instead of making a choice.
example: Sakurai's answer to convenience-first design documents: players aren't concerned about why developers do what they do, only whether the game is good.
review_question: Which parts of this spec exist for our convenience rather than the player's experience?
keywords: player first ideal spec plan B hedging feasibility programmer collaboration compromise developer convenience proposal commit

principle: Make sure everyone knows the goal and their piece's role in it
why: Roles only produce a game when they work in tandem, and nothing gets done without mutual understanding. Art made without knowing its gameplay function can bury the terrain; animators who think gameplay is the designers' job put weak poses on the hit frame; people who match a reference without grasping a character's essence miss what makes it feel right. And everyone finishing their assigned tasks doesn't guarantee a finished game.
how_to_apply: Share the project's objectives with every role, not only the leads, and mix professions in subteams with the director involved in each. Tell artists which elements have collision, tell animators when and where collision is active, and give everyone working on a character a short statement of its core essence. Keep a visible picture of everything still needed to ship.
anti_pattern: Treating art as standalone pictures; assuming the game will ship because everyone completed their own list.
example: A Mii Fighter Nakoruru costume matched her King of Fighters XIV look but felt off until a revision captured her essence. Sakurai's common stage note: "your backdrop's outshining your terrain."
review_question: Can each teammate say what the game is about and why their current task matters to it?
keywords: shared goals alignment vision context role clarity big picture purpose understanding cross-discipline subteams essence

principle: Show the whole team the whole game, every day
why: On big projects people can be like a worker making one screw without knowing it becomes a car, and working without the larger picture is stressful. Team-wide emails often go unread, but a page with something new every day gets read on people's own initiative. For a director joining an existing team, regular reports also mean the team isn't taking direction from a total stranger.
how_to_apply: Post a daily report: one current screenshot at the top, then 3-5 topics (news, what you're working on, checklists, issues to fix, and sometimes a game you played or current events), with comments open. Put key announcements there instead of in mass email, and invite teammates to post what they finished. Every few months, or every period, have each discipline or subteam present its finished work to everyone, even though scheduling it is a hassle.
anti_pattern: Relying on mass email for important information; skipping team presentations because they're hard to organize.
example: Sakurai wrote a Daily Report every working day from Smash Bros. Brawl on. When he said he'd reveal the next fighter (Sephiroth) there at 5 p.m., the dev team alone brought the server down.
review_question: When did every team member last see the current build as a whole?
keywords: daily report standup status update newsletter screenshot of the day progress visibility information sharing showcase demo day team presentation

principle: Playtest with fresh outsiders and children, and watch instead of asking
why: Developers know the game too well to be the standard. An outsider who has played grows familiar too, so you can't call the same person back as fresh a second or third time. Children always give honest reactions, showing where controls are hard and what bores them. Problems some players have, like 3D motion sickness, stay invisible on a team where nobody feels them.
how_to_apply: With permission, invite staff members' children and their friends, make it feel like a fun session with snacks, stand back and note where they struggle or lose interest. Rotate in new testers who start from the very beginning, treating each one as a one-time first impression. Recruit testers prone to motion sickness to check camera comfort. Share the reactions with the team.
anti_pattern: Asking testers what they think instead of watching what they do; reusing an outsider as if they were still fresh; signing off on difficulty or comfort with only the team's judgment.
example: Playing the original Super Smash Bros., one child shouted "Whoa! Look how far he flew!" at a Falcon Punch's knockback.
review_question: When did someone who had never played this build play it from the start while we watched in silence?
keywords: playtesting user testing outside testers fresh eyes children kids observation first impressions usability motion sickness blind test

principle: Delegate execution to specialists and testers; keep the director supervising
why: On the early Smash games, Kirby Air Ride, Meteos and Kid Icarus: Uprising, Sakurai entered or decided every parameter himself on top of supervision, approvals and marketing, which he says he should never have done; on the earliest games it took all he had just to finish. Dedicated play testers who battle every day are more attuned to balance than the director. Specialists do their best work on pieces they're attached to or excel at, and some playful details are better left to trusted partners than dictated.
how_to_apply: Build tools and pipelines so a few planners can enter and tune data; staff dedicated play testers and trust their analysis; give specialties such as post-processing a clear owner. Let composers pick pieces they're attached to, and otherwise assign by strength. Keep the director playing the build and supervising instead of doing data entry.
anti_pattern: A director who is the only person able to change values; dictating every detail of creative work you've handed off.
example: From Smash Bros. for 3DS/Wii U a small team of planners handled tuning, and on Ultimate Sakurai only supervised. He still plays about 30 minutes of multiplayer at lunch. HIKE designed this channel's Grab Bag gesture visuals with no instruction from him.
review_question: What is the director doing personally that someone else could do as well or better?
keywords: delegation trust specialists play testers planners tuning parameters bottleneck micromanagement director workload ownership

principle: Step in personally when delegated core work stalls
why: Trusting people with their work doesn't mean leaving a stalled core alone indefinitely. When assets already exist, clear new specs and a director's return can rescue a project quickly. Sakurai remembers Iwata never telling him how to approach his games' content, yet jumping in to help teams whenever problems arose.
how_to_apply: Let leads own their work, but watch the core: if the central gameplay still isn't working after a long stretch, step back in, write fresh specs and rebuild the logic on the finished assets. When tuning stops giving the results you expect, have strong programmers hunt for code bugs, since no parameter can fix broken code. When someone reports they're stuck, take the baton and reassign, re-scope or change approach.
anti_pattern: Leaving stalled core gameplay delegated indefinitely; dictating content when what the team needs is hands-on help.
example: After a year of delegated development on Kirby Air Ride, not a single Warp Star worked right. At the lead programmer's request Sakurai returned as director, they wrote new specs, and the game was finished in three and a half months, with courses and machines mostly done. In Melee's final stretch Iwata worked directly with the programmers to find code bugs.
review_question: Is any delegated core system still not working after repeated attempts?
keywords: intervene rescue stalled project step in rebuild hands-on leadership unblock escalation director involvement trust

principle: As director, own the trimming when plans slip
why: Hardware limits, delayed deadlines and growing workloads always knock plans off course. It's faster when the director recognizes the problems and cuts than when compromises come out of battles between cost-focused producers and quality-focused directors. Just about any finished game is the result of trimming and hard work.
how_to_apply: When plans slip, anticipate the damage and offload the heavy or flammable cargo: drop or scale back the riskiest work and reset the course. Cut detail no player will see, but allow harmless extras that cost no schedule or performance. Set hard requirements early and pare content until they hold. Before the costliest late phase, check whether the project can actually be finished. Thank the team at the end, because finishing usually means painful cuts.
anti_pattern: Waiting for a producer to force the cuts; spending effort on details nobody will ever see.
example: Sakurai asked the stage team to tone down car tires that turned in the backdrop of Inkling's stage, something truly nobody would see. On Smash for 3DS he considered 60 FPS an absolute must and pared things down until it held.
review_question: What are we still building that we'd cut if we were honest about the schedule?
keywords: scope cuts trimming triage prioritization cut features schedule slip deadline overscope feature creep kill your darlings

principle: Protect individuality: intervene when tuning sands distinctiveness down
why: Balancing purely on strength levels everything out: weaknesses get patched, strengths get cut, and every character ends up average, and average is mediocre. Sakurai wants each fighter highly unique and player opinions divided, and accepts some unfairness in isolated parts for it. Echo chambers and outside pressure can push a game toward the ordinary, while a unique vision gives it distinctive strength.
how_to_apply: Delegate balance analysis, but have the director step in mainly when a proposed change threatens a character's or the game's individuality. Tell the tuning team to keep characters unique by amplifying shortcomings to offset advantages. Listen to the team's concerns and adapt to them, but separate those from pressure that would only make the game more ordinary.
anti_pattern: Sanding every outlier toward the mean; letting every loud opinion steer the design.
example: Sakurai says that when he does speak up about Smash balance, it's most often because a fighter's individuality is being threatened.
review_question: Has this round of changes made any character or system less distinctive?
keywords: individuality uniqueness distinctiveness character identity balance homogenization average mediocre vision protect quirks echo chamber

principle: Judge work by its purpose, not your mental image, and know when to stop
why: The director's goal isn't to make everything conform to personal ideals. Work that differs from what you pictured is fine if it meets the goal and the quality is there, and sometimes it turns out better. Supervision often brings a half-step when you hoped for a whole one, and swinging big and then pulling back can feel like changing direction every round; the director and the artist share responsibility for the result.
how_to_apply: State each asset's goal in one sentence (for the dojo wall: it must look like wooden boards actually broke) and approve anything that meets it. Approve sounds that fit the game even when they differ from what you imagined. Flag flaws as soon as you see them, but if several rounds still don't reach the bar, put it in the game as-is and spend your time elsewhere. Aim for first-try approvals by being clear about what you want from the start.
anti_pattern: Rejecting good work for not matching the picture in your head; feedback rounds that never end; swinging direction each round.
example: Smash Ultimate's Mishima Dojo destructible wall took several rounds of retouched feedback (sawn-looking cuts, boards twisting like metal, copy-pasted patterns, splinters hanging into the fighters' path) before it read as broken wood. Sakurai says he accepts work and moves on surprisingly often.
review_question: What is this asset's one-sentence goal, and does the current version meet it?
keywords: acceptance criteria approval good enough diminishing returns feedback rounds perfectionism convergence definition of done ship it

principle: Lead by request and respect, never by rank
why: People with ideas are powerless without others. A director's instructions travel downstream, but they are really requests made from the bottom up to the people doing the work. Nobody likes a demanding customer, so acting superior only breeds resentment. Every teammate is an ally, and a disagreement doesn't make you enemies. The industry is small, so fights and badmouthing come back to you.
how_to_apply: Phrase direction as requests to the people who'll do the work. Address everyone politely in name and tone, including brand-new and much younger hires. Treat disagreements as normal between allies. Raise issues as constructive feedback about the work, never as complaints about a person behind their back. Don't act subservient either, and leave every team on good terms.
anti_pattern: Barking orders; acting superior or subservient; badmouthing coworkers; abandoning a project midway to jump to the next job.
example: Sakurai addresses team members politely even when they're new hires much younger than him. Directors at other companies sometimes ask him about former teammates who are interviewing with them.
review_question: Would the team describe the lead's instructions as requests or as orders?
keywords: respect leadership style humility hierarchy rank politeness team culture conflict ally reputation small industry

principle: Meet trouble with calm analysis and shared responsibility, not blame
why: Sakurai remembers Iwata using logic rather than instinct: where most people would lose their temper or take offense, he stayed calm and offered analysis or suggestions. Results come from a whole chain (visuals, title, advertising, competing titles, timing, platform), so poor sales can't be pinned on one person, and in supervision the director and the artist share responsibility.
how_to_apply: When something goes wrong, analyze the cause and propose a fix before reacting. In post-release reviews, look across the whole chain instead of naming a culprit. Treat friction between roles as a question of mutual support: what can you do so the other side can do their best work?
anti_pattern: Losing your temper or taking offense; pinning a failure on a single person.
example: Sakurai credits Iwata, by then head of Nintendo's corporate planning division, with working directly alongside the programmers to find the code bugs stalling Melee.
review_question: When we last reviewed a problem, did we analyze causes or look for someone to blame?
keywords: blame calm conflict resolution blameless postmortem analysis temper shared responsibility failure review sales flop

principle: Give everyone an open, answered channel for opinions and requests
why: People with different skills, standpoints and tastes notice different problems, in the game and in how the team is run, but some won't speak up unless it's easy. Hearing everyone matters even if some posts get lost. After a big change in how a team works, many people share the same problems, and asking early surfaces them.
how_to_apply: Set up an opinion board where anyone can post about how development is going, and have the director reply with their thinking or forward items to the right team. Survey everyone soon after a big workflow change and fix the common problems first. Make time for one-on-ones. On the listening end, be flexible and decide quickly.
anti_pattern: Posts that get lost with no reply; assuming people will raise things without an easy way to do it.
example: Sakurai set up an opinions board whenever he joined a team. His survey shortly after Smash Ultimate went remote in April 2020 found shared problems with desks and chairs, reference monitors, internet, playtesting and social contact.
review_question: Where can the most junior teammate post a concern today, and who answers it?
keywords: opinion board suggestion box feedback channel survey one-on-one listening team voice input retrospective

principle: Separate the director's content role from the producer's business role
why: The director has the final call on content and is best placed to own the concept, since shaping it is hard without a grasp of the game's core appeal. Producers weigh development cost against projected sales, handle staffing and marketing (a good game doesn't matter if nobody knows about it) and take interviews because directors are busy and essential to the team. Their viewpoints differ, but both want a quality product.
how_to_apply: Write down who owns content and concept and who owns budget, staffing and publicity. On a tiny team one person can wear both hats, but know which hat a decision belongs to. Build enough trust that differences of opinion don't turn into standoffs. If you go independent, estimate how much company management would eat your creative time before you hire.
anti_pattern: Handing the concept to someone who doesn't grasp the core appeal; letting cost-versus-quality fights stand in for decisions.
example: Sakurai often slots into a producer's role because Smash fighter reveal movies are marketing. He runs Sora Ltd. with almost no production staff so management doesn't eat his directing time.
review_question: Who owns the concept, and who owns the budget, staffing and publicity?
keywords: director producer roles responsibilities budget staffing marketing publicity concept owner team structure business creative split

principle: Budget for overhead: ten people produce about seven people's work
why: Running a team takes management time: someone has to handle workloads, outside communication and creative supervision, and a strong creator promoted to lead stops producing their old output. The bigger the team, the longer it takes to get everyone on the same page, including tools, security and rules. Big changes cost output too: Sakurai estimated remote work cut productivity by about 30%.
how_to_apply: Plan at roughly 70% effective output from headcount, with more overhead as the team grows. Name who handles workload management, external communication and quality supervision. Backfill a promoted lead's production work. Set up shared tools and rules early. On a team of just a few people, expect closer to full output.
anti_pattern: Planning as if headcount equals output; expecting a newly promoted lead to keep their old individual output.
example: Sakurai's rule of thumb: depending on the situation, ten people can generally produce seven people's worth of work.
review_question: Does our schedule assume everyone spends all their time producing?
keywords: management overhead team size productivity estimation scheduling headcount capacity planning lead promotion remote work

principle: Give every task and bug a ticket with one owner and a status
why: Work that lives only in conversation slips through the cracks; whoever holds a ticket owns the work, so responsibility and progress are obvious. Bugs found on old builds don't help, programmers aren't always the right fixers, and every fix risks a new bug, so a disciplined loop beats carefulness alone.
how_to_apply: Split each content piece into tickets per discipline (spec, model and rig, animation, programming, effects, sound effects, balancing), each with one owner, a status and a deadline a lead reviews, and leave slack between dependent tasks. For bugs: test only on the latest daily build, file a ticket once the bug can be reproduced, grade severity (Class S for hangs and save corruption, Class A for progression blockers), route it to the discipline that owns the problem, have the tester verify the fix in several configurations, and mark it resolved instead of deleting it.
anti_pattern: Tasks with no owner; downstream staff forced to start on unfinished upstream work; sending every bug to programmers; deleting closed tickets.
example: Smash Bros. sometimes ran CPU battles all night to find bugs, and near a project's end testers in Japan, North America and Europe pass save data back and forth.
review_question: Does every open task and bug have exactly one owner and a current status?
keywords: tickets task tracking bug tracker issue ownership status severity triage QA reproduction steps regression daily build

principle: Present ideas fast: core idea first, no justifications or alternatives
why: Creators have to communicate their ideas, and Sakurai's secret is speed: trim the fat and get to the heart of the topic. Speed isn't the same as short; a 200-page proposal works if each page moves quickly like a comic panel. A wall of text read aloud is annoying because people just read ahead. Defining a new game by comparison invites the question of why not just play the original.
how_to_apply: Open with the core idea and drop justifications, alternatives and Plan B. Use one image and about two lines of text per slide, group slides into categories so people know where they are, and talk around the slides instead of reading them. Explain even the basics simply. Describe what's new rather than "X, but with Y".
anti_pattern: Long preambles; reading slides aloud; pitching a new game as a variant of an existing one.
example: Sakurai's Smash Bros. Ultimate proposal ran over 200 PowerPoint pages, nearly all one image and two lines of text, presented quickly.
review_question: Does the pitch open with the core idea, with no justifications or alternatives in the way?
keywords: presentations pitching proposals slides meetings communication brevity speed clarity deck

principle: Build a warm team: thank, celebrate and play together
why: Sakurai sees a good director-team relationship as the way game development should be. Small fun events act as icebreakers, captioning the daily screenshot helped the team unwind, and kid playtests drove the team forward through hard stretches. Finishing usually means tough decisions and cut content, so master-up can feel wounding, and that's when thanks matter most.
how_to_apply: Turn giveaways into quick games (list items on the daily page, let people sign up, pick winners by rock-paper-scissors, a match in your own game or a secret rule). Keep snacks in the review room. Thank the staff explicitly at master-up. When forming a core team, favor people who love the game or genre.
anti_pattern: Handing things out at random; treating the end of a project as just a deadline passed.
example: Sakurai's team has given him a wide variety of birthday presents, which he calls proof of a good relationship. The Game Arts core team for Brawl had played so much Melee that their analog stick ridges were worn down.
review_question: When did the team last do something together that wasn't work?
keywords: team morale culture celebration gratitude thanks icebreaker fun events motivation snacks recognition team building

principle: Line up the next plan before the team disbands
why: Teams scatter when a project ends, and directors usually go straight from one job to the next. Sakurai finished Smash Ultimate's 200-plus-page proposal on the same day as Smash for 3DS/Wii U's final video presentation, because staying ahead was the only way to keep the dev team together.
how_to_apply: During the tail end of a project, draft the follow-up proposal, including feature lists and per-character adjustments. Use any gap before a new team assembles to write design documents and win over key stakeholders.
anti_pattern: Starting the next plan from nothing after the team has already moved on.
example: Before Brawl's team assembled, Sakurai wrote the design documents and pitched each character to its original creator.
review_question: If this project ended next month, is a plan ready that would keep the team together?
keywords: next project pipeline continuity team retention proposal planning roadmap sequel

principle: Make every call for the player, not for the developers' convenience
why: Players don't care why developers did something; they only care whether the game is good, and they won't cut you slack because development was hard. Every developer shares one goal, entertaining players, and that same goal is what keeps you motivated through a hard project.
how_to_apply: When a spec or compromise exists to make development easier, ask whether players would accept it; keep it only if it is a sensible efficiency trade they won't notice, otherwise look for alternatives together with the programmers. When you feel lost or unmotivated, ask how the decision in front of you entertains the player and let that decide. Remember that real people will buy what you make.
anti_pattern: Design documents that put the developers' jobs ahead of the player experience; expecting players to forgive problems because development was difficult.
example: Sakurai's answer to design documents that prioritize developer convenience (ep 21); his rule for when you've lost your way: entertain players (ep 7); remembering that actual people will buy the game (ep 67).
review_question: Which decisions in this build were made for our convenience, and would a player accept each one?
keywords: player first player perspective player experience developer convenience compromise entertain players purpose motivation customer

principle: Treat each project as a professional assignment, not a hobby
why: Once money, sales and numbers are involved, game development is a job like any other; indie developers become professionals too, and being a pro means responding to demand. Once you understand what makes games fun, you can make any kind of experience regardless of your own taste. Sakurai says he makes games because it is what he is best at and suited for, not because they are the games he wants to play.
how_to_apply: At kickoff, write down the genre, goal and audience the project must serve and design to that brief. On tasks that aren't to your taste, find what makes them interesting and do them well anyway. Give a sequel the same full effort as an original, and practice working in styles outside your specialty so you can match a set style.
anti_pattern: Designing games for yourself; only putting effort into work you personally enjoy; coasting on a series' name.
example: An experienced gamer making Kirby's Dream Land for newcomers, and Meteos despite not being good at block puzzles; an artist who loves cute things texturing lifelike zombies and roaches; artists on one team matching a single visual style.
review_question: Can you state the genre, goal and audience this game must serve, and does the build serve them rather than your own taste?
keywords: professionalism professional assignment brief job not a hobby personal taste career genre audience sequel range

principle: Refuse easy-way-out compromises: the hardship fades, the game endures
why: You forget the difficulty of a project but never the parts you got wrong, because flaws stay in the game for good. Every player multiplies your effort: if 1,000 people play, the impact is 1,000 times your hardship. Most creative works also have to do something extra to stand out from the crowd.
how_to_apply: Before taking a shortcut, ask whether you'll regret it once the game ships. Set up an efficient workflow first, then put the effort you save into what players will actually experience. Decide which special touches will set the game apart and commit to them.
anti_pattern: Taking the easy way out with too many compromises. Equally, needless hardship: Sakurai is explicit that effort should serve customers, not be suffering for its own sake.
example: The ending of Kirby's Adventure, where the screen shakes when it was supposed to flash white, a slip he still remembers; Melee's orchestral arrangements and first CG movie, whose storyboards he drew over his New Year's holiday; Smash Ultimate's 29 million-plus sales, about the population of Australia.
review_question: Which compromise in this build will you still regret when the game has been out for years?
keywords: polish compromise shortcut regret quality bar extra effort stand out hardship impact multiplied efficiency

principle: Start now: motivation arrives after your hands are moving
why: Turning a 0 into a 1 is hard, and overthinking while unmotivated goes nowhere; motivation comes later, once you've started. The best way to improve is steady output, and the words you tell yourself set the course of your actions: those who act are the ones who win.
how_to_apply: Take the first physical step at once: open the document and type a line, open the canvas and draw. Cut off social media, video sites and games before a work block. Psych yourself up out loud and start. Save planning tricks such as visualizing tasks for after you've begun. If you want to make games, sit down and make one with whatever tool you have.
anti_pattern: Waiting to feel motivated; overthinking what the work means before doing it; waiting for better tools.
example: His exaggerated advice to work as if a bomb in the room will go off unless you start now (ep 83); 'Do it! Come on! Go!' (ep 212); Family BASIC, bought with six months of allowance, is what showed him he could make games (ep 118).
review_question: What is the very first physical action on this task, and why haven't you taken it yet?
keywords: motivation procrastination getting started just do it action momentum productivity distractions focus

principle: Manufacture urgency, and favor speed over endlessly polishing drafts
why: Thinking you can finish whenever lets work drift, while telling yourself only a few hours remain gets things done. Momentum counts for a lot: the longer a proposal sits, the less fresh it gets. With limited time, over-working every line to prevent misunderstanding costs succinctness.
how_to_apply: Give each task a short self-imposed time limit, set well ahead of the real deadline, and frame milestones as something closing in on you. Once the outline and main points are itemized, write the whole draft in one push. Accept small imperfections in proposals, scripts and presentations and live with the results.
anti_pattern: Treating work as something you can finish whenever; leaving it to the real last day like summer homework; ruminating over every detail of a draft.
example: He went from last to first in a middle-school race by imagining a three-meter machine chasing him (ep 171); he wrote the channel's scripts in about a month, roughly 12 a day: 'Short and snappy! Speed above all else!' (ep 261).
review_question: Does this task have a near, self-imposed deadline, and is any draft stalling because you keep polishing it?
keywords: deadline urgency speed momentum time limit power of suggestion hot and fast perfectionism drafts pace

principle: Take a lot in: play many current games to the end, reflectively
why: A director needs to grasp the scope of modern games so that what they deliver is on par; Sakurai calls this a must. Input you don't reflect on goes in one ear and out the other. Fun is relative to its time, so judging everything by the games of your youth blinds you to the present.
how_to_apply: Play as many different current games as you can rather than one title at length, and try to reach each ending. While playing or watching, note what works and why. Choose the input form that suits you (film works too if you reflect on it). Before claiming old games were better, replay one next to a recent game.
anti_pattern: Sinking all your play time into one game; passive consumption; holding modern games to nostalgic standards.
example: Sakurai keeps playing many games even when busy and always tries to see the ending (ep 126); he tells fans who have put thousands of hours into his competitive games to be sure to play other games too (ep 220).
review_question: How many recent games in or near your genre have you finished this year, and what did you write down about each?
keywords: input research playing games broad input reflect study competitors modern games nostalgia references media diet

principle: Put a lot out: keep a small, steady, low-pressure output habit
why: You won't succeed without steady output, and regular writing is training. A habit survives for years when each installment costs little time, uses strengths you already exercise, and isn't done out of obligation; working out of duty or for the sake of the industry takes a major toll. Habits compound: his column habit is what led to the channel.
how_to_apply: Commit to a recurring output such as a devlog, column, daily team report or daily screenshot. Time-box each installment to a short fixed slot. Publish what you think is good instead of writing for an imagined audience. Before starting a side project, fix its total run and the size of each edition so it fits beside your main work.
anti_pattern: Taking on routine work out of obligation; overthinking each installment; open-ended side projects that grow until they compete with development.
example: His Weekly Famitsu column ran 18 years and 9 months, 640 articles, usually written in about an hour (ep 98); a Daily Report every workday and the Screenshot of the Day (ep 123, 126); PRESS START planned from the start as a 10-year run of 14 to 16 pieces per concert (ep 116).
review_question: What do you produce on a fixed rhythm, and is each installment small enough to survive your busiest month?
keywords: output habit routine devlog column daily report consistency sustainable time-box obligation side project writing

principle: Clear every review the same day, and protect a block for your own work
why: Every review that waits keeps teammates waiting, and delaying a key member's decision can put a whole team behind; quick replies also make the second and third rounds easier, and putting things off just makes the next day worse. But being open to reviews all day breaks a lead's schedule into erratic pieces.
how_to_apply: Take review requests through one channel with a fixed subject line and handle them first come, first served. Reply the same day, ideally as soon as the current review is done, and explain any changes to everyone involved. Set a delivery cutoff so reviews never start late at night, and reserve a fixed period (mornings, or after a cutoff) with no reviews at all for your own tasks.
anti_pattern: Letting requests pile up overnight; leaving yourself open to supervision all day; reviews arriving so late they wreck your sleep.
example: Sakurai's email-only 'Review Request' workflow, answered within the day no matter how many pile up (ep 177); his channel editors had to deliver by 8 PM after 11 PM deliveries left him short of sleep (ep 261).
review_question: How many review requests or decisions are more than a day old, and when is your protected no-review block?
keywords: reviews same day turnaround supervision inbox email decision speed cutoff time blocking productivity bottleneck habits

principle: Define the problem's theme, then list many ideas before pruning
why: If you try to think of something from nothing you have no starting point, so ideas naturally won't come. Producing many candidates, even silly or unrealistic ones, gets you past the feeling of having nothing, and minor variants of failed ideas often lead to the answer. Sakurai treats improving games and coming up with new ideas as learnable skills.
how_to_apply: Write the problem as a simple one-line theme. List broad solution types and note why each fails in this context. For every failure, look for a variant that fixes its flaw. Keep thinking actively instead of waiting for inspiration, and prune only once the list is long.
anti_pattern: Brainstorming with no defined problem; throwing out minor or silly ideas too early.
example: 'How to put out a fire in some ruins': no water nearby; sand is scarce but dirt might work; a bucket is too small but a bigger one might do (ep 237).
review_question: Can you state in one line the problem you're solving, and how many candidate solutions have you written down?
keywords: ideation ideas brainstorming problem solving creativity stuck creative block theme quantity over quality

principle: Ask why other games work, then rebuild instead of mimicking
why: Copying something fun won't make your game feel original; reexamining why other games do things raises your chances of making something fresh. If your game is too close to another, players can just play the original, and to stand out you need something that can't be found elsewhere.
how_to_apply: Before borrowing a mechanic, write down why it works in its source and whether that reason applies to your game. Deconstruct the fun into its parts (usually risk and reward), analyze it, and rebuild it as your own mechanic. If you start from an homage, list many reasons a player would pick yours over the original, not just one.
anti_pattern: Mimicking features without understanding them; riding an original's coattails with a single point of difference.
example: Kirby Air Ride's charge-and-release drifting came from deconstructing why drifting is fun, not from imitating racing games (ep 57).
review_question: For each borrowed mechanic, can you say why it works in its source and what makes your version yours?
keywords: originality copying imitation homage deconstruct analyze rebuild innovation fresh mimic why

principle: Train a keen personal eye, and put your own take into the game
why: The one thing the skilled directors Sakurai knows share is a sensibility that latches onto tiny details and perceives what others miss, in visuals, game essence, animation and story. Directors use their own thoughts and feelings to set their games apart; the role, like a game, calls for a touch only that person can offer. That quirkiness still needs balance and the ability to communicate it.
how_to_apply: When reviewing your build or someone else's game, write down the small details most people would overlook and what you would change. For each major decision, state your personal take and how it differs from the genre's usual answer, and keep the difference on purpose. Practice explaining the idea until teammates can repeat it back.
anti_pattern: Assuming there is one standard way to direct and copying it; idiosyncrasy you can't communicate to a team.
example: In supervision he flags tiny flaws, such as an extraneous mark on a face or hair poking into an eye highlight, as soon as he finds them (ep 253).
review_question: What in this game could only have come from you, and could your team explain it?
keywords: sensibility unique perspective director personal touch eye for detail originality vision taste quirky observation

principle: Notice echo chambers and seek opinions from outside your circle
why: A flood of agreement makes you feel right even though plenty of people disagree, and an insular world hides problems that need solving. It happens with design ideas and with reviews every day. If you can't stay objective, your game ends up unbalanced, whether you play it safer or push it further. Online opinions about what is strong or weak gain momentum and seem truer than they are.
how_to_apply: When an idea gets nothing but praise, ask people outside that circle what is wrong with it. Before acting on reviews or social reactions, check whether you are only seeing the voices that agree. Form your own verdict on a game before reading what others think. When online claims spread, check them against data and actual play.
anti_pattern: Letting in only the opinions that validate you.
example: Despite online talk of strong and weak fighters, Smash Ultimate's worldwide online data put every fighter's win rate between 47.18% and 51.43% (ep 218).
review_question: Who outside your usual circle has criticized this idea, and what did they say?
keywords: echo chamber criticism objectivity feedback bias social media reviews outside opinions validation community

principle: Keep your deliberate direction; don't let outside voices sand it off
why: Sometimes taking a game in your own 'unbalanced' direction is what feels best, and it beats being swayed by other people; a unique vision gives a game distinctive strength. Decisions made by majority converge on the safest, most mediocre ideas, and ideas opposed during planning often turn out fun once built.
how_to_apply: Sort feedback into team concerns you should adapt to and outside pressure that would only make the game more ordinary, and protect the deliberate quirks. Let the person who holds the big picture make creative calls instead of counting votes, and use polls only as input. Back the call with reasons and with everything the team knows.
anti_pattern: Being swayed until the game loses its identity; settling creative direction by headcount; the opposite failure, dictating with paper-thin reasoning.
example: Metal Gear Solid 3's wound-treatment system reportedly had only four supporters on the team at first, yet turned out fun (ep 158); Sakurai polls his team out of curiosity but keeps the final call, as with the Mii Fighter outfit's white socks (ep 158).
review_question: Which distinctive choices have been softened because of outside pressure, and did those changes fix real problems?
keywords: conviction vision unique direction majority vote mediocre criticism outside pressure identity distinctive

principle: Steer by your concept when fatigue and doubt set in
why: Development is long, and once fatigue sets in it is easy to wonder what is supposed to be fun. The concept is like a lighthouse: change course and you get lost, and scrapping work wastes months of artists' and programmers' effort and demoralizes the team. Fun is hard to see on paper, so teams often only grasp it once the game is playable.
how_to_apply: Write the concept as one clear statement before production and don't move forward until it's that clear. When doubting, check decisions against it, and amplify emergent fun only if it heads toward the concept. In proposals, commit to the ideal spec instead of hedging with alternatives, then course-correct with the team.
anti_pattern: Changing direction midway because the game isn't turning out as expected; leaving a Plan B in the proposal so someone else has to decide.
example: People have told Sakurai after a project shipped, 'Now I see what you were getting at' (ep 187).
review_question: Can you state the concept in one line, and does the change you're considering move toward it?
keywords: concept lighthouse direction staying the course doubt fatigue plan b commitment conviction staying true

principle: Treat a rejection as your job to show the appeal better
why: A proposal has to make the people who provide funding and talent think 'We should definitely do this', so showing the game's appeal is the presenter's responsibility. A game unlike anything before runs into preconceptions, and proactively searching for new ways to explain it pays off later. Poor results rarely trace to one person.
how_to_apply: When a pitch is rejected, rework how it demonstrates the fun instead of blaming the reviewers. Describe the game on its own terms rather than by comparison. If press or partners dismiss the game, explain it to players yourself. When something underperforms, review the whole chain instead of hunting for one culprit.
anti_pattern: Telling yourself the other party has no taste; pinning failure on a single person.
example: When magazines ignored his document explaining the first Smash Bros.' push and pull, he turned it into the Smash Bros. DOJO!! site himself (ep 143, 245).
review_question: If this pitch were rejected tomorrow, what would you change about how it shows the fun?
keywords: rejection pitch proposal criticism resilience communicate appeal blame preconceptions setback persuasion

principle: Never fight or badmouth coworkers: the industry is small
why: Developers move between teams constantly, so someone you wronged may join your next team years later, and directors do ask about former teammates. Treating people poorly gets you excluded, and dislike comes straight back to you. You are responsible for your workplace's atmosphere, and fixating on difficult people steals attention from supportive ones. Company work is mutual support on a path you chose.
how_to_apply: Raise problems directly as constructive feedback, ideally with a proposed fix. If a situation doesn't suit you, step back instead of escalating. Finish or hand off your work before leaving. Never speak ill of anyone. Follow a partner company's rules. Meet trouble with calm analysis, and treat directions to others as requests, not orders.
anti_pattern: Fighting, acting selfishly, leaving on bad terms, abandoning a project to jump to the next job, holding grudges, thinking of your job as forced on you.
example: Directors at other companies ask Sakurai about former team members who are interviewing with them (ep 249); Mr. Iwata stayed calm and offered analysis where most people would lose their temper (ep 259).
review_question: If every teammate on this project joined your next one, would you be glad?
keywords: conflict reputation coworkers small industry respect professionalism workplace atmosphere feedback cooperation career

principle: Break in by finishing your own game and letting originality show
why: Making a game yourself is the quickest, if not only, way into the industry: you see which problems arise and how to solve them, and even designers need to think like programmers. Many people want to make games, so an imitative idea won't help your case. Imitation is fine while learning, and finishing anything at all is a feat.
how_to_apply: Start small in whatever tool you can get and finish it. Get people to play it (friends, free online release, or a sale if you're confident), find out what they think, then improve it or carry the lessons forward. Send an original game with your applications even if you don't meet every listed requirement, and enter open proposal calls.
anti_pattern: Waiting for ideal tools; submitting an imitative showcase; not applying because you lack one listed requirement.
example: Family BASIC on the Famicom was how Sakurai learned he could make games (ep 118); before entering the industry he won Sega's Associate Planner Certificate No. 004 through a public proposal promotion (ep 149).
review_question: Is there a finished, original game you could hand to someone today?
keywords: career breaking in portfolio first game indie job application originality student junior finish your game

principle: Keep a new idea sealed until its first draft is written
why: Talking about an idea makes you feel fulfilled, which releases the internal pressure that gives a proposal its force. A design document written without sharing a word burns hotter than one compiled from a brainstorm. Posting ideas or progress on social media vents the same pressure.
how_to_apply: Whenever you want to tell someone about the idea, write it into the document instead. Hold back work-in-progress posts while it takes shape. Consult colleagues for weak points and new ideas only once the draft is finished. Picture how people will react to keep yourself going.
anti_pattern: Talking an unfinished proposal through; using a group brainstorm in place of your own draft; venting ideas on social media mid-creation.
example: His balloon and pressure-cooker metaphors for internal pressure (ep 144).
review_question: Did you finish a full first draft before pitching or posting about it?
keywords: internal pressure secrecy proposal draft brainstorming social media sharing ideas creative energy

principle: Turn negative thoughts into questions about how to improve
why: Each time you think, say or post a defeatist idea it becomes a little more true, because your thoughts and words set your attitude. Negative feelings are fine to have, and used as motivation they can be a bigger opportunity for change than a positive outlook.
how_to_apply: Stop voicing or posting defeatist lines about your work. Rewrite each one as a question and act on the answer: 'my work feels pointless' becomes 'what are some ways I can make it better?'
anti_pattern: Repeating negative ideas out loud or on social media; mistaking this for forced positivity that denies the feeling.
example: His examples of self-talk to avoid: 'I'm running out of money', 'There's barely any point in working', 'Life's just not fun' (ep 212).
review_question: What negative statement about this project have you repeated lately, and what improvement question does it hide?
keywords: mindset self-talk negativity motivation reframing attitude social media defeatism mental health

principle: Protect your body: exercise a little and fix your workstation
why: People who exercise tend to be far more productive than people who don't. Screens close to your eyes cause strain, and nothing works as well as changing the work environment; missing desks and chairs cause health problems. Overdoing it backfires.
how_to_apply: Do at least a little regular exercise, for example pedaling an exercise bike through play sessions. Keep about a meter between your eyes and the monitor (move it back if it is under 60 cm, and use a larger screen to compensate) and match brightness to the room.
