Make sure everyone has a proper desk and chair. Ramp up gradually and stop if something hurts.
anti_pattern: Overdoing it; long sessions with a screen close to your eyes; treating glasses or eyedrops as a substitute for fixing the setup.
example: Two-hour exercise-bike sessions, and legs hurt from climbing around 500 stairs (ep 24); severe eye strain during Smash Ultimate's development (ep 81); Sora buying desks and chairs for remote staff (ep 66).
review_question: Is your screen about a meter away, and when did you last exercise?
keywords: health exercise eye strain ergonomics monitor distance desk chair sleep burnout sustainable pace wellbeing

principle: Give one project all of you, and keep overhead off creative time
why: A project that needs its director's full time suffers when attention is split. Creators who go independent and hire staff often get bogged down in the management needed to keep employees paid, leaving no time for the game itself.
how_to_apply: Before taking a demanding lead role, decline or finish competing commitments. Focus on one directing job at a time. Before going independent, estimate how much of your time company management would eat. Keep a daily block that belongs only to your own tasks.
anti_pattern: Juggling other agreements while leading a project that needs everything; hiring staff by default and losing your creative time to running a company.
example: For Brawl, Sakurai turned down his other projects except Mushiking, which was already in progress (ep 132); Sora Ltd. stays a near-staffless contracting company so he can be a 'wandering director' (ep 53).
review_question: What else is competing for your attention on this project, and can you clear it?
keywords: focus commitment one project at a time overhead management independent studio freelancing time

principle: Picture the real people who will play, and let that fuel you
why: Imagining how people will react, and which parts they'll love, gives you the strength to push on. Real people will buy what you make, and what children love can shape their tastes for life. Imagining a presentation also organizes your thinking and can reveal new insights.
how_to_apply: While writing and developing, picture specific reactions to specific parts of the game. Mentally present your current build to customers and note what you would change. During hard stretches, share outside players' reactions with the team.
example: A child shouting 'Whoa! Look how far he flew!' at a Falcon Punch while playtesting the original Smash Bros. (ep 248); Smash Ultimate as the top game in a 2019 CoroCoro Comic survey (ep 124).
review_question: Which moment in this build do you picture players loving, and has anyone outside the team reacted to it yet?
keywords: motivation audience player reactions imagine presentation children morale purpose empathy

principle: Respect the labor behind every game, and judge it by its own goals
why: Every game has its own values, goals and audience, so ranking games on one scale misses what makes them great. Developers go through cuts and hardship to finish, and many games never ship at all. Creators who leave the industry often succeed elsewhere, and everyone has the right to choose their own path.
how_to_apply: Evaluate a game against what it set out to do for its intended players. Approach other developers' games with gratitude for the struggle behind them. Frame awards as celebration, not a race. Don't write off creators who disappear from view, and give yourself the same freedom to start something new.
anti_pattern: Choosing one universal 'best' game; treating sales as a measure of ingenuity; calling vanished creators washed up.
example: The Game Designers Award, judged on originality by directors of unique games (ep 13); master-up often leaving the team feeling wounded rather than triumphant (ep 87); Sakurai starting a YouTube channel while still making games (ep 176).
review_question: When you critique another game, are you judging it against its own goals and audience?
keywords: gratitude respect critique other developers awards judging empathy industry culture career change

principle: Study your genre's roots, then carve a new path
why: The path today's creators walk was carved by their predecessors. Playing the foundational games shows how clever ideas built on top of each other, and knowing that path is the basis for creating your own.
how_to_apply: Play landmark games of your genre and note which mechanic each introduced and what it cost. Then aim your own design at something those games didn't do instead of retracing them.
anti_pattern: Learning a genre only from its latest entries; retracing an old path instead of extending it.
example: Scramble's separate shot and bomb buttons and fuel gauge laid groundwork for side-scrollers like Gradius; Donkey Kong popularized jumping; Moon Patrol had possibly the first parallax scrolling (ep 155); 1986's jumps in storage capacity (ep 209).
review_question: Which classic first did what your core mechanic does, and what does yours add?
keywords: history classics arcade foundational games study roots retro conventions predecessors genre

principle: Don't let convenient tools or obvious answers fence in your ideas
why: If you're too tied to convenient systems, it's hard to step away from them and you set mental limits on what's possible; creation is about freedom. The obvious choice isn't always right, and proactively searching for new solutions tends to pay off.
how_to_apply: Regularly ask which 'impossible' ideas are only the limits of a tool or convention. Before adopting the standard solution (a stock rig, a raw leaderboard, a template site), consider at least one alternative built for your game.
anti_pattern: Treating a tool's defaults as the boundary of what's possible.
example: Realistic skeleton rigs limit joints to 180 degrees, while great animation pushes past common sense (ep 236); Smash's Global Smash Power instead of a standard leaderboard (ep 170).
review_question: Which limit in your design comes from a tool's default rather than from the game?
keywords: tools limits conventions creativity freedom thinking outside the box defaults constraints

principle: Use advice to sharpen your own judgment, not to replace it
why: Sakurai says the foundation is the viewer's own experience, skill and way of thinking; his lessons are only a boost, and mileage varies. Knowledge has meaning only when someone uses it.
how_to_apply: Test each lesson against your own build, keep what fits, and keep making and playing games to build the judgment the advice depends on.
anti_pattern: Following design rules blindly; collecting advice without applying any of it.
example: He calls the channel a 'boost' and closes the series with 'If nobody uses it, it might as well not exist!' (ep 1, 261).
review_question: Which piece of advice did you apply this week, and did it actually fit your game?
keywords: advice judgment learning experience rules of thumb apply knowledge mileage may vary

principle: Treat making the game known as seriously as making it good
why: An unknown game may as well not exist. Development and marketing are multiplicative, two wheels on one axle: the success of one is proportional to the other. With an estimated 10,000+ games listed on Steam in 2021 alone, nobody finds games by chance, and publicity alone usually isn't enough to draw people in.
how_to_apply: From early in development, plan what the dev team itself will contribute to promotion (reveal videos, an official site, a demo, presentations) and budget the time for it. Ask the publisher for the marketing and operations plan so you can suggest ideas while they can still be acted on. Think about how each piece of news will reach people scrolling social feeds.
anti_pattern: Assuming a good game will be discovered on its own; treating marketing as someone else's department, separate from development.
example: Sakurai is a director, not a producer, yet takes on many producer duties apart from money because marketing is that vital: fighter reveal movies, the Smash Bros. DOJO!! site and the Mr. Sakurai Presents videos (ep 80, 234, 245).
review_question: What is the dev team's own plan for making this game known, and is it in the schedule?
keywords: marketing visibility discoverability promotion awareness launch sales publicity multiplicative two wheels one axle

principle: Make every marketing image match how the game actually feels
why: Until people play, they judge a game by its title, box art, screenshots and videos. If the image and the reality don't match, you fail to reach the people the game would resonate with and you disappoint the ones who were misled into buying it. A half-baked demo does the same damage through word of mouth.
how_to_apply: Compare your title, cover, screenshots, trailer and demo with actual moment-to-moment play and fix anything that sets the wrong expectation. Surprises are fine as long as the overall picture matches. Go indirect or subversive only if it still captures the heart of the game. A tech demo is acceptable only if it truthfully shows how the game will run.
anti_pattern: Painting a misleading picture for the sake of surprise, 'a banana that tastes like an apple'.
example: The Japanese Kirby Super Star's plain wooden-box cover, an idea from Shigesato Itoi, looked unrelated to the vibrant game but got to its heart; even so, Sakurai says showing the game for what it is works better (ep 101).
review_question: Would a buyer who saw only your store page and trailer get the game they expected?
keywords: honest marketing representation expectations box art screenshots misleading truthful store page cover art

principle: Get to real gameplay as fast as possible in every trailer
why: People judge quickly whether a game is fun, and they can't be expected to buy a game if they can't tell what kind of game it is. Viewers skip long logos and intros, and however much work goes in, a trailer will never be on the level of a film, so its job is to show what only the game offers. New IP and indie titles can't rely on a name the way famous series can.
how_to_apply: Treat a gameplay trailer as a required deliverable, including on your store page. Cut opening logos, long movies and character intros; lead with what makes the game appealing and save story and world for later. If you don't open on raw gameplay, open on footage that clearly illustrates the systems or an honest tech demo. Watch it as a stranger and trim whatever delays the game.
anti_pattern: Store-page trailers with no gameplay at all; teaser-only reveals for a new or indie title; trying to compete with films on cinematics.
example: Sakurai won't buy a game without a trailer unless there's a very good reason, and has almost made a habit of skipping trailer openings (ep 186, 17).
review_question: How many seconds into your trailer does real gameplay appear?
keywords: trailer gameplay footage reveal video first seconds store page teaser intro logos hook show the actual game

principle: Ship in the best shape possible: patches can't win back players who left
why: No matter how much a game improves through patches, it means nothing if players have already given up on it. A perfect release is all but impossible for modern games (they are enormously complex, developers barely get to play the final build, and the market finds one-in-a-thousand bugs), but that is a reason to aim high from day one, not an excuse.
how_to_apply: Set the release quality bar as if no update will ever come. Lock content early enough to play a near-final build, and check difficulty on the actual retail hardware after late optimization. After launch, treat player videos and reports as your biggest test pass.
anti_pattern: Shipping rough on the assumption that patches will fix it later.
example: A bug that one player in a thousand sees is unlikely to show up in testing, but after launch that player can upload a video for everyone (ep 231); late optimization made Meteos faster and harder than intended (ep 141).
review_question: If no patch were ever possible, would you ship this build?
keywords: launch quality patches updates day one bugs release polish first impression ship it

principle: Choose your audience from a top-down market view, not your own taste
why: Players' styles have branched widely, so relying on your own likes and dislikes misreads the market. Tastes branch apart with age: the market is broadest at the trunk, among younger players before everyone finds their branch, while aiming squarely at one branch can make its players fall in love with a game. Demographic lines are blurry; 'beginners' spans all ages and genders.
how_to_apply: Map the current player segments and decide deliberately which one the game serves. Define the target by experience level or need rather than age or gender. For broad reach, use orthodox, broadly appealing design; for a niche, commit fully to that branch's values. Set the risk level of your rules to fit the audience you chose.
anti_pattern: Picking the audience from personal preference alone; treating demographic slices as hard boundaries.
example: The original Kirby was designed for 'beginners', never 'for children', yet has enough oomph that advanced players enjoy its controls (ep 226); Nintendo's top sellers are hits with younger generations (ep 112).
review_question: Who exactly is this for, described by experience and needs, and why that group?
keywords: target audience targeting market segments beginners niche broad appeal demographics trunk branch

principle: Don't let market research generate your concept
why: Targeting and market research are built on what has already been made, so they show only the safe main road others have walked, not the path to what comes next. Following that road makes work more average and mediocre, and it sells less. Innovators stand alone because they walk untraveled paths, yet they open new roads for everyone.
how_to_apply: Form the concept first and use data to check its risks, not to pick it. When research says a genre is booming, ask how crowded it will be when you release and what you offer that the others don't. Keep graphs and research out of the pitch; spend that space on what is new.
anti_pattern: Chasing whatever genre the data says is selling now; deciding creative direction by what the majority already likes.
example: Around the NES-to-SNES transition, research showed RPGs selling, so many Japanese companies made Dragon Quest and Final Fantasy-like games and dove into an overcrowded market (ep 226).
review_question: Did the core idea come from data about what already sells, or from something new you want to offer?
keywords: market research data trends genre chasing innovation mediocre copycat safe road originality

principle: Count every game, old or new, as competition for players' time
why: For the player, time spent on something old is worth the same as time on something new, and subscription services put back catalogs right beside new releases. Games take many hours and a higher effort to start than low-barrier phone content, and a huge play-time number can scare buyers off rather than attract them.
how_to_apply: List what your target player could spend the same hours on (current releases, older games, subscription catalogs, phone and social media) and write down why they would pick yours. Measure against the best games in the genre. Offer something fresh that can't be found elsewhere, and lead with fun rather than an hour count.
anti_pattern: Assuming your only competition is this year's releases; assuming a game you find fun will find players; advertising '300 hours of content!' as the main attraction.
example: Subscription video services pit every new film against decades of back catalog (ep 72); being told a game has 300 hours of content before you start is likely to put you off (ep 250).
review_question: Why would your target player spend tonight on your game instead of the best older game in its genre, or their phone?
keywords: competition player time back catalog subscription phones attention positioning play time hours

principle: When a trailer shot feels good enough, zoom in and go bolder
why: Sakurai's most frequent notes on reveal footage were all ways of pushing past adequate: bolder framing, a changed angle of view, more interaction between characters, a balance of serious and comic, and cutting to the music. Shallow depth of field and focus pulls can make big things look small.
how_to_apply: Run every trailer shot through five checks: zoom in and go bolder; tweak the angle of view to transform the layout; add interactions between characters; balance serious and comic beats; sync to the music. Remove depth-of-field focus shifts unless a shot truly needs one. Polish faces and highlights that will be seen up close.
anti_pattern: Settling for safe, adequate framing.
example: Smash fighter reveals (ep 163); a focus shift from background to foreground in Sora's reveal that Sakurai had removed (ep 174); Kazuya's eye glint made stronger and sharper for his reveal (ep 165).
review_question: For each trailer shot, have you tried a tighter, bolder framing and synced it to the music?
keywords: trailer framing camera zoom bolder angle of view music sync cinematography reveal polish shot

principle: Explain an unusual game's essence to players yourself
why: A game unlike anything before runs into preconceptions; people dismissed the first Smash Bros. before release, and a document explaining its depth sent to magazines had little impact. Proactively searching for new ways to explain pays off later. The director knows the game's content and its fun best.
how_to_apply: Write a plain explanation of how the game plays, its core essence and where its push and pull lies, and publish it directly to players as a guide if the press won't run it. Have the person who knows the game best write it or at least review it, and delegate production tasks like screenshots.
anti_pattern: Relying only on press coverage to explain an unusual game; waiting for others to discover its depth.
example: 'The Secrets of Smash Bros.' became the Smash Bros. DOJO!! players' guide, which Sakurai hand-coded in an HTML editor (ep 245, 143); Nintendo's own sales staff and wholesalers rejected the idea of its characters fighting before they had played it (ep 27).
review_question: If players misunderstand your game's depth, where can they read the designer's own explanation?
keywords: smash bros dojo players guide explain game essence developer communication misunderstood preconceptions direct to players

principle: Post updates on a fixed, frequent schedule fans can make a habit
why: People come to a site excited to see something new, and that works well once it becomes a daily routine; something new every day gets read where a mass email doesn't. Official posts carry the game's voice, so someone who knows it should check every one.
how_to_apply: Release one new detail on a set cadence (Brawl's Dojo posted every weekday). Have the director write or review each post and the team help with production tasks. Review every official social and website update before it goes out. Shape news for people scrolling social feeds, and keep the announcements off your personal account.
anti_pattern: Irregular information dumps; unreviewed official posts; flooding your personal social account, which can rub people the wrong way.
example: Brawl's Smash Bros. DOJO!! updated five times a week in six languages; during Melee's brutal development Sakurai updated the site himself and replied to comments (ep 245); he checks every official Twitter and website update even though he doesn't write them (ep 80).
review_question: What is your update cadence, and could a fan predict when the next update arrives?
keywords: update schedule cadence community blog devlog social media posts dojo regular news

principle: Keep one official home base, shaped around your game's content
why: Social media delivers information in short bursts, but a game still needs one place that delivers all of it. A site made in a standard fashion won't fit every game; a game with many elements needs a site that goes in depth to match.
how_to_apply: Maintain one canonical site alongside a blog and official social accounts. Build its sections from your actual content (characters, modes, techniques, online play, stages, music, events) and add features the game needs. Have someone who knows the design review the layout and every update.
anti_pattern: Scattering information only across social posts; a generic template that doesn't fit the game.
example: Smash Ultimate's site covers fighters, modes and techniques, 100+ stages, Pokemon and Assist Trophies, a built-in music player, reveals and Mr. Sakurai Presents videos, a blog, and tournament and photo-contest info (ep 143).
review_question: Is there one place where a player can find everything about your game, organized the way your game is?
keywords: official website home base hub landing page site structure social media information

principle: Make storefront art strong enough to earn the click
why: On storefronts with an almost endless lineup, people use a game's banner to decide whether to look at it at all; if the visuals don't draw them in, they won't play. Once a game is in stores, its cover art is crucial for getting potential players interested.
how_to_apply: Treat banner, capsule and cover art as critical assets, not afterthoughts, and test whether they make people want to click. Keep them honest to the game (see MKT-02).
anti_pattern: Assuming good gameplay will be found regardless of presentation.
example: Steam's almost endless lineup, where players judge games by their banners (ep 152).
review_question: Shown as a small banner among dozens of others, does your key art make a stranger want to click, and does it represent the game?
keywords: store page banner capsule art key art cover art thumbnail storefront steam discoverability

principle: Triage post-launch work: fatal bugs first, the rest is a bonus
why: Crashing bugs must be fixed, but balance tweaks and quality-of-life features are a free bonus that ties up the director and key staff who could start the next game (for one-off releases; games-as-a-service may differ). Every fix can create new bugs, and changing core systems late forces wide re-testing. DLC and updates stretch the schedule.
how_to_apply: Rank post-launch work by severity. Plan people and time for fixes that slip past master-up. Prefer narrow, contained fixes over changes to core systems, and re-run broad checks before releasing each patch. Use online and tournament data as reference for balance. Budget DLC as a real schedule extension.
anti_pattern: Rushing a hotfix out without re-checking; touching core AI or global difficulty code in a late patch; treating DLC and updates as free.
example: When Smash Ultimate's CPU fighters felt too hard at launch, the patch lowered Challenger fight difficulty and added a Very Easy option to World of Light instead of changing core CPU code (ep 141); Smash for 3DS/Wii U released in 2014 but development only wrapped in spring 2016 because of DLC (ep 135).
review_question: Is each post-launch task a fatal fix, or a bonus worth keeping key staff from the next game?
keywords: patches post-launch updates DLC hotfix triage balance patch regression live ops maintenance

principle: Budget a demo as its own small game, and release it only when balanced
why: Demos are very effective at getting people to try a game, but making one is far more work than players think: from the moment you decide on one you maintain two builds with separate management, updates, tuning and QA, spoiler data must be stripped, and removing data breaks things. A half-baked demo raises the risk that people write the game off.
how_to_apply: Decide early whether you'll make a demo and schedule it as its own deliverable with near-final QA. Keep spoiler content in separable files and check the demo build for leftovers. If the pre-release build isn't balanced, consider a post-launch demo made from the finished game and accept a smaller splash.
anti_pattern: Treating a demo as a quick slice of the full game; releasing an unbalanced demo on the idea that something is better than nothing.
example: Pre-COVID expo demos were somewhat easier because players couldn't keep them; downloadable demos may be more effective than ever (ep 122).
review_question: Does your demo have its own schedule and QA pass, and does it represent the final game's balance?
keywords: demo trial build QA leaks spoilers datamining word of mouth vertical slice

principle: Build assets and tools so they double as marketing material
why: In-game assets like character artwork may be used outside the game, trailers need models that hold up at higher resolution, and the best gameplay footage comes from being able to re-shoot a moment from any angle.
how_to_apply: Produce key art and renders at a quality and format marketing can reuse. Make touched-up revisions of game models for pre-rendered CG and build trailer sound from the game's own sound effects. Give the team replay and debug-camera tools (pause, rotate characters, zoom, change angle) for capturing footage and screenshots.
anti_pattern: Assets made only for the in-game use case, forcing marketing to remake or make do.
example: Fighter artwork made with outside use in mind (ep 80); reveal gameplay segments recorded with debug and replay features to find the best camera angles (ep 163); the Screenshot of the Day captured with debug-mode controls (ep 195).
review_question: Can your team capture a beautiful, repeatable shot of any moment without replaying it live?
keywords: key art assets reuse marketing assets replay debug camera footage capture screenshots

principle: Demo by playing: show every key feature in a close match
why: Showing people a game directly is probably the most effective form of presentation, and you can't demo a game whose content you don't understand. Real stakes, like a genuine chance of failure, are what make live play thrilling.
how_to_apply: Before a demo, write a checklist of what the footage must show (for a fighter: every special move, the super move and as many regular moves as possible) and keep matches relatively close. Learn the content thoroughly, check the stage setup, and when playing live keep real stakes such as high difficulty and no restarts.
anti_pattern: Demoing without understanding the game's content; one-sided matches; a badly set-up play environment on stage.
example: Sakurai played every DLC fighter himself in Mr. Sakurai Presents (ep 207); at PRESS START 2012 he played a Kid Icarus: Uprising Air Battle live with the orchestra at Intensity 9.0 with zero defense, where a Game Over would have ended the performance (ep 227).
review_question: Does your demo plan guarantee every key feature appears, in a match that stays close?
keywords: live demo presentation showcase stage play gameplay demonstration Mr. Sakurai Presents checklist

principle: Present your game on its own terms, not as "X but with Y"
why: If your game really is that close to another, people may just play the original, and a company should avoid copycat accusations. References mean different things to different generations, so a comparison can mislead. Only a sequel in the same series should sell itself by pointing to other games.
how_to_apply: Rewrite your pitch or announcement so it describes the core experience without naming another game, and check that people can still picture it. Sum the game up in one line naming its audience or its hook. Keep 'it's like X' for informal talk with people you know share the reference.
anti_pattern: Headlining with a comparison; assuming your own play history is your audience's reference point.
example: 'Mario' can mean Super Mario Bros. on the NES, Mario Odyssey, or just the character, depending on who hears it (ep 161); each of Sakurai's works captioned in a single line (ep 2).
review_question: Can you describe your game's hook in one line without naming another game?
keywords: pitch positioning comparison elevator pitch one line hook messaging originality copycat

principle: Make a sequel's reveal prove it beats its predecessor
why: A sequel that repeats the original can expect roughly half the sales. People buy a sequel based on how well the last game was made and whether the new one looks clearly more fun; if it is the same scale with similar content, fans feel they've already experienced it.
how_to_apply: Write in one line how the sequel is more fun and more impactful than the last game, and make the reveal show exactly that. If a returning player would think 'I've already played this', expand the system or the content before announcing.
anti_pattern: Remaking the same game at the same scale; assuming a sequel sells on its name.
example: Smash Ultimate's 'Everyone is here!' concept, possible because the team and tools carried over (ep 160); Melee's concept of powering up everything (ep 40).
review_question: What does your reveal show that the previous game couldn't do?
keywords: sequel reveal announcement headline concept series franchise marketing sales

principle: Hear fans through deliberate channels, but keep the plan yours
why: Recurring requests show what an audience wants, and a well-run survey can inform big decisions. Direct replies to fans built a relationship before social media, though risk management may leave less freedom for that today. A project planned completely in advance can't change course on comments, and off-topic or mocking comments mostly show the point didn't get through.
how_to_apply: Collect wishes with structured tools, such as a survey that discounts repeat votes, at the planning stage. Answer persistent requests with dedicated content. Decide in advance which parts of the plan are open to audience input and which are fixed, and read reactions with the echo-chamber caution in CRAFT-12.
anti_pattern: Letting the comment section steer a plan midstream; ignoring a request your audience keeps repeating.
example: A past fan survey with about 1.8 million valid votes informed Smash Ultimate's new fighters (ep 160); after followers kept begging for his cat, he gave her a whole video (ep 39); with every channel script written in advance, he couldn't take viewer requests (ep 261).
review_question: Where do fans' wishes enter your plan, and where are they deliberately kept out?
keywords: community fans feedback requests surveys comments engagement audience listening social media

principle: Plan from the start to reach a global audience in their languages
why: Reaching players worldwide at the same time takes coordination with regional partners, and it multiplies the audience for every update. Text written ahead of time also serves subtitles, translation and checks.
how_to_apply: If you want a global audience, plan localization of updates and videos from the start, line up regional partners, and write scripts or copy early so translators work from final text.
anti_pattern: Treating localization of marketing as an afterthought.
example: Brawl's Dojo ran in six languages (Japanese, English, Spanish, French, German and Italian) with help from Nintendo of America and Nintendo of Europe (ep 245); Sakurai planned the channel as Japanese-only, then chose English versions to reach as many people as possible (ep 261).
review_question: Will players in your other target languages get each update at the same time as the first language?
keywords: localization translation global audience languages subtitles regional marketing

principle: Don't lock expensive movies behind progress; they'll be shared anyway
why: People post in-game movies online before a game is even out, so movies meant as progression rewards stop being rewards. A showcase that isn't tied to game progress can be enjoyed by everyone and works as marketing instead.
how_to_apply: Assume any in-game movie will be uploaded at or before launch. Turn showcase cinematics into marketing everyone can watch, and reward progression with things that keep their value after someone uploads them.
anti_pattern: Spending heavily on in-game movies as rewards for pushing through a mode.
example: Brawl's per-fighter movies in Subspace Emissary were posted online from pre-release copies, so Sakurai stopped making movies that cut in during gameplay and made fighter reveals instead, 37 of them (ep 163).
review_question: Which of your rewards lose their value once someone uploads them?
keywords: cutscenes rewards spoilers leaks movies showcase reveal marketing progression

principle: Pick a title that shortens into something memorable
why: Players will abbreviate a title, and a name that shortens well may be easier to remember. The words in a title also carry nuance about the game's tone.
how_to_apply: While naming, list the short forms players are likely to use and favor names that shorten well. Choose words for the tone they imply.
example: Super Smash Bros. becomes just 'Smash' (ep 101); Mr. Iwata chose 'Brothers' so the fighting reads as friends settling a little disagreement (ep 259).
review_question: What will players shorten your title to, and does that and the full title fit the game's tone?
keywords: title naming abbreviation name memorable tone branding

principle: Keep every tunable number out of the code
why: If values are hard-coded, every tweak means diving into code and going through a programmer, yet parameters keep being tuned for balance to the very end, long after the programmer's job is done. Code is the bones and parameters are the muscles: change the muscles and the same bones behave in drastically different ways.
how_to_apply: Have programmers read every value that might need tuning (attack power, speeds, decelerations, timings) from a parameter table kept outside the code that planners can edit at any time. Build characters or vehicles as parameter sets on one shared behavior, with only a few true types in code. When a mode needs different physics, give it its own parameter set. When the game's tempo changes, retune every parameter instead of porting old values.
anti_pattern: Writing tunable numbers directly into code; one person as the only one who can change values; carrying old values into a game whose speed changed.
example: A move with attack power 10, where the code makes the move happen and the 10 is a separate parameter (46). Kirby Air Ride's machines differ only by parameters apart from star versus bike types (59). Brawl's fighters needed a second jump and movement parameter set for the Subspace Emissary (108). Ultimate's raised tempo meant none of Smash for's parameters could be reused (160).
review_question: Can a designer change any damage, speed or timing value without touching code or waiting for a programmer?
keywords: parameters data-driven design tuning values hard-coded magic numbers spreadsheet config tables balance data designer tools

principle: Keep game speed independent of frame rate and processing speed
why: Games use frames as their unit of time, and distance equals time times speed, so whatever counts time controls how far and fast everything moves. His NES and SNES games counted screen interrupts, so PAL versions at 50 fps ran at 5/6 speed. In Meteos, game speed was tied to processing speed, so late optimization sped the game up and made it harder than tuned. A dropped frame is not slowdown unless your logic makes it so.
how_to_apply: Drive game logic from a clock that does not depend on how many frames are drawn or how fast the processor runs. When diagnosing performance, tell frame drops (less redrawing) from true slowdown (the game itself running slower). Find every timing that still depends on processing speed (enemy speeds, time limits, decay timers). Lock processing speed and frame timing before final balance, and redo tuning if they change.
anti_pattern: Logic tied to a refresh rate that varies by region or platform; treating a performance gain as purely good when it also changes game speed.
example: NES/SNES PAL ports at 5/6 speed (5). Meteos became harder after late optimization (141, 74). The Mushiking pet got hungry faster on the production unit than on the dev board (92).
review_question: If the frame rate halves or the processor gets faster, does the game still run at the same speed and difficulty?
keywords: frame rate independence game speed slowdown frame drops PAL 50Hz processing speed timing bugs fixed timestep delta time

principle: Set the frame-rate target early and cut content until it holds
why: 60 and 30 fps differ both in look and in how smoothly they control. 60 is ideal; 30 is an acceptable standard because 60 costs about half your visual performance. For Smash on 3DS, Sakurai treated a stable 60 as an absolute must and pared things down until it held, where many 3DS games ran at 30 or dropped stereoscopic 3D. A faithful port can still lose its mood if it runs choppy.
how_to_apply: Choose the target at the start of the project, per game. Budget for the worst-case scene (the maximum number of characters and effects) rather than the average. When one platform is weaker, let it set the shared limits, and cut or simplify features rather than lower the target. Profile every stage or level at maximum load.
anti_pattern: Dropping to 30 fps or cutting a headline feature late to fit everything in; budgeting for typical rather than peak load.
example: Smash for 3DS: four players, stereoscopic 3D, items, Pokemon and Assist Trophies at a stable 60; Ice Climbers, two characters at once, were too much (135). Ultimate's roughly 115 base stages had to hold 60 with eight fighters on Switch (99). The NES Ghosts 'n Goblins kept every enemy in place but lost its smooth, creepy feel to a low frame rate (156).
review_question: Does the heaviest possible scene hold the frame-rate target on the weakest platform you ship on?
keywords: frame rate 60fps 30fps performance budget worst case performance target stable frame rate porting weaker hardware optimization

principle: Verify the final build on real retail hardware before sign-off
why: Sakurai tuned Mushiking on a custom dev board just under one square meter and never played the production handheld; probably because of a processing-speed difference, the pet gets hungry faster than planned and almost always wants food, adding unintended stress. Smash Ultimate's CPUs felt too hard at launch and he still does not know why. When you work with computers, sometimes there is no telling what you will get.
how_to_apply: Before sign-off, play the finished game on production units, not just dev kits. Compare timer-driven systems (hunger, fatigue, growth), time limits and enemy speeds against design values. Schedule a final difficulty pass after late optimization lands. When several team members independently report the same feel problem, treat it as real even without a cause.
anti_pattern: Tuning only on development hardware; assuming a build that worked on the dev board will behave the same on retail units.
example: Sodatete! Kouchuu Ouja Mushiking's hunger rate (92, 141). Meteos' late speed-up (141). Smash Ultimate's launch CPU difficulty (141).
review_question: Has someone played the final build on a retail unit and checked every timing-sensitive value against the design?
keywords: retail hardware testing dev kit vs production final build verification timing differences difficulty regression sign-off

principle: Remove input and display lag from every test, demo and capture setup
why: Even a game with great response time is ruined by lag, and many people do not recognize lag when they see it. Display latency comes from picture post-processing; at 60 fps every 16.67 ms is a frame of delay. Sound can lag on its own through a home theater system. Lag and frame rate also change how heavy a button feels, so a laggy setup misleads tuning.
how_to_apply: Before any demo, playtest, event or capture, press jump in an instantly responsive 2D game on that exact setup and confirm the character moves the moment you press. Switch TVs to Game Mode or Low Latency Mode, or turn off every picture-enhancing setting. Check audio separately and try an analog connection or low-latency audio. Convert listed display times to frames. Check yourself instead of trusting that someone else did, and rule out display lag before retuning feel.
anti_pattern: Assuming a setup is fine because someone has played on it; judging lag with a 3D game; TV post-processing left on.
example: At E3 2018's Treehouse: Live, the Smash Ultimate setup's lag ruined the controls until Sakurai pointed it out (8). NES Kirby via Nintendo Switch Online as a jump test (8). Sakurai swapped to his low-lag recording monitor mid-session (156). Score-chasers seek out CRTs, which need no buffer (252).
review_question: Was the feel of this build judged on a display chain verified to add no lag?
keywords: input lag display latency game mode low latency mode TV settings response time audio latency demo setup events playtest

principle: Aim testing at the places where systems fight over control
why: Full coverage is impossible: Ultimate's 89 fighters give about 8,000 pairings before movesets, items, extra players, stages, hazards and spirits multiply in. A game that takes dozens of hours to finish might need thousands to tens of thousands of hours to test fully. Bugs cluster where one thing forcibly controls another, where scenes change, at extreme geometry, in growth and parameter systems, and where AI logic modes contradict.
how_to_apply: Estimate the test matrix early so you know where to prioritize. Put the first and heaviest passes on grabs, throws and restraints, especially on a target mid special move; on scene-changing supers (restrain, release, nothing leaks between scenes); on extreme and V-shaped terrain; and on every parameter, growth or unlock system. List the conditions each AI behavior mode responds to and test cases where two modes disagree. Let machines help: run CPU-versus-CPU battles overnight, and near the end pass save data between regions for worldwide testing.
anti_pattern: Brute-forcing combinations with no prioritization; holding the game to a completely bug-free standard.
example: Smash Ultimate's hot spots: grabbing a fighter mid special move, Final Smashes with scene changes, Stage Builder V-shaped terrain, Spirits (136). Overnight CPU battles and Japan, North America and Europe passing save data (208).
review_question: Which interactions in this build let one system seize control of another, and have they been tested first?
keywords: QA test planning combinatorial explosion test matrix edge cases risk-based testing automated testing bots soak test state conflicts

principle: Ship as if no patch will come; treat updates as a bonus
why: Modern games are too complex to be perfect at release, every fix restarts testing so developers barely get to play the finished game, and the market is the best bug tester: a one-in-a-thousand bug will show up in a player's video. But no patch matters once players have given up. A completely bug-free standard belongs to banks and airports and would make releasing games practically impossible.
how_to_apply: Set release quality as though no update will ever ship. Lock content early enough to spend time on near-final builds. After launch, fix crashing and fatal bugs as a must, and weigh balance and quality-of-life updates as optional work against freeing the director and key staff for the next game. Watch player videos and reports as your biggest test pass. Budget the schedule for updates and DLC, which stretch it.
anti_pattern: Shipping rough on the assumption that patches will fix it; treating post-launch updates as free.
example: Smash for 3DS/Wii U released in fall to winter 2014 but development only wrapped in spring 2016 because of updates and DLC (135). The one-in-a-thousand bug that gets uploaded after launch (231).
review_question: If no patch ever shipped, would this build be acceptable to players on day one?
keywords: launch quality patches updates post-launch support day one patch content lock triage DLC schedule

principle: Make the edit-and-test tuning loop a single button press
why: Tuning is where you iterate most, so it must be as efficient as possible. On the original Smash and Melee, one conversion took ten minutes even for the smallest tweak, plus a reboot, with hand-edited text files, so Sakurai wrote every parameter himself. With a fast pipeline, more people can tune more values more deeply, and the director can supervise instead of entering data.
how_to_apply: Build a conversion tool, for example a spreadsheet add-in, that pushes edited parameters to every active dev kit or test build in one press, without a reboot. Give planners and other team members access so a small tuning team can work while the director reviews. Back them with play testers who keep playing the current build.
anti_pattern: Multi-minute conversions and reboots per tweak; a director who enters all the data while also supervising, approving and marketing.
example: Bandai Namco Studios' Excel add-in updates all active dev kits with one button press (46). From Smash for 3DS/Wii U, a small team of planners took over parameter entry; on Ultimate Sakurai only supervised (135, 220).
review_question: How many seconds pass between changing a value and playing with it, and how many people can do it?
keywords: iteration speed hot reload live tuning pipeline conversion dev kits tools workflow fast iteration delegation

principle: Make parameters unmistakable with plain-language names, units and formulas
why: Several people usually tune parameters later, so each one's meaning must be crystal clear to anyone; terse names like X-velocity get misread. Specs and parameters do not work if you cannot convey speed, so units matter. Hiding rarely used fields reduces human error, and formulas keep related values in balance. You will not get far with tuning if you cannot explain things clearly.
how_to_apply: In specs, write each tunable as a bracketed plain-language phrase with a placeholder value, such as [Special startup X-velocity is O] and [Special X-deceleration is O/frame], under the rule that anything in brackets becomes a parameter, and keep a list pairing each phrase with its value. State a unit for every speed (pixels per frame for sprites, km/h or m/frame for real-scale 3D) and every time (frames at your target rate). Hide rarely adjusted fields in the editor, and link dependent values with formulas, such as one move at 1/2 another's power.
anti_pattern: Unitless values; cryptic labels; a flat sheet where every field looks equally important.
example: Sakurai's bracket notation for a dash that decelerates as it goes (68). Smash attack parameters in Excel with hidden fields and formulas (46). Mario's top speed of about 1 pixel per frame on a 256-pixel-wide NES screen; Kirby Air Ride speeds in km/h (84).
review_question: Could a new planner read any parameter's name and know what it does and in what unit?
keywords: spec sheets parameter naming units brackets notation formulas spreadsheet hidden columns documentation pixels per frame frames

principle: Spend processing where players look, and cut what nobody sees
why: Console hardware is not as powerful as most people think, so you must decide which elements are major and which minor. Players mostly look at the center of the screen, foundations are usually off-screen, and fighters are often small. The less you process an object, the more of it you can put on screen. Fingers are complex for their size and particles always cost something, so every effect and joint competes for the same budget.
how_to_apply: Rank assets by how much they are actually seen and spend polygons and texture detail in that order: in front of the camera and on playable surfaces first. Set model budgets by on-screen size, raised for models also shown up close elsewhere. Build LOD only when the gain is worth the labor. Prefer cheap light and color work in the asset over heavy per-object shaders. Lock finger joints and swap a few pre-made poses. Use billboards for flashes, particles and simple objects. Allow playful details only when they meet deadlines and cost no performance.
anti_pattern: Detail nobody will ever see; over-investing in small on-screen elements; LOD by default; fully simulating every finger on crowded screens.
example: Smash stages put skysphere detail in front of the camera; Inkling's stage had backdrop car tires that turned, which he asked to tone down (44). Super Mario 64's rolling iron balls are billboards (153). The N64 Smash fighter was about 300 polygons, about 200 with three or more fighters (40).
review_question: Which costly elements in the busiest scene would players never notice if they were cheaper?
keywords: optimization performance budget LOD level of detail billboards particles polygon budget processing cost prioritization major minor elements

principle: Calibrate for every controller, platform and regional hardware variant
why: Every console's analog stick is slightly different, so the lowest tilt that registers has to be configured each time. Flick dashes cause accidental dashes, so Ultimate exposes sensitivity. A D-pad gives only 0 or 1, so an analog-dependent game cannot simply support it. The NES lacked the cartridge pins for expansion audio, so several games sounded different abroad. Confirm and cancel sit in different places by platform, and the same speed value gives different results on screens with different pixel counts.
how_to_apply: Set and test the stick dead zone per platform or controller. Expose sensitivity for gesture inputs like flicks. Before promising support for an input device, check whether your mechanics need analog values. List each target's audio, input and button conventions and provide fallbacks. Recheck raw pixel speeds on every resolution. Account for peripheral costs: a twin-stick add-on for 3DS added about 5% processor load, too much for a game already at the limit.
anti_pattern: One stick-sensitivity value for every console; relying on hardware features only some versions have.
example: Analog tilt sensitivity per console (19); adjustable flick sensitivity in Smash Ultimate (154); Smash cannot be played with a D-pad (175); Famicom versus NES expansion audio (239); a 3DS twin-stick peripheral that added about 5% processor load in Kid Icarus: Uprising (125).
review_question: Has each supported controller and platform version been checked for dead zone, button conventions and missing features?
keywords: analog stick dead zone tilt sensitivity controller calibration platform differences confirm cancel buttons hardware variants regional differences ports

principle: Build debug commands for the test setups you use most
why: Without the right debug features, the team spends time inventing workarounds. Teams use debug mode every day, so its convenience has a huge impact on productivity. A separate debug controller is a real pain to hunt down, and debug menus bloat easily.
how_to_apply: Add direct commands for frequent setups, such as setting every character to a chosen damage percentage. Put debug functions on button combinations of the normal gameplay controller. Include capture tools (pause, rotate characters, zoom, change camera angle). Regularly reorganize and prune the debug menu, and strip it from the release build.
anti_pattern: Workarounds like temporarily changing a move's damage to set up a test; a separate debug controller; a bloated, disorganized debug menu.
example: Before Smash could set damage directly, the team made Fox's forward tilt deal 100% damage (195). Screenshot of the Day was captured with debug pause, rotation, zoom and angle controls, though fighters could not be moved nearer or farther (195).
review_question: Can a tester reach any common test situation in a few seconds from the normal controller?
keywords: debug mode developer mode cheats debug menu test setup commands productivity QA tools screenshot mode

principle: Add view toggles that isolate exactly what you are checking
why: Capes and clothes hide poses, and older workarounds such as scaling or removing the cape were clumsier; the transparency feature did not take long to build. Per-element display toggles are, in his words, another must-have and were used often. Effects pack information into an instant, and collision has to be distinguishable from backdrop, so both need dedicated views.
how_to_apply: Add a dev-mode option to make any selected model part, or the whole model, translucent or hidden. Add an on/off toggle for every display element. Add a view that highlights every collision surface (his example marks them in red). Add slow-motion and background-off toggles for effect review. Make these views available to reviewers outside the team.
anti_pattern: Editing the model (scaling or deleting parts) just to inspect an animation.
example: Smash Ultimate's caped fighters checked with transparency; a 3D fighting game developer whose tools could disable clothes and swaying objects (217). Collision surfaces shown in red (30). Ultimate's effects recorded with slow motion on and backgrounds off (79).
review_question: Can a reviewer hide, fade or slow any element to see exactly the thing under review?
keywords: debug visualization display toggles transparency collision view slow motion isolate layers render toggles animation review tools

principle: Run bugs through tickets with repro steps, severity and the right owner
why: Having programmers playtest wastes their time, so projects use dedicated bug testers. Bugs found on the wrong version are not helpful and can cause problems. A ticket makes responsibility obvious and makes it less likely anything is overlooked. Programmers are not always the right fixers: artists fix character problems and animators fix animations. Visualizing tasks is vital.
how_to_apply: Require everyone to test on the latest daily build. Have testers work from design documents and checklists in subteams by game area. File a ticket only once the bug can be reproduced. A manager assigns a class (S for hangs or possible save corruption, A for progression blockers, lower classes sometimes waived on purpose) and routes it to the discipline that owns it. After a fix the tester confirms it in a variety of configurations, then marks it resolved rather than deleting it. Cross-reference or merge related tickets and rebalance overloaded people. Track all other work as tickets with one owner, a status and a deadline too.
anti_pattern: Reports from outdated builds; tickets with no repro steps; deleting closed tickets; tasks that live only in conversation.
example: Smash's bug-testing process (208); one character split into spec, model and rig, animation, programming, VFX, SFX and balancing tickets (94); bug reports with reproduction steps routed by one person (50).
review_question: Is every known bug a ticket with repro steps, a severity class, an owner and a verified fix?
keywords: bug tracking tickets severity triage bug reports reproduction steps QA workflow daily build issue tracker class S class A blocker crash save corruption

principle: Regression-test every fix, and keep late fixes narrow
why: Fixing one bug can introduce others, which is sometimes called enbugging, so even an urgent fix cannot ship right away; every fix means redoing plenty of other checks. Changing core systems late forces wide re-testing.
how_to_apply: Pair each fix with a regression pass over related systems before releasing a patch, and verify it in several configurations. For late or post-launch problems, prefer contained changes, such as lowering specific encounters or adding an easier option, over rewriting core AI or global difficulty code.
anti_pattern: Rushing a hotfix out without re-checking; touching core systems in a late patch when a narrow change would do.
example: Smash Ultimate's too-hard launch CPUs were addressed by lowering Challenger fight difficulty and adding Very Easy to World of Light, instead of changing core CPU functions (141).
review_question: What else could this fix break, and has that been re-checked?
keywords: regression testing hotfix patch enbugging fix verification contained fix late changes risk

principle: Fix the code before you tune the numbers
why: Even with correct parameters, mistakes in the code mean almost no amount of adjustment gives the result you want, which wastes the tuner's time. Even correct frame counts can be broken by code or data errors, and a trained sense of timing is how you notice.
how_to_apply: When tuning stops responding the way you expect, stop adjusting and have strong programmers hunt the underlying bugs. Play each move against its spec; when it feels off, inspect the code and data before touching the numbers.
anti_pattern: Tuning parameters on top of buggy code.
example: In Melee's final stretch, Satoru Iwata worked directly with the programmers to find code problems; without him Sakurai doubts it would have released before the end of 2001 (259).
review_question: When a parameter change does not produce the expected result, does anyone check the code before changing it again?
keywords: debugging tuning parameters code bugs balancing verification spec vs implementation frame data mismatch

principle: Name files so they sort sensibly and read at a glance
why: With a category-first scheme, anyone can read a name and know the move, and everything stays neat when sorted. Direction-first names or words for strength would make a huge mess when sorted. Names that are too short are easy to type but hard to understand. Romanized Japanese makes things harder for people who do not speak it: it is not just you who needs to understand your game.
how_to_apply: Define the scheme at project start: broad category first, then modifiers, then numbers for strength or sequence. Sort a folder by name and check related files group in a sensible order; if not, reorder the name parts. Use English when other or overseas teams may join. Test names on someone new to the project. Use one ID scheme across folders, files and tracking spreadsheets.
anti_pattern: Modifiers before the category; words for strength; cryptic abbreviations; romanized native-language names on international projects.
example: Smash labels: Attack11 to Attack13 for jab steps, Attack4 for smash, AttackS4 for side smash, AttackAirF for forward aerial, SpecialHi for up special, with N, Hi, S and Lw for directions (22). Sakurai's channel used category letter plus episode code for folders, files and the schedule (261).
review_question: Sorted alphabetically, do this folder's files group and order the way the team thinks about them?
keywords: file naming conventions asset naming labels sorting folders organization internal names English international teams

principle: Keep every file on a server with locking, merging and history
why: A large game is split into tens of thousands to millions of files with possibly hundreds of people editing them. Locking stops two people editing one file, but keeping a huge file locked to one person is inefficient, conflicting uploads still happen, and reversion, where changes vanish and the file returns to its old state, happens often. In theory there should be no issues; in practice it is a constant source of headaches.
how_to_apply: Put every file under a management tool on a server. Lock a file to edit it, upload when done to unlock. For large files several people need at once, allow simultaneous edits, let the tool merge, and name someone to resolve leftover conflicts by hand. When work goes missing, check version history first, since the tool backs up every edit.
anti_pattern: Passing copies around by hand; one person holding a huge file locked while others wait; assuming the tool makes lost work impossible.
example: General overview with no game-specific example (172).
review_question: If someone's change vanished today, could it be recovered from history, and who resolves merge conflicts?
keywords: version control source control file locking merge conflicts revert history backup asset management

principle: Turn hard memory and processing limits into design tricks
why: Limits reward ingenuity: Super Mario Bros. delivered far more game than Mario Bros. with 40 KB against 24 KB. Kirby's Dream Land was designed mostly for 512 kilobits (64 KB), so art was shared and mirrored, and enemy movement was hand-authored to match terrain with no collision checks, which was wasteful to make but light on processing. All you can do is work within your game's limits and aim for the best effect possible.
how_to_apply: Decide which resource is scarce. If memory is, share and flip art, cap animation frames, store sprites as stacked bitplanes and compress runs. If processing is, trade memory for it with hand-authored paths or frame animations instead of simulation. On size-limited media, test compression on your biggest asset sets early before cutting content. When space or time is tight, use presets or placeholder art so the budget goes into behavior.
anti_pattern: Asking for more resources before trying technique; cutting content to a download before testing compression.
example: Waddle Dee and Waddle Doo share a back half, two characters in the ROM space of 1.5; Gordo is one image flipped; Coner and Cappy have no terrain collision (100). Kirby's defeat stars are hand-placed per frame (244). Ultimate's music fit in a quarter of Smash for's space on a cartridge capped at about 16 GB (160). Family BASIC's 2 KB of program space made its built-in character presets crucial (118).
review_question: Which resource is actually scarce in this build, and are you trading the plentiful one for it?
keywords: memory limits ROM budget compression sprite reuse mirroring flipping retro constraints processing budget hand-authored animation run-length encoding bitplanes

principle: Reuse debug tools for footage, screenshots and player-facing aids
why: Smash's reveal gameplay was recorded by team members using debug and replay features to find the best camera angles, then checked and restructured repeatedly. The Training Mode trajectory guide began as a debug feature Sakurai requested; he worried it might reveal too much but included it because it is easy to understand.
how_to_apply: Build replay playback with a free debug camera so trailer and screenshot shots can be re-framed from recorded play. Review debug overlays for ones that would teach players, weigh whether they reveal too much, and ship the clear ones in a training mode.
anti_pattern: Capturing trailer footage live with no way to re-shoot an angle.
example: Fighter reveal gameplay segments (163); the Training Mode trajectory guide and Screenshot of the Day (195); in-engine reveal footage captured by footage specialists (50).
review_question: Can a moment of play be replayed and re-shot from any angle, and which debug views would help players learn?
keywords: replay system photo mode debug camera free camera trailer capture footage screenshots training mode overlays

principle: Treat a pre-release demo as a second build with its own QA
why: Demos are very effective at getting a game noticed, but if you are not careful one becomes almost another small game. People will find spoiler data left in a build, and removing data greatly raises the chance of breaking something. From the moment you decide on a demo you maintain two versions, and anything public needs nearly as much testing as the final game. A half-baked demo can get the game written off.
how_to_apply: Decide early and schedule the demo as its own deliverable with its own tuning, updates and near-full QA. Keep spoiler content in separable files so it can be stripped cleanly. Audit the demo build for leftovers, then retest thoroughly. Release a pre-launch demo only when it is balanced enough to represent the game; otherwise consider a post-launch demo and accept the smaller splash.
anti_pattern: Treating a demo as a quick slice; leaving spoiler data in it; releasing an unbalanced demo.
example: General advice; he contrasts pre-COVID expo demos with downloadable ones (122).
review_question: Could someone mining this demo's files find anything you have not announced?
keywords: demo build trial version spoilers datamining leaks separate build QA marketing demo

principle: Build CPU players from data and give them human reflexes
why: The computer has no eyes, so it must decide from data: the opponent's position and status, its own attack ranges, movement range and attack timing, and the opponent's attack data. CPUs that react faster than a human feel extremely unfair. Logic that switches mid-match can contradict itself, more often as criteria multiply. A CPU that perfect-shields every attack could be invincible, but that would not be fun.
how_to_apply: Convert each character's reach, attack timing and movement range into data the AI can query, and feed it the opponent's attack data, position and status. Add a reaction delay. Organize behavior into modes that switch with match state and test cases where two modes conflict. Tune high levels toward offense rather than waiting or perfect defense, and cap perfect blocks and dodges.
anti_pattern: Superhuman reaction speed; high-level CPUs that turtle; piling on behavior criteria without checking for contradictions.
example: Smash Ultimate's CPUs have a reflex delay, are briefly confused by reversed controls, and were tuned for offense over defense (221).
review_question: Can the CPU do anything a human physically could not, and where do its behavior modes disagree?
keywords: AI CPU opponents bots reaction time behavior modes decision data difficulty fairness fighting game AI

principle: Seed randomness with an unpredictable value
why: Computers can only do things in a predetermined way, so they cannot produce true randomness, and players can reset or repeat actions to always get the result they want.
how_to_apply: Factor the system's internal clock or another indefinite value into random number generation.
anti_pattern: Predictable random results that resetting can exploit.
example: General caution in his randomness episode (189).
review_question: Can a player reset or repeat an action to force a random outcome?
keywords: RNG random number generator seed manipulation reset abuse clock

principle: Match real-time online players within their local region
why: Smash needs fully synchronous communication, a major disadvantage compared with asynchronous games like Mario Kart, so lag makes it choppy unless players are close; higher input density makes online frame skips stand out. Matchmaking that is too narrow finds no one, while too broad gives lopsided matches.
how_to_apply: For synchronous games, matchmake within the local region, not just the country. Consider lowering input density where online play will lag. Tune matchmaking range against population, especially in low-population regions and hours.
anti_pattern: Country-wide or global matching for frame-tight synchronous play.
example: Super Smash Bros. Brawl's online play versus Mario Kart (108); Ultimate's matchmaking balance (170).
review_question: How far apart can two matched players be before the connection breaks the feel?
keywords: netcode online matchmaking latency region synchronous asynchronous lag online play

principle: Keep reference hardware, cables and displays organized and calibrated
why: Old games remain working tools for a developer, so they must be quick to reach. With many consoles connected, labels show what is plugged in where. Each monitor shows color slightly differently, which is fatal for art checks, and tinted office lighting skews art. Organizing is a pain, but it gets worse if you do not stay on top of it.
how_to_apply: Keep reference consoles connected through a selector, label every cable, adapter and selector input, give each console a switchable outlet and ventilation. Calibrate team monitors by eye against one shared reference screen and light review areas neutrally. Verify the display chain for lag before tests.
anti_pattern: Unlabeled tangles of cables; approving art on a monitor known to crush shadows.
example: Sakurai's custom six-door game cabinet with a selector and Tepra labels (216). A Mewtwo image losing its shadow on one monitor; an office lit yellow whose art came out bluish (184).
review_question: Can anyone on the team switch to any reference platform in minutes and trust the screen they are looking at?
keywords: dev environment reference library hardware setup cable labels monitor calibration test station organization

principle: Set the game's risk by its target player, not by your own skill
why: Sakurai wanted the first Kirby to be as accessible as possible for new players, so inhaling and flying both lowered the risks they faced, even when staff asked 'Are you sure about this?'. In his view more game essence means less broad appeal, and a minor risk to a veteran can be a brick wall to a newcomer. The same reasoning ran the other way when the audience changed: Brawl slowed down for casual Wii players, and Uprising aimed at hardcore players.
how_to_apply: Write down the target player before tuning any risk. For newcomers, soften the harshest penalties while keeping some (flight over pits, but falling still costs a life). For experts, let them raise the risk themselves. Re-check risk whenever the platform or audience shifts.
anti_pattern: Making a game unreasonably hard so it lasts longer; tuning risk to the development team's skill.
example: Kirby's Dream Land: inhale before an approaching enemy gets dangerous, six hits of health, flight at any time. Melee was so fast it was hard on newcomers, so Brawl's speed was a little slower. Uprising's Fiend's Cauldron let players bet hearts on higher intensity, though Sakurai later felt the game came out too hardcore.
review_question: Who is this game for, and does its harshest penalty suit that player?
keywords: target audience difficulty risk accessibility beginners casual hardcore penalty kirby dream land brawl

principle: Layer optional depth on a core that a novice can finish
why: When Kirby's Adventure came out, the NES market had matured and few beginners were starting on it, so the game had to satisfy both groups. The copy ability sat on top of inhale-and-spit: novices could finish with the core, while experienced players dug into abilities for tricks. Extras for one audience were kept off the critical path. Smash's configurable rules carried the same idea into multiplayer: play what you want, how you want.
how_to_apply: Play through using only the core verbs and confirm the game can be finished that way. Put depth systems and audience-specific extras where players choose them: a map entrance, a rule toggle, an optional mode. Make sure the depth layer gives each encounter something to look forward to.
anti_pattern: Requiring the depth system to progress; forcing extras on players who don't want them.
example: Kirby's Adventure: copy abilities, plus three one-button minigames entered from the world map. Super Smash Bros.: chaotic four-player matches with items, or tense one-on-one without. The first Kirby was made for beginners but has enough 'oomph' that advanced players enjoy the controls.
review_question: Can a novice finish using only the core, and what does the optional layer give veterans?
keywords: optional depth layered design beginners and experts copy ability optional content accessibility skill ceiling kirby's adventure

principle: Build the concept as the answer to a named problem
why: Sakurai says most of his concepts are logical: they solve a problem. He felt combo-heavy fighters lost push and pull, since after the first hit the opponent's skill stopped mattering, so Smash used accumulated damage and ring-outs. Too many games took too long to beat, so Kirby Super Star became an omnibus. He felt FPS and TPS games were stuck in by-the-book theory, so Uprising rethought the genre. For Meteos he first worked out the genre's risk and reward, then asked whether blocks even had to be erased.
how_to_apply: Write the pain point of the genre or the brief in one sentence, then design a core rule that removes it. Test the answer: does it change what the player actually does, or only what the action is called? If it only renames, keep going.
anti_pattern: Cosmetic novelty that renames the standard verb; treating an 'antithesis' as rejection rather than a response to something you respect.
example: Smash's accumulated damage and ring-outs; Meteos' matched blocks that blast off into space, enabling secondary ignitions and air docking; Kirby Super Star's cork board of short scenarios.
review_question: What specific problem does our core rule solve, and does it change what the player does?
keywords: concept problem solving genre innovation push and pull core rule smash bros meteos originality

principle: Let the platform's unique strength and the market gap shape the concept
why: For Kid Icarus: Uprising, glasses-free 3D meant depth had to be part of the fun, and Touch! Generations already covered casual DS players, so he made a meaty shooter for hardcore players. For Smash for 3DS and Wii U he framed the platforms as the 'one' and the 'many' and gave each version modes built on that. The N64 analog stick inspired flick input, GameCube streaming audio allowed orchestral music in Melee, and the Wii's built-in online made online play essential for Brawl. He also warns against shoehorning in every function of new hardware.
how_to_apply: List what the target hardware does that others can't and which audiences competitors already serve, then aim the concept at the gap. If shipping on several platforms, give each at least one mode built on its own strength while sharing mechanics, animation and balance. Skip peripheral functions that don't serve the game.
anti_pattern: Versions that differ only in graphical power; using every gimmick a device offers.
example: Smash Run on 3DS (five minutes of power-up collecting on a huge map, since everyone has their own screen) versus 8-Player Smash and Smash Tour on Wii U. Brawl deliberately didn't use every Nunchuk or pointer function.
review_question: What does our platform do uniquely, and which part of our design depends on it?
keywords: platform hardware strengths market gap concept multiplatform kid icarus uprising smash 3ds wii u flick input

principle: Choose the concept your situation can finish, and uniquely enables
why: Two prototypes won praise, but the team needed a finished game soon and the RC adventure would have taken two years, so the fighter became Smash. A racer was judged quicker to make than an action game to accompany the Kirby anime. Kirby's Adventure went to the NES because setting up an SNES environment would take too long. Ultimate kept the same studio, team and tools on similar hardware, which made bringing back every fighter feasible: Sakurai saw it as the one chance.
how_to_apply: Estimate each candidate concept's development time. Inventory what carries over (team, tools, assets, hardware architecture) and look for the bold idea that inventory makes cheap. Pick the concept that fits both the schedule and that one-time opportunity.
anti_pattern: Chasing a concept the team can't finish in time; ignoring an ambition that only your current situation makes affordable.
example: Dragon King: The Fighting Game chosen over the RC robot adventure; Kirby Air Ride as the quicker-to-make companion to the anime; Ultimate's 'Everyone is here!', with only seven missing veterans to rebuild.
review_question: Given our team, tools and remaining time, which concept can we actually finish, and what does our situation make uniquely possible?
keywords: feasibility scope concept selection production continuity schedule smash prototype ultimate everyone is here

principle: Change a feature's context before cutting it
why: On the NES's larger screen Kirby could fly past almost any challenge. Sakurai considered removing flight but changed its context instead: a bigger info panel limited vertical space and made characters read bigger, mid-boss fights stayed on one screen, and flight got slower, and he felt it ended up nicely balanced. Kirby Super Star made co-op scrolling work by restructuring roles (a lead the camera follows and a Helper who can be off-camera) instead of dropping the request.
how_to_apply: When a signature mechanic breaks balance or a request seems impossible, list the context levers (screen space, arena bounds, speed, camera, player roles, HUD) and try them before cutting the feature.
anti_pattern: Cutting a signature mechanic that a context change could rebalance; giving every co-op player equal pull on the camera in a jump-heavy side-scroller.
example: Kirby's Adventure's flight; Kirby Super Star's Helper system with its 'Space Jump' warp back to the lead. In Dream Land he accepted that flight could skip enemies because the Game Boy screen was so small.
review_question: Before cutting this feature, which context lever have we tried changing?
keywords: rebalance context camera co-op helper flight hud signature mechanic kirby's adventure kirby super star

principle: Build variety as rule-changing parameters on one shared core
why: Kirby Air Ride's machines feel totally different but share one underlying behavior: apart from star versus bike types, everything is parameters, so a machine's character changes by tweaking a few numbers. Each Meteos planet changes block shapes, field width, launch behavior, music and sound, so the controls feel drastically different and players pick favorites. Smash for 3DS/Wii U's 'variable character strength' framework powered several modes at once. Uprising's weapons change Pit's speed, not just damage.
how_to_apply: Implement one shared behavior, then express each vehicle, stage, character or weapon as a parameter set that changes how it plays (size, gravity, speed, field shape, piece types) plus its own audio. Keep strength-varying layers out of modes that need a level playing field.
anti_pattern: Character select that only swaps art or barely changes skills; separate code for every variant.
example: Air Ride's machines; Meteos planets such as Boggob (gains height with each jump), Hevendor (blocks vanish when matched) and Brabbit (moves very slowly); Smash Run, Smash Tour, custom moves, Mii Fighters and amiibo on one parameter layer.
review_question: Do our characters, stages or vehicles change the rules, or only the art?
keywords: parameters variety data-driven characters stages vehicles shared behavior kirby air ride meteos planets variable strength

principle: Tune and test on the final build and the real hardware
why: Meteos' game speed was tied to processing speed, so a late optimization made it faster and harder than Sakurai's per-planet tuning intended. Sodatete! Kouchuu Ouja Mushiking was tuned on a custom board and never played on the production handheld, and the Mushi gets hungry faster than planned. Smash Ultimate's CPU fighters felt too hard at launch for reasons he still doesn't know. 'When you're working with computers, sometimes there's no telling what you might get.'
how_to_apply: Lock processing speed and frame timing before final balance tuning. After any optimization, replay difficulty and timer-driven systems on the retail unit. When a launch problem is too risky to fix at its core, ship a narrow, contained fix.
anti_pattern: Shipping without playing on production hardware; changing processing speed after tuning.
